<!-- paragraphesansboite-1: body_md -->
Throughout this document, we use the following notations:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $(x,y)$ denotes the cartesian coordinates, and $(r,\theta )$ denotes the polar coordinates with $\theta  \in [0,2\pi )$,
    \item for~any $r>0$, $B(0,r)$ is the disc of $\mathbb{R}^2 $ of radius $r$ centered at $(0,0)$,
    \item $k_{i} := \omega  \sqrt{\rho _{i} /\mu _{i} }$ with $i=0,1$ is the wave number in $\Omega $, resp.\ in the layer,
    \item $\mathbb{P} := \mathbb{N}+ \frac{\pi }{\Theta } \mathbb{N}$,
	\item $R_{\mathrm{s}} := \operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{supp}f_{\mathrm{s}})$, which is positive by assumption on $f_{\mathrm{s}}$,
	\item $\mathbf{r} := r$ in $\Omega $ and $\mathbf{r}:=x$ in $\Lambda$,
    \item $\alpha  := e^{-\mathrm{i}\Theta }$.
\end{itemize}
In addition, we use the following conventions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathbb{N}:=\{0,1,2,3,\dots \}$,
    \item $\mathbb{N}^* :=\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, $\mathbb{R}^* :=\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ and likewise for $\mathbb{Z}^*$, $\mathbb{Q}^*$ and $\mathbb{C}^*$,
    \item $\mathbb{R}_+ :=[0,\infty )$, $\mathbb{R}_+^* :=(0,\infty )$ and likewise for $\mathbb{R}_-$ and $\mathbb{R}_-^*$.
	\item For any $n,m\in \mathbb{N}^*$ and any open set $O\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$, $H^{m} _{\mathrm{loc}} (O)$ denotes the set of functions that are $H^{m}$ on every open subset of $O$ whose closure is a compact subset of $O$. Similarly for $L^2 _{\mathrm{loc}}$.
\end{itemize}
If needed, a more complete list of the notations can be found at the end of this document, see page~\pageref{nomenclature}.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-1 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-2: body_md -->
$\Im(\omega ) \neq 0$ est une hypothèse technique liée au fait que nous considérons un cadre académique comportant une couche semi-infinie. Dans ce cas, $\Im(\omega ) = 0$ nécessiterait de définir une condition de rayonnement spécifique, ce qui est difficile. Dans le cas plus réaliste d'un obstacle borné partiellement recouvert par une couche mince, il est possible d'utiliser une condition de rayonnement classique de Sommerfeld. Notez que l'hypothèse $\Im(\omega ) \neq 0$ n'a que peu d'impact sur l'analyse asymptotique.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-2 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-3: body_md -->
Tout au long de ce document, nous utilisons les notations suivantes :
\begin{itemize}
    \item $(x,y)$ désigne les coordonnées cartésiennes et $(r,\theta )$ désigne les coordonnées polaires avec $\theta  \in [0,2\pi [$,
    \item pour tout $r>0$, $B(0,r)$ est le disque de $\mathbb{R}^2 $ de centre $(0,0)$ et de rayon $r$,
    \item $k_{i} := \omega  \sqrt{\rho _{i} /\mu _{i} }$ avec $i=0,1$ est le nombre d'onde dans $\Omega $, resp.\ dans la couche,
    \item $\mathbb{P} := \mathbb{N}+ \frac{\pi }{\Theta } \mathbb{N}$,
	\item $R_{\mathrm{s}} := \operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{supp}f_{\mathrm{s}})$, qui est strictement positif par hypothèse sur $f_{\mathrm{s}}$,
	\item $\mathbf{r} := r$ dans $\Omega $ et $\mathbf{r}:=x$ dans $\Lambda$,
    \item $\alpha  := e^{-\mathrm{i}\Theta }$.
\end{itemize}
De plus, nous utilisons les conventions suivantes :
\begin{itemize}
	\item les intervalles ouverts sont notés $]a,b[$ dans la partie en français (i.e. ce chapitre) mais $(a,b)$ partout ailleurs, et de même pour les intervalles semi-ouverts,
    \item $\mathbb{N}:=\{0,1,2,3,\dots \}$,
    \item $\mathbb{N}^* :=\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, $\mathbb{R}^* :=\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ et de même pour $\mathbb{Z}^*$, $\mathbb{Q}^*$ et $\mathbb{C}^*$,
    \item $\mathbb{R}_+ :=[0,\infty [$, $\mathbb{R}_+^* :={]0,\infty [}$ et de même pour $\mathbb{R}_-$ et $\mathbb{R}_-^*$.
	\item Pour tous $n,m\in \mathbb{N}^*$ et tout ouvert $O\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$, $H^{m} _{\mathrm{loc}} (O)$ désigne l'ensemble des fonctions qui sont $H^{m}$ sur tout ouvert $O'\subset O$ tel que $\overline{O'}$ est compact dans $O$. De même pour $L^2 _{\mathrm{loc}}$.
\end{itemize}
Si besoin, une liste plus complète des notations se trouve à la fin de ce document page~\pageref{nomenclature}.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-3 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-4: body_md -->
\begin{itemize}
	\item La condition $\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} U_{p,\ell } = \mu _{0} \partial _{y} u_{p-1,\ell }$ est incluse dans le problème \eqref{eq: eq vol champs de couche fr} vérifié par $U_{p,\ell }$, tandis que $u_{p,\ell } = U_{p,\ell }$ est incluse dans le problème \eqref{eq: eq vol champs lointains fr} satisfait par $u_{p,\ell }$, de sorte que la construction est récursive par rapport à $p$ : $u_{p-1,\ell }$ permet de construire $U_{p,\ell }$, ce qui permet de construire $u_{p,\ell }$.
	\item Le champ de couche $U_{p,\ell }$ satisfait un problème unidimensionnel par rapport à $Y$, la variable $x$ jouant le rôle d'un paramètre.\\
\end{itemize}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-1ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-4 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-5: body_md -->
\label{def: X dans C[[X]]} 
We denote $X := (\delta _{n,1} )_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \in \mathbb{C}[[X]]$.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-5 -->
<!-- demo-1: body_md -->
It~is easy to prove by induction. First, one can verify that $(\delta _{n,0} )_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is the multiplicative neutral element of $\mathbb{C}[[X]]$. Hence $X^{0} = (\delta _{n,0} )_{n}$. Then if we assume $X^{k} = (\delta _{n,k} )_{n}$ for a given $k$, we can deduce
\[X\cdot X^{k} = (\delta _{n,1} )_{n} \cdot  (\delta _{n,k} )_{n} = \bigg(\sum_{i=0}^n \delta _{i,1} \cdot \delta _{n-i,k} \bigg)_{\!n} = (\delta _{n,k+1} )_{n} .\]
<!-- end demo-1 -->
<!-- demo-2: body_md -->
By~\cref{X^k dans C[[X]],def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}, we have $a_{k} X^{k} = (a_{k} \delta _{n,k} )_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ for~any $k\in \mathbb{N}$. Next, for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $\{n\in \mathbb{N} \mid a_{k} \delta _{n,k} \neq 0\}\subset \{n\}$ is finite, so $(a_{k} X^{k} )_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ has finite support on each coordinate. Hence we can write
\begin{equation}{}
    \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{k=0} ^{\infty } a_{k} X^{k} = \bigg(\sum_{k=0}^\infty  a_{k} \,\delta _{n,k} \bigg)_{\!n\in \mathbb{N}} = (a_{n} )_{n\in \mathbb{N}} .
\end{equation}
Note that we can change the index of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ from $n$ to $k$ as it~is only a bound variable.
<!-- end demo-2 -->
<!-- demo-3: body_md -->
For~any $i\in I$ and $j\in J$, let us denote $(a_{i,n} )_{n} :=f_{i}$ and $(b_{j,n} )_{n} :=g_{j}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Direct by~definition of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}.
    \item \Cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]} states that $\lambda f_{i} = (\lambda a_{i,n} )_{n}$ for~any $i\in I$. In addition, for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $\{i\in I \mid \lambda  a_{i,n} \neq 0\}$ is included in $\{i\in I \mid a_{i,n} \neq 0\}$ which is finite because $(f_{i} )$ has FSEC. So $(\lambda  f_{i} )_{i\in I}$ has FSEC. Moreover, 
    \begin{align*}
        \lambda  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} f_{i} &= \lambda  \cdot \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} a_{i,n} \bigg)_{\!n} && \text{by \cref{def: fsum dans C[[X]]}} \\
        &= \bigg(\lambda  \sum _{i\in I} a_{i,n} \bigg)_{\!n} && \text{by \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}}  \\
        &= \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} \lambda  a_{i,n} \bigg)_{\!n} \\
        &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \lambda  f_{i} && \text{by \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}} 
    \end{align*}
    \item \Cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]} states that $f_{i} +g_{i} = (a_{i,n} +b_{i,n} )_{n}$ for~any $i\in I$. For~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $\{i\in I \mid a_{i,n} +b_{i,n} \neq 0\}$ is included in $\{i\in I \mid a_{i,n} \neq 0\} \cup  \{i\in I \mid b_{i,n} \neq 0\}$ which is finite because $(f_{i} )$ and $(g_{i} )$ has FSEC. So $(f_{i} +g_{i} )_{i\in I}$ has FSEC. Moreover,
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} f_{i} +\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} g_{i} &= \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} a_{i,n} \bigg)_{\!n} + \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} b_{i,n} \bigg)_{\!n} && \text{by \cref{def: fsum dans C[[X]]}} \\
        &= \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} (a_{i,n} +b_{i,n} ) \bigg)_{\!n} && \text{by \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}}  \\
        &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \,(a_{i,n} +b_{i,n} )_{n} && \text{by \cref{def: fsum dans C[[X]]}} \\
        &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \,(f_{i} +g_{i} ) && \text{by \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}} 
    \end{align*}
    \item One can verify that $(h_{k} )$ has FSEC similarly to point 2. Next, for~any $k\in I\cup J$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$, let us define $c_{k,n} :=a_{k,n}$ if $k\in I$ and $c_{k,n} :=b_{k,n}$ if $k\in J$. We can write:
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}

        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}}

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}}

        &= \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} a_{i,n} +\sum _{j\in J} b_{j,n} \bigg)_{\!n} && \text{by \cref{def: operations basiques dans C[[X]]}}  \\

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}}

    \end{equation}
    For~any $n\in \mathbb{N}^*$, $\{i\in I \mid a_{i,n-1} \neq 0\}$ is finite, so $(Xf_{i} )_{i}$ has FSEC. Finally,
    \begin{align*}

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}}

        &= \bigg(0 , \sum _{i\in I} a_{i,0} , \dots ,\sum _{i\in I} a_{i,n-1} ,\dots \bigg)_{n} && \text{by \cref{eq: preuve proprietes de fsum 5}} \\
        &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}}

        &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} Xf_{i} && \text{by \cref{eq: preuve proprietes de fsum 5}}

    \item Left to the reader.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}

    \item[3.] For~any $i\in I$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} +\Psi _{i} )\subset \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cup \operatorname{supp}(\Psi _{i} )$. So for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}^m$, $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} +\Psi _{i} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ is included in $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}\cup \{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Psi _{i} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ which is finite.
    \item[4.] For~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}^m$, $\{k\in I\cup J \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Upsilon _{k} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ is included in $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}\cup \{j\in J \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Psi _{j} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ which is finite.
\end{itemize}

For~any $(i,j)$, let us denote $(f _{i,j,q} )_{q\in \mathbb{R}^m} := \Phi _{i,j}$. Let $i\in I$. Hence $(\Phi _{i,j'} )_{j'\in J}$ has CLFS. Similarly, one can verify that $(\Phi _{i',j} )_{i'\in I}$ has CLFS for~any $j\in J$.\\
Then, $\operatorname*{\mathchoice

\begin{align*}

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}

\end{align*}
with $\pi _{1} :(i,j)\mapsto  i$. Therefore $\big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}

\begin{align*}
    \operatorname*{\mathchoice

    &= \bigg( \sum _{i\in I} \sum _{j\in J} f _{i,j,q} \bigg)_{\!q\in \mathbb{R}^m} && \text{by \cref{def: fsum}}  \\
    &= \bigg( \sum _{(i,j)\in I\times J} f _{i,j,q} \bigg)_{\!q\in \mathbb{R}^m} && \text{because these sums have finite support} \\
    &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}}

Similarly, one can show $\operatorname*{\mathchoice

For~any $d\in \mathbb{R}$, we have $\iota (f _{d} )=( \widetilde{f }_{d,d'} )_{d'\in \mathbb{R}}$ where $\widetilde{f }_{d,d'} :=f _{d}$ if $d'=d$ and $\widetilde{f }_{d,d'} :=0$ otherwise. Hence $\operatorname{supp}(\iota (f _{d} ))$ is equal to $\{d\}$ if $f _{d} \neq 0$ and to $\varnothing $ otherwise. So, for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}$, $\{d\in \mathbb{R} \mid \operatorname{supp}(\iota (f _{d} ))\cap B\neq  \varnothing  \}$ is equal to $\{d\in \mathbb{R} \mid f _{d} \neq 0 \text{ and } d\in B\} =\operatorname{supp}((f _{d} )_{d} )\cap B$. If one of these sets is finite, then so is the other one.

The first statement is a direct consequence of \cref{def: fsum d'ensembles,SF 1D de composantes pures} item 2. Next, let $I$ be a set and let $(\Phi _{i} )_{i\in I} \in \big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in A} \tilde{E}_{d} )^{I}$ that has collectively locally finite support. For~any $i\in I$, let us denote $(f _{i,d} )_{d\in \mathbb{R}} :=\Phi _{i}$. By~\cref{def: fsum}, we have $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} =\big(\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d} \big)_{d\in \mathbb{R}}$ and this family has locally finite support by \cref{les SF sont stables par fsum}.
\begin{itemize}
    \item If $d\in A$, then $\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d}$ has only a finite number of non-zero terms and these terms all belong to $\tilde{E}_{d}$. Since $\tilde{E}_{d}$ is a vector space, we deduce $\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d} \in  \tilde{E}_{d}$.
    \item If $d\in \mathbb{R} \setminus A$, then all the $f _{i,d}$ vanish, so $\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d} =0$.
\end{itemize}
Using the first part of the present lemma, we deduce $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \in \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in A} \tilde{E}_{d}$.

For~any $i\in I$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(f(\Phi _{i} )) \subset  \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )+\deg f$. Therefore, for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}$, $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(f(\Phi _{i} ))\cap B \neq  \varnothing \} \subset  \{i\in I \mid (\operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )+\deg f)\cap B \neq  \varnothing \} = \{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap (B-\deg f) \neq  \varnothing \}$ which is finite by assumption. So~$(f(\Phi _{i} ))$ has collectively locally finite support. Now, for~any $i\in I$, let $(f _{i,d} )_{d\in \mathbb{R}} :=\Phi _{i}$. We have:
\begin{align*}
    \tilde{f}\bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \bigg) &= \tilde{f}\left( \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d} \bigg)_{\!d\in \mathbb{R}} \right) && \text{by~definition of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ (\cref{def: fsum})}  \\
    &= \left(f\bigg(\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d-\deg f} \bigg)\right)_{\!d\in \mathbb{R}} && \text{by~definition of }  \tilde{f} \\
    &= \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} f(f _{i,d-\deg f} )\bigg)_{\!d\in \mathbb{R}} && \text{by linearity of $f$ on E}  \\
    &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \big(f(f _{i,d-\deg f} )\big)_{d\in \mathbb{R}} && \text{by~definition of }  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}} \\
    &= \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \tilde{f} (\Phi _{i} ) && \text{by~definition of }  \tilde{f}
\end{align*}
Finally, with the abuse of notation $f:= \tilde{f}$, we obtain the aimed formula.

<!-- demo-13: body_md -->
We treat only the positive case, as the negative case is entirely similar. Let $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f_{1} ,\dots ,f_{k}$ be linear maps $E\rightarrow E$ that have a positive degree s.t.\ $f=\sum_{i=1}^k f_{i}$. Let $d_{f} :=\min \{\deg  f_{i} \mid i\in [\![1,k]\!]\}$. Since $\Phi \in E^{+}$, there exists $d_{\Phi } \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.\ $\operatorname{supp}(\Phi )\subset [d_{\Phi } ,\infty )$. So, for~any $i\in [\![1,k]\!]$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(f_{i} (\Phi ))\subset \operatorname{supp}(\Phi )+\deg  f_{i} \subset [d_{\Phi } +d_{f} ,\infty )$. This implies $\operatorname{supp}(f(\Phi ))\subset [d_{\Phi } +d_{f} ,\infty )$ and $f(\Phi )\in E^{+}$. Moreover, iterating this result gives:
\[\forall n\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad  \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi ))\subset [d_{\Phi } +nd_{f} ,\infty ).\]

Thus $(f^{n} (\Phi ))_{n}$ has collectively locally finite support. Finally it~is easy to see that $\operatorname{supp}\big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty f^{n} (\Phi )\big)\subset  \bigcup _{n\in \mathbb{N}} \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi )) \subset [d_{\Phi } ,\infty )$, so $\operatorname*{\mathchoice

        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n} f^{n} (\Phi ) \in E^{+}$.

Let us treat only the positive case. Let $d_{\mathcal{F}} :=\min \{\deg f \mid f\in \mathcal{F}\}$, let $d_{I} \in \mathbb{R}$ be s.t.\ $\bigcup _{i\in I} \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} ) \subset [d_{I} ,\infty )$ and, for~any $i\in I$, let $d_{i} := \inf (\operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} ))$. We also denote $g:=\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f$. Using \cref{les SF sont stables par fsum}, we get $\operatorname{supp}\!\big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \big) \subset  \bigcup _{i\in I} \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\subset [d_{I} ,\infty )$ which proves $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \in E^{+}$.\\
Moreover, like in the proof of \cref{existence des serie geometrique d'op 1D}, we have $\operatorname{supp}(g^{n} (\Phi _{i} )) \subset [d_{i} +nd_{\mathcal{F}} ,\infty )$ for~any $i\in I$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. So, for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}$, $\{(i,n)\in I\times \mathbb{N} \mid \operatorname{supp}(g^{n} (\Phi _{i} ))\cap B \neq \varnothing  \}$ is included in $\{(i,n)\in I\times \mathbb{N} \mid d_{i} +nd_{\mathcal{F}} \leqslant \sup  B \}$. This last set is finite for the following reasons.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $d_{i} >-\infty $ for~any $i$ because $\Phi _{i} \in E^{+}$.
    \item $d_{\mathcal{F}} >0$.
    \item For~any $M\in \mathbb{R}$, $\{i\in I \mid d_{i} <M\}$ is finite. To prove this statement, let us take $M\in \mathbb{R}$. The set $B_{M} :=[d_{I} ,M]$ is bounded, so $I_{M} :=\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap B_{M} \neq  \varnothing \}$ is finite. Therefore $\{i\in I \mid d_{i} <M\}\subset \{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap (-\infty ,M] \neq  \varnothing \}\subset I_{M}$ is finite.
\end{itemize}
Hence, $\big(g^{n} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{(i,n)\in I\times \mathbb{N}}$ has collectively locally finite support. Therefore \cref{Fubini pour fsum} (Fubini) states
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: fsum et le crochet commutent en 1D preuve 1}}
    \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} g^{n} (\Phi _{i} ) = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty g^{n} (\Phi _{i} ).
\end{equation}
\Cref{Fubini pour fsum} also states that the $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$-sums in \cref{eq: fsum et le crochet commutent en 1D preuve 1} are well-defined, and in particular that the family $\big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice

It~is easy to see that the maps $f_{1} \circ \cdots \circ f_{n}$ have a degree, so \cref{fsum commute avec les op a degre dans les SF 1D} allows us to swap $\operatorname*{\mathchoice

\[\operatorname*{\mathchoice

        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}

First, let us assume that $(\Phi _{i} )_{i}$ has CLFS. For~any $i\in I$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(\tilde{\iota}(\Phi _{i} ))=\{0\}\times \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )$. So, for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}^2 $, $I_{B} :=\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\tilde{\iota}(\Phi _{i} ))\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ is equal to $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap B' \neq \varnothing \}$ with $B':=\{d\in \mathbb{R} \mid (d,0)\in B\}$. $B'$ is bounded, so $I_{B}$ is finite and $\big(\tilde{\iota}(\Phi _{i} )\big)_{i}$ has CLFS.\\
Conversely, let us assume that $\big(\tilde{\iota}(\Phi _{i} )\big)_{i}$ has CLFS. Then, for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}$, the set $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\Phi _{i} )\cap B\neq \varnothing \}$ is equal to $\{i\in I \mid \operatorname{supp}(\tilde{\iota}(\Phi _{i} ))\cap (B\times \{0\}) \neq \varnothing \}$ which is finite, so $(\Phi _{i} )_{i}$ also has CLFS.\\

    &= \tilde{\iota}\left( \bigg(\sum _{i\in I} f _{i,d} \bigg)_{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 } \right) && \text{by~definition of } \tilde{\iota} \\

For~any $g\in \mathcal{F}$ and $\Psi  \in \prod _{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 } E_{d}$, let us denote 
\[\deg _{v} g:=v\cdot \deg g \qquad \, \text{ and } \qquad  \operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Psi ) = \{v\cdot (d,p) \mid (d,p)\in \operatorname{supp}(\Psi )\}.\]
Let $M_{f} :=\min \{\deg _{v} g \mid g\in \mathcal{F}\}$. Since $\Phi \in E^{v}$, there exists $M_{\Phi } \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.\ $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi ) \subset [M_{\Phi } ,\infty )$. For~any $g\in \mathcal{F}$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(g(\Phi ))\subset \operatorname{supp}(\Phi )+\deg  g$ so $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (g(\Phi ))\subset  [M_{\Phi } +\deg _{v} g,\infty )\subset [M_{\Phi } +M_{f} ,\infty )$. This implies $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (f(\Phi )) \subset [M_{\Phi } +M_{f} ,\infty )$, thus $f(\Phi )\in E^{v}$. Moreover, iterating this result gives: 
\[\forall n\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad  \operatorname{supp}_{v} (f^{n} (\Phi ))\subset  [M_{\Phi } +n M_{f} ,\infty ) .\]
Hence for~any bounded set $B\subset \mathbb{R}^2 $, $\{n\in \mathbb{N} \mid \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi ))\cap B \neq  \varnothing \}$ is included in $\{n\in \mathbb{N} \mid M_{\Phi } +n M_{f} \leqslant \sup _{b\in B} v\cdot b \}$ which is finite because $M_{f} >0$. Thus $(f^{n} (\Phi ))_{n}$ has collectively locally finite support. Finally, $E^{v} _{M} :=\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 ,\,v\cdot (d,p)\geqslant M} \epsilon ^{p} E_{d}$ is closed under $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ by \cref{fsum des Ed dans les SF 2D}, so $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n} f^{n} (\Phi ) \in E^{v} _{M} \subset E^{v}$.

The proof is almost identical to the one of \cref{inverse de id-f dans les SF 1D}. The steps that were justified by \cref{fsum commute avec les op a degre dans les SF 1D,existence des serie geometrique d'op 1D} are now justified by \cref{existence des serie geometrique d'op 2D,les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D} resp., which are the analogous results for formal series with index in $\mathbb{R}^2 $.

\def\mathcal{I}_{#}1{\mathcal{I}_{#1}}                         
\def\mathcal{I}'_{#}1{\mathcal{I}'_{#1}}                   
\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $f:=\sum _{g\in \mathcal{F}} g$. Let us show that, for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{I}_{n} :=\big(f^{k} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{(i,k)\in I\times [\![0,n]\!]}$ has collectively locally finite support (CLFS). We start by proving that $\mathcal{I}'_{n}:=\big(f^{n} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{i\in I}$ has CLFS for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, by induction on $n$.
\begin{itemize} 
    \item For $n=0$, $\mathcal{I}'_{0} =(\Phi _{i} )_{i\in I}$ has CLFS by assumption.
    \item Let $n>0$. Let us assume that $\mathcal{I}'_{n-1}$ has CLFS and prove that $\mathcal{I}'_{n}$ has CLFS. \Cref{les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D} shows that $\big(g\circ f^{n-1} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{i\in I}$ has CLFS for~any $g\in \mathcal{F}$. By~sum (i.e.using \cref{proprietes de fsum} item 3), we deduce that $\mathcal{I}'_{n}$ has CLFS.
\end{itemize}
Now, $\big(f^{k} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{(i,k)\in I\times \{n\}}$ is in bijection with $\mathcal{I}'_{n}$, so it has CLFS by \cref{proprietes de fsum} item 5. Finally, by finite disjoint union of families that have CLFS (see \cref{proprietes de fsum} item 4), we get that $\mathcal{I}_{n}$ has CLFS.\medskip

\underline{Step 2:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us show that $\mathcal{I}:=\big(f^{k} (\Phi _{i} )\big)_{(i,k)\in I\times \mathbb{N}}$ has CLFS. Like in the proof of \cref{existence des serie geometrique d'op 2D}, we define for~any $g\in \mathcal{F}$ and $\Psi  \in \prod _{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 } E_{d}$:
\[\deg _{v} g:=v\cdot \deg g \qquad \, \text{ and } \qquad  \operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Psi ) = \{v\cdot (d,p) \mid (d,p)\in \operatorname{supp}(\Psi )\}.\]
Let $M_{\mathcal{F}} :=\min \{\deg _{v} g \mid g\in \mathcal{F}\}$ and let $M_{I} \in \mathbb{R}$ be s.t.\ $\bigcup _{i\in I} \operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi _{i} ) \subset [M_{I} ,\infty )$. Using \cref{les SF sont stables par fsum}, we get $\operatorname{supp}_{v} \!\big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \big) \subset  \bigcup _{i\in I} \operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi _{i} )\subset [M_{I} ,\infty )$ which proves $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{i\in I} \Phi _{i} \in E^{v}$.\\
Let $B\subset \mathbb{R}^2 $ be a bounded set and $A :=\{(i,n)\in I\times \mathbb{N} \mid \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi _{i} ))\cap B \neq \varnothing  \}$. We need to show that $A$ is finite. Like in the proof of \cref{existence des serie geometrique d'op 2D}, we have $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (f^{n} (\Phi _{i} )) \subset [M_{I} +n M_{\mathcal{F}} ,\infty )$ for~any $i\in I$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
    A &= \{(i,n)\in I\times \mathbb{N} \,\mid\, \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi _{i} ))\cap B \neq \varnothing  \text{ and } M_{I} +n M_{\mathcal{F}} \leqslant  \sup _{b\in B} v\cdot b\}\\
    & = \{(i,n)\in I\times [\![0,n_{B} ]\!] \,\mid\,  \operatorname{supp}(f^{n} (\Phi _{i} ))\cap B \neq \varnothing \} \qquad  \text{with }  n_{B} := \left\lfloor { \frac{1}{M_{\mathcal{F}}} \Big(\sup _{b\in B} v\cdot b -M_{I} \Big)}\right\rfloor 
\end{align*}
because $M_{\mathcal{F}} >0$. Since $\mathcal{I}_{n_{B} }$ has CLFS by step 1, $A$ is finite. Therefore, $\mathcal{I}$ has CLFS.\medskip

\underline{Step 3:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} One can conclude using \cref{Fubini pour fsum} (Fubini) and \cref{les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D} item 2. This part is entirely similar to the end of the proof of \cref{fsum et le crochet commutent en 1D} and we do~not repeat it.

\defP_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu #}1{P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu #1}} 
By~\cref{def: espaces A}, we have $\mathcal{A}(D)=\sum _{d\in \mathbb{R}} \mathcal{A}_{d} (D)$, so it suffices to show that the sum is direct. We will only treat the case $D=\Omega $ because the other three are similar.\\
Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and, for~any $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$, $d_{j} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f _{j} \in \mathcal{A}_{d_{j}} (\Omega )$. We assume that $d_{1} <d_{2} <\cdots <d_{n}$ and $\sum_{j=1}^n f _{j} =0$. Let us show that $\forall j\in [\![1,n]\!],\; f _{j} =0$. Let us fix $\theta \in (0,\Theta )$. By~definition of $\mathcal{A}_{d_{j}} (\Omega )$, we have for~any $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$:                                                   
\[\exists P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j} \in \mathbb{C}[T] ,\; \forall r>0,\qquad  f _{j} (r,\theta )=r^{d_{j}} P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j} (\ln  r).\]
Let us assume by contradiction that there exists $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$ s.t.\ $P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j} \neq 0$. Let $j_{0} :=\max \{j\in [\![1,n]\!] \mid P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j} \neq 0 \}$. Then we have
\[0 = \sum_{i=1}^n f _{i} (r,\theta ) \sim  r^{d_{j_{0}}} P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j_{0} } (\ln r) \quad \ \mathrm{when} \ r\rightarrow \infty ,\]
so $P_{\theta\mkern-1mu,\mkern1mu j_{0} } =0$. This is absurd, so we have: $\forall j\in [\![1,n]\!],\forall r>0,\; f _{j} (r,\theta )=0$. Since this holds for~any $\theta $, we deduce $f _{j} =0$ for~any $j$.

<!-- demo-24: body_md -->
Let $d\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\mathcal{B} :=\{z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] \ \big|\ (q,k,j)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}^2  \text{ s.t.\ }  q+k=d \text{ and } [(q\in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } q\leqslant k) \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  j>0]\}$. Separating real and imaginary parts, it~is enough to show that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega )\cap \mathcal{C}^{0} (\Omega ,\mathbb{R})$. The proof uses the fact that $\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] = r^{q+k} \,\Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} (\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big]$ for~any $(q,k,j)$ and has two steps:
\begin{itemize}
	\item First, we show that the subspaces of $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega )$ in which $|q-k|$ is equal to a given number are in direct sum.                                                                                                                   
	Since $q+k=d$, for a given value of $|q-k|$, $(q,k)$ can take at most two values.
	\item Then we separate the different powers of $\ln r$, by looking at the behavior when $r\rightarrow \infty $, similarly to \cref{decomposition de A en sev}.
\end{itemize}\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} For~any $a\in \mathbb{R}_+$, let us denote
\[E_{a} := \operatorname{Span}\!\big(\big\{z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} P(\log (\alpha z))] \ \big|\ (q,k,P)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{R}[T],\; q+k=d \text{ and } |q-k|=a\big\}\big).\]
Let us first show
\[\mathcal{A}_{d} = \bigoplus_{a\geqslant 0} E_{a} .\]
Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $0\leqslant a_{1} <\cdots <a_{n}$ and, for~any $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$, $f _{j} \in E_{a_{j}}$. Let us assume $\sum_{j=1}^n f _{j} =0$ and prove: $\forall j\in [\![1,n]\!],\; f _{j} =0$. For~any $j\in \mathbb{N}$, $f _{j}$ is a sum of terms of the form $\psi :z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} P(\log (\alpha z))]$ with $(q,k,P)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{R}[T]$, $q+k=d$ and $|q-k|=a_{j}$. Such a function can be written in polar coordinates as
\[\psi (r,\theta ) =  r^{d} \,\Im\big[e^{\pm \mathrm{i}a_{j} (\theta -\Theta )} P(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))\big].\]
It is well known from the theory of ODE that, for~any $a\in \mathbb{R}$ and $Q\in \mathbb{C}[T]$, $f:\theta \mapsto e^{\pm \mathrm{i}a\theta } Q(\theta )$ is a solution of $(\partial _{\theta } ^2 +a^2 )^{m_{Q}} f=0$ for some $m_{Q} \in \mathbb{N}$. Hence there exists an integer $m$ s.t.\ we have:
\[\forall j\in [\![1,n]\!],\qquad  (\partial _{\theta } ^2 +a_{j} ^2 )^{m} f _{j} =0.\]
Thus, for~any $r_{0} >0$, the functions $f _{j|\{r=r_{0} \}}$ with $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$ belong to distinct generalized eigenspaces of the operator $\partial _{\theta } ^2 $ in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty } (0,\Theta )$. Since these spaces are in direct sum, we deduce $f _{j|\{r=r_{0} \}} =0$ for~any $j$, and finally $f _{j} =0$ on $\Omega $.\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 2:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $a\in \mathbb{R}_+$ and let us show that $\mathcal{B}\cap E_{a}$ is a basis of $E_{a}$. By~construction $\mathcal{B}\cap E_{a}$ generates $E_{a}$, so it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{B}\cap E_{a}$ is linearly independent. There exists $(q,k)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}$ s.t.\ $q+k=d$ and $|q-k|=a$. There are two cases.
\begin{itemize}
	\item \underline{Case 1: $q\not\in \mathbb{N}$.\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} In this case, we have $\mathcal{B}\cap E_{a} =\{z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] \mid j\in \mathbb{N}\}$. Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and $(\lambda _{j} ) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be s.t.\ $f := \sum_{j=0}^n \lambda _{j} \,\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] =0$ and let us prove $(\lambda _{j} )=0$. We assume by contradiction that $(\lambda _{j} ) \neq 0$. Without loss of generality, we can assume $\lambda _{n} \neq 0$. We have for~any fixed $\theta \in (0,\Theta )$:
	\begin{multline*}
		0=r^{-d} f (r,\theta ) = \smash{\sum_{j=0}^n \lambda _{j} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} (\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big]} \\
		\underset{r\rightarrow \infty }{\sim} \lambda _{n} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \ln ^{j} r] = \lambda _{n} \sin ((q-k)(\theta -\Theta )) \ln ^{n} r.
	\end{multline*}
	Taking $\theta $ s.t.\ $\sin ((q-k)(\theta -\Theta )) \neq 0$ we get $\lambda _{n} =0$. This is absurd and concludes this part of the proof.\smallbreak

	\item \underline{Case 2: $q\in \mathbb{N}$ and $q=k$.\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} The reasoning is similar to the previous case, but $\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \. \overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]$ does~not belong to $\mathcal{B}$, so we ignore $\lambda _{0}$, we have $n\geqslant 1$ and we have:
	\[0=r^{-d} f (r,\theta ) = \sum_{j=1}^n \lambda _{j} \Im\big[(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big] \underset{r\rightarrow \infty }{\sim} \lambda _{n} \Im\!\left[ \binom{n}{1} \ln ^{n-1} \!r \cdot  \mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta )\right] = \lambda _{n} n \ln ^{n-1} \!r\cdot  (\theta -\Theta ).\]
	Again this implies $\lambda _{n} =0$.\smallbreak

	\item \underline{Case 3: $q\in \mathbb{N}$ and $q\neq k$.\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Up to switching $q$ and $k$, we can assume $q>k$. Then we have 
	\[\mathcal{B}\cap E_{a} =\{z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] \mid j\in \mathbb{N}\} \cup  \{z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{k}} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{q}} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] \mid j\in \textcolor{red!93!black}{\mathbb{N}^*}\}.\]
	Let $(\lambda _{j} )_{j\in [\![0,n]\!]}$ and $(\nu _{j} )_{j\in [\![1,n]\!]}$ be s.t.
	\[f := \sum_{j=0}^n \lambda _{j} \.\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] + \sum_{j=1}^n \nu _{j} \.\Im[(\alpha z)^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{k}} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{q}} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ] =0\]
	and let us prove that $(\lambda _{j} )$ and $(\nu _{j} )$ vanish. If $n=0$, then it~is clear that we have $\lambda _{0} =0$, so $(\lambda _{j} )$ and $(\nu _{j} )$ vanish. Now let us assume $n>1$. We assume by contradiction $\lambda _{n} \neq 0$ or $\nu _{n} \neq 0$. We have
	\[0=r^{-d} f (r,\theta ) =\sum_{j=0}^n \lambda _{j} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} (\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big] \textcolor{red!93!black}{ {}-{} }  \sum_{j=1}^n \nu _{j} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(\textcolor{red!93!black}{q-k})(\theta -\Theta )} (\ln r \textcolor{red!93!black}{ {}-{} } \mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big]\]
	Applying $(r\partial _{r} )^{n-1}$ (which is like differentiating $n-1$ times w.r.t.\ $\ln r$), we obtain:
	\begin{align*}
		0 &= \lambda _{n} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \,n!\. (\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta )) \big] + \lambda _{n-1} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \.(n-1)! \big]  \\
		&\quad \ - \nu _{n} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \,n!\. (\ln r-\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))\big] - \nu _{n-1} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \.(n-1)! \big] 
	\end{align*}
	Thus we reduced the problem to an expression similar to the case $n=1$. Dividing by $(n-1)!$, this yields
	\[0 = \big[n (\lambda _{n} -\nu _{n} )\ln r + (\lambda _{n-1} -\nu _{n-1} )\big] \,\Im[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )}] + n(\lambda _{n} +\nu _{n} ) \,\Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )}\,\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta )\big].\]
	Since $\Im[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )}]$ and $\Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )}\,\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta )\big]$ are linearly independent functions of $\theta $, and $\ln r$ and 1 are linearly independent functions of $r$, we deduce $\lambda _{n} +\nu _{n} =\lambda _{n} -\nu _{n} =0$, so $\lambda _{n} =\nu _{n} =0$. This is absurd and concludes the proof.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end demo-24 -->
<!-- demo-25: body_md -->
There are two cases whether the coefficient of degree $m$ of $\Im[\alpha ^{d} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{m} ]$ vanishes or not.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item If $d\in \mathbb{R} \setminus \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$, then $\alpha ^{d} \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \mathbb{R}$, so: $\forall m\in \mathbb{N},\; \deg \Im[\alpha ^{d} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{m} ] =m$. Therefore, $(\Im[\alpha ^{d} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{m} ])_{m\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}[T]$. So~writing $Q$ in this basis gives a unique solution of \cref{eq: resolution de Im[alphad P(T-iTheta)]=Q}.
	\item If $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$, since $\alpha ^{d} \in \mathbb{R}$, we have: $\forall m\in \mathbb{N},\; \deg \Im[\alpha ^{d} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{m} ] =m-1$. So in this case $(\Im[\alpha ^{d} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{m} ])_{m\in \mathbb{N}^*}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}[T]$. Thus, $F:P\mapsto \Im[\alpha ^{d} P(T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )]$ is surjective and its kernel is the set of constant polynomials. Its restriction to $E:=\{P\in \mathbb{R}[T] \mid P(0)=0\}$ is therefore an isomorphism and we set $L_{d}:= (F_{|E} )^{-1}$. Finally, for~any $Q\in \mathbb{R}[T]$ we have $F^{-1} (\{Q\})= \{L_{d}(Q)\}+\operatorname{Ker} F$.
\end{enumerate}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-1ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
<!-- end demo-25 -->
<!-- demo-26: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
	\item $\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d}$ is clearly solution of \cref{eq: pb de Laplace homogene dans A(Omega)} for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$. Conversely, let $f $ be a solution.	Let us denote 
	\[\forall d\in {\textstyle \tau\mathbb{N}^*},\;\forall r\in \mathbb{R}_+^*, \quad  c_{d} (r) := \frac{2}{\Theta } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } f (r,\theta )\,\sin (d\theta )\,\mathrm{d}\theta .\]
	Using separation of variables and $f _{|\partial \Omega } =0$, it~is easy to show that we have
	\[f =\sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} c_{d} (r) \sin (d\theta )\]
	with convergence in $H^2 (\Omega \cap \{r_{1} <r<r_{2} \})$ for~any $0<r_{1} <r_{2} <\infty $. Since $\Delta f =0$, we have $(r \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r} )^2 c_{d} = d^2 c_{d}$ for~any $d$. Hence we get: $\forall d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*, \exists a_{d} ,a_{-d} \in \mathbb{C}, \forall r\in \mathbb{R}_+^*,\; c_{d} (r) = a_{d} r^{d} +a_{-d} r^{-d}$.\\
	Moreover, by~definition of $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$, there exists $q\in \mathbb{R}_+^*$ s.t.\ $f \in \sum _{d\in [-q,q]} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega )$. Therefore
	\[\forall d\in {\textstyle \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \cap (q,\infty ),\quad  a_{d} = \lim _{r\rightarrow \infty } r^{-d} c_{d} (r) = \lim _{r\rightarrow \infty } \frac{2}{\Theta } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \underbrace{r^{-d} f (r,\theta )}_{\longrightarrow \,0}\,\sin (d\theta )\,\mathrm{d}\theta  =0.\]
	Similarly, looking at $r\rightarrow 0$ one gets: $\forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap (-\infty ,-q),\; a_{d} =0$. This yields
	\[f  = \sum _{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\cap [-q,q]} a_{d} \.\operatorname{sgn}(d) \,\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d}\]
	(where $\operatorname{sgn} (d):=d/|d|$), which is a finite sum. Therefore, $f $ is in the desired span.
	\item Any solution of the system vanishes in $\Lambda$, so point 2 easily follows from point 1.
\end{enumerate}

<!-- demo-27: body_md -->
\Cref{pb de Laplace homogene dans A} shows the uniqueness of the solutions $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}}$ and $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$, so only their existence remains to prove. We will build $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}}$ (resp.\ $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$) when $\psi_\Omega$ (resp.\ $\psi_\Gamma$) is part of the basis of $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ (resp.\ $\mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$) given by \cref{decomposition de A en sev,base de A Omega} (resp.\ \cref{rq: base de A couche et Gamma}). This induces a unique way to extend $\psi_\Omega \mapsto \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}}$ and $\psi_\Gamma \mapsto \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$ into linear maps, and the images of these extensions will remain solutions of \cref{eq: operateur R Omega Omega,eq: operateur R Gamma Omega} by linearity of the problems.
\begin{itemize}
	\item First, let us solve \cref{eq: operateur R Gamma Omega} for the basis function $\psi_\Gamma:x\mapsto  x^{d} \ln ^{j} \!\,x$, with $d\in \mathbb{R}$ and $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Let us look for a solution $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$ of the form $z\mapsto \Im[(\alpha z)^{d} P(\log (\alpha z))]$ with $P\in \mathbb{R}[T]$. As~the real part of an analytic function, this function is harmonic. Moreover, we have $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}_{|\Gamma } = x^{d} \.Q(\ln x)$ with $Q:=\Im[\alpha ^{d} P(T-i\Theta )]$ using the notation of \cref{eq: def Im[alphad P(T-iTheta)]}. Thus, by \cref{resolution de Im[alphad P(T-iTheta)]=Q}, if we take $P:=L_{d}(T^{j} )$, then we have $\Im[\alpha ^{d} P(T-i\Theta )]=T^{j}$ and $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}_{|\Gamma } =\psi_\Gamma$. Hence $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$ solves \cref{eq: operateur R Gamma Omega}. In addition, it~is clear that $\psi_\Gamma \mapsto \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$ has degree 0.                   
	\item Now let us solve \cref{eq: operateur R Omega Omega} for the basis function $\psi_\Omega:z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ]$ with $(q,k,j)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}^2 $ s.t.\ we have $(q\in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } q\leqslant k)\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  j>0$ (see \cref{base de A Omega}). Given that $\Delta  =4\partial _{z} \partial _{ \bar{z}}$, we have for~any $q_{1} \in \mathbb{R}$, $k_{1} \in \mathbb{N}$, $P_{1} \in \mathbb{R}[T]$ and $u_{1} :z\mapsto  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q_{1}} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k_{1}} P_{1} (\log (\alpha z))]$,
	\[\Delta u_{1} = 4\,\Im[(\alpha z)^{q_{1} -1} \, k_{1} \overline{\alpha z}^{k_{1} -1} (q_{1} P_{1} +P_{1} ')(\log (\alpha z))].\]
	So~taking $q_{1} :=q+1$, $k_{1} :=k+1$ and $P_{1} \in \mathbb{R}[T]$ a solution of $4k_{1} (q_{1} P_{1} +P_{1} ') = P_{\psi}$, we have $\Delta u_{1} = \psi_\Omega$ in $\Omega $.
	\begin{itemize} 
		\item If $q_{1} =0$, $P_{1}$ is unique up to a constant, Moreover, writing $\sum_{i=0}^n a_{i} \.T^{i} :=P$, we have
		\[f _{1} = -a_{0} \,\Im[(\alpha z)^{k_{1}} ] + \sum_{i=1}^m a_{i} \,\Im\big[\overline{\alpha z}^{k_{1}} \log (\alpha z)^{i} \big] \]
		where each term belongs to the basis of $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$. So for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$ different from $k_{1}$, we have $\sigma _{d} (f _{1} )=0$, while $\sigma _{k_{1}} (f _{1} )=-a_{0} =-P_{1} (0)$ if $k_{1} \in \mathbb{N}\cap \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$. Taking $P_{1} (0):=0$ thus gives: $\forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*,\; \sigma _{d} (u_{1} )=0$.
		\item If $q_{1} \neq 0$, there exists a unique solution $P_{1}$. Given that $q_{1} \neq 0$ and $k_{1} \neq 0$, \cref{def: sigma} implies that: $\forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*,\; \sigma _{d} (u_{1} )=0$.
	\end{itemize}
	Since $u_{1|\Gamma }$ may not vanish, we finally define $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}} :=u_{1} -R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}(u_{1|\Gamma } )$. It is easy to verify that it solves \cref{eq: operateur R Omega Omega} and $\psi_\Omega \mapsto \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}}$ has degree 2.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end demo-27 -->
<!-- demo-28: body_md -->
\Cref{pb de Laplace homogene dans A} shows the uniqueness of $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\Delta}}{u_{\Delta}}$, $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ and $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$, so only their existence remains to prove.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Let us define $R_{\Delta}:\mathcal{A}(\Omega ) \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_{\perp} (\Pi )$ by:
	\[\forall \.\psi_\Omega \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega ),\qquad  R_{\Delta}(\psi_\Omega) := \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
		R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}(\psi_\Omega) &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
		0 &\text{ in }\Lambda
	\end{array}\right.\]
	Then it~is easy to verify that $R_{\Delta}(\psi_\Omega)$ is a solution of \cref{eq: operateur R Omega Pi}. Moreover, $R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}$ is linear and has degree 2, so $R_{\Delta}$ has the same properties.

	\item By~\cref{decomposition de A en sev}, it suffices to build $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ when $\psi_\Lambda= x^{d} \,Q_{\psi} (\ln x,Y)$ with $d\in \mathbb{R}$ and $Q_{\psi} \in \mathbb{C}[T,Y]$. In addition, by~\cref{rq: base de A couche et Gamma}, $Q_{\psi}$ is uniquely defined from $\psi_\Lambda$, so $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ can be built in terms of $Q_{\psi}$. We look for $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ of the form $x^{d} \,Q_{u} (\ln x,Y)$ in $\Lambda$ with $Q_{u} \in \mathbb{C}[T,Y]$. Then necessarily we have \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}l}
		\partial _{Y} ^2  Q_{u} & Q_{\psi} \\[0.5mm]
		\partial _{Y} Q_{u} (\cdot ,0)&0 \\[0.5mm]
		Q_{u} (\cdot ,-1) & 0
	\end{array}\right.\]
	This uniquely determines $Q_{u}$. Now we define $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ in $\Omega $ as $R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}(x^{d} \.Q(\ln x,0))$. This makes $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ continuous on $\Gamma $, so we have $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}} \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$. Moreover, $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}_{|\Omega } \in \mathcal{A}_{\perp}(\Omega )$, so $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}} \in \mathcal{A}_{\perp}(\Pi )$. Finally, it~is easy to see that $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\partial_Y^2}}{u_{\partial_Y^2}}$ is a solution of \cref{eq: operateur R couche Pi}.
	
	\item Similarly, it suffices to build $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}$ when $\psi_\Gamma= x^{d} \,P_{\psi} (\ln x)$ with $d\in \mathbb{R}$ and $P_{\psi} \in \mathbb{C}[T]$. Like in point 2, we take $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}_{|\Lambda} :=x^{d} \,Q_{u} (\ln x,Y)$ and $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}_{|\Omega } := R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}(x^{d} \.Q(\ln x,0))$ for some $Q_{u} \in \mathbb{C}[T,Y]$. Then we have $\partial _{Y} {\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscru_{\mathrm{N}}}{u_{\mathrm{N}}}}_{|Y=0^{-}} = x^{d} \,\partial _{Y} Q_{u} (\ln x,0)$ so it suffices to take $Q_{u}$ as a solution of: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}l}
		\partial _{Y} ^2  Q_{u} & 0 \\[0.5mm]
		\partial _{Y} Q_{u} (\cdot ,0) & P_{\psi} \\[0.5mm]
		Q_{u} (\cdot ,-1) & 0
	\end{array}\right.\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end demo-28 -->

It suffices to verify it when $f $ has the form $\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} P(\log (\alpha z)) ]$ in $\Omega $ and $x^{d} \,Q(\ln x,Y)$ in $\Lambda$, with $q\in \mathbb{R}$, $k\in \mathbb{N}$, $d=q+k$, $P\in \mathbb{C}[T]$ and $Q\in \mathbb{C}[T,Y]$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item We have $\partial _{x} ^2 f (x,Y) = x^{d-2} (d(d-1)+(2d-1)\.\partial _{T} +\partial _{T} ^2 )\.Q(\ln x,Y)$ which is in $\mathcal{A}(\Lambda)$.
	\item Let $\psi : z\mapsto  (\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} P(\log (\alpha z))$. From $\partial _{z} \psi  = \frac{1}{2} (\partial _{x} \psi -\mathrm{i}\partial _{y} \psi )$ and $\partial _{ \bar{z}} \psi  = \frac{1}{2} (\partial _{x} \psi +\mathrm{i}\partial _{y} \psi )$ it follows that $\partial _{y} f  = \Im[\partial _{y} \psi ] = \Re[\partial _{z} \psi  -\partial _{ \bar{z}} \psi ]$. Therefore, \begin{align*}
		\partial _{y} f _{|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} &= \Re[\alpha  (\alpha x)^{q-1} \,\overline{\alpha x}^{k} (qP+P')(\log (\alpha x)) -(\alpha x)^{q} \, \overline{\alpha }\,k\,\overline{\alpha x}^{k-1} P(\log (\alpha x))] \\
		&= x^{q+k-1} \Re[\alpha ^{q-k} ((q-k)P+P')(\ln x-\mathrm{i}\Theta )] \ \ \in \ \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )
	\end{align*}
	\item Since $\Delta  =4\partial _{z} \partial _{ \bar{z}}$, we have $\Delta f  = 4\,\Im[(\alpha z)^{q-1} \,k\.\overline{\alpha z}^{k-1} (qP+P')(\log (\alpha z))]$ which is in $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$.
\end{enumerate}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-1ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}

Let $\mathbf{v}^{0} := ( \mathrm{id}+k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta})(\mathbf{u}^0)$. By~\cref{inverse de id-f dans les SF 1D}, $\langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle $ maps $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ to itself, and it~is the inverse of $ \mathrm{id}+k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta}$ on $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$, so we have $\mathbf{u}^0 = \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle (\mathbf{v}^{0} )$. In addition, \cref{operateurs R} states that we have $\Delta \circ R_{\Delta}= \mathrm{id}$, $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ R_{\Delta} =0$, $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ R_{\Delta}=0$ and $\sigma _{d} \circ R_{\Delta} =0$ for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$, as operators on $\mathcal{A}(\Pi )$. These relations then generalize to the extensions of these operators to $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$. Hence we deduce:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $(\mu _{0} \Delta  +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )\circ \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle  = \mu _{0} \Delta  \circ ( \mathrm{id} +k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta})\circ \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle =\mu _{0} \Delta $,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle  = \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 $,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle  = \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}}$,
	\item and $\sigma _{d} \circ \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta} \rangle  = \sigma _{d}$ for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, \cref{eq: equations de bfuDA} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi preuve 1}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{v}^{0} & 0&\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{v}^{0} & g^{0} &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \mathbf{v}^{0} _{|Y=0^{-}} & h^{0} &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{v}^{0} ) & s_{d} & \ \forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
Let us denote $(g^{0} _{d} )_{d\in \mathbb{R}} :=g^{0}$, $(h^{0} _{d} )_{d} :=h^{0}$ and $(\mathbf{v}^{0} _{d} )_{d} :=\mathbf{v}^{0}$ the coordinates of the formal series $g^{0}$, $h^{0}$ and $\mathbf{v}^{0}$. Since $\Delta _{|\Omega }$ has a degree, and $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 $ and $\partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}}$ have degree 0, \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi preuve 1} is equivalent to:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi preuve 2}}
\forall d\in \mathbb{R},\qquad  \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{v}^{0} _{d} & 0&\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{v}^{0} _{d} & g^{0} _{d} &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \mathbf{v}^{0} _{d|Y=0^{-}} & h^{0} _{d} &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{v}^{0} _{d} ) & s_{d} & \ \text{if } d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}

Then \cref{pb de Laplace homogene dans A,operateurs R} show that, for~any $d\in \mathbb{R}$, the set of solutions of \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi preuve 2} in $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )$ is
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\big\{f = \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2}(g^{0} ) + \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}(h^{0} ) + c\. \phi_{d} \ \big|\ c\in \mathbb{C},\, \sigma _{d} (f )=s_{d} \big\}$ if $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$,
	\item and $\big\{ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2}(g^{0} ) + \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}(h^{0} )\big\}$ otherwise.
\end{itemize}
Moreover, in the first case, we have $\sigma _{d} \circ R_{\Delta} =\sigma _{d} \circ R_{\partial_Y^2} =\sigma _{d} \circ R_{\mathrm{N}}=0$ by \cref{operateurs R}, so $c=s_{d}$. Therefore, \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi preuve 2} is equivalent to $\mathbf{v}^{0} = \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2}(g^{0} ) + \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}(h^{0} ) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} s_{d} \,\phi_{d}$. Thanks to the assumptions on $g^{0}$, $h^{0}$ and $(s_{d} )$, this $\mathbf{v}^{0}$ indeed belongs to $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end demo-31 -->

This is similar to \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi}. Let $R_{1} :=-R_{\partial_Y^2}\circ \partial _{X|\Lambda} ^2 $, $R_{2} :=\frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} $ and $\mathbf{v}^{\infty } := ( \mathrm{id}-R_{1} -R_{2} )(S^\infty)$. By~\cref{inverse de id-f dans les SF 1D}, $\langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle $ send $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ to itself and is the inverse of $ \mathrm{id}-R_{1} -R_{2}$ on $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$, so we have $S^\infty = \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle (\mathbf{v}^{\infty } )$. Moreover, \cref{operateurs R} implies that we have:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\Delta \circ R_{1} =\Delta \circ R_{2} =0$,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ R_{1} =-\partial _{X|\Lambda} ^2 $ and $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ R_{2} =0$,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ R_{1} =0$ and $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ R_{2} =\frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}}$,
	\item and $\sigma _{d} \circ R_{1} =\sigma _{d} \circ R_{2} =0$ for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.
\end{itemize}
These relations first hold for the original operators on the spaces $\mathcal{A}$, and are then generalized to their extension to $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}$. This implies:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\Delta \circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle =\Delta $,
	\item $(\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  + \partial _{X|\Lambda} ^2 )\circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle  = \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ ( \mathrm{id}-R_{1} )\circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle  = \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ ( \mathrm{id}-R_{1} -R_{2} )\circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle  =\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 $,
	\item similarly $(\mu _{0} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} - \mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} )\circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle =\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}}$.
	\item and $\sigma _{d} \circ \langle R_{1} ,R_{2} \rangle =\sigma _{d}$ for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, \cref{eq: equations de SDA} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pb de Poisson dans A Pi preuve}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{v}^{\infty } & F^{\infty } _{\Omega } &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{v}^{\infty } & F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \mathbf{v}^{\infty } _{|Y=0^{-}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{v}^{\infty } ) & s_{d} & \ \forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
Similarly to the proof of \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi}, the only solution of \cref{eq: pb de Poisson dans A Pi preuve} in $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ is $ \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} R_{\Delta} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } )+ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} ) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \! s_{d} \.\phi_{d}$, which ends the proof.
<!-- end demo-32 -->

\label{ansatz: existence de bfuDApl et SDApl} 
In the rest of this chapter, we consider a family $(\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ and a family $(S^\infty_{p,\ell } )_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}}$ of elements of $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ s.t., for any $p\in \mathbb{P}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, we have:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: eq vol bfuDApl}}
	\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } & -(\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\mathbf{u}^0_{p-2,\ell } &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell |Y=0^{-}} & \mu _{0} \.\partial _{y} \mathbf{u}^0_{p-1,\ell |y=0^{+}}  &\text{ on }\Gamma  
	\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: eq vol SDApl}}
	\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  S^\infty_{p,\ell } & -\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \.S^\infty_{p-2,\ell } &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \Delta  S^\infty_{p,\ell } & -\omega ^2 \rho _{1} \.S^\infty_{p-2,\ell } &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{0} \.\partial _{Y|Y=0^{+}} S^\infty_{p,\ell } - \mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} S^\infty_{p,\ell } & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
By~convention, we are taking $\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } =0$ and $S^\infty_{p,\ell } =0$ for~any $p\in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{P}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$.
