For~any $d\in \mathbb{R}$, let us denote $E_{d} :=\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ]$, so that we have $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Pi ) =\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d,p\in \mathbb{R}} \epsilon ^{p} E_{d}$. \Cref{sec: series d'op de SF 2D} considers the space
\[E^{v} := \bigcup _{M\in \mathbb{R}} \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\substack{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 \\ v\cdot (d,p)\geqslant M}} \epsilon ^{p} E_{d}\]
where $v\cdot (d,p)$ denotes the scalar product of $\mathbb{R}^2 $. Moreover, \cref{existence des serie geometrique d'op 2D} shows that, if we have $v\cdot \deg R>0$ for~any $R\in \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon$, then $\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle $ is well-defined on $E^{v}$. Thus, if we take $v:=(\pm 1,2)$ we have $v\cdot w>0$ for any $w\in \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}} \setminus \{0\}$, which implies $\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )\subset E^{v}$ and $(\forall R\in \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon,\, v\cdot \deg R>0)$. Hence $\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle $ is well-defined on $\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )$.\\
\defq{\mathbf{q}} 
                    
Next, let $S:=\sum _{R\in \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon} R$ and $\Phi \in \mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )$ and let us show that $( \mathrm{id}-S)(\Phi )$ and $\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle (\Phi )$ belong to $\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )$. Let $q \in \mathbb{R}^2 $ be s.t.\ $\operatorname{supp}(\Phi )\subset  \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q$. For~any $R\in \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon$, we have
\[\operatorname{supp}(R(\Phi )) \subset  \operatorname{supp}(\Phi ) +\deg R \subset \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q +\mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}} \subset  \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q\]
because $\mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}$ is a cone, so it~is stable by addition. Hence $\operatorname{supp}(S(\Phi ))\subset \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q$, which implies in particular $( \mathrm{id}-S)(\Phi )\in \mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )$. By~induction, we also deduce $\operatorname{supp}(S^{n} (\Phi ))\subset \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q$ for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Hence, by \cref{fsum des Ed dans les SF 2D}, we obtain:
                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
\[\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle (\Phi ) \.:=\. \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty S^{n} (\Phi ) \.\in  \!\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{(d,p)\in \mathchoice{K^{\pm}}{K^{\pm}}{K^{\mkern-1mu \pm}}{K^{\pm}}+q} \!\epsilon ^{p} E_{d} \,\subset \, \mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi ).\]
Finally, by \cref{inverse de id-f dans les SF 2D}, $ \mathrm{id}-S$ is invertible on $E^{v}$ and we have $( \mathrm{id}-S)^{-1} =\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle $. Since $\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )$ is stable by these operators, we also have $( \mathrm{id}-S_{|\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )} )^{-1} =\langle \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon\rangle _{|\mathcal{A}^\pm_\epsilon(\Pi )}$.
<!-- end demo-34 -->
<!-- demo-35: body_md -->
Let $S:=\sum _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}} R$ and $\Psi := ( \mathrm{id}-S)(u)$. By~\cref{Rmaicro defini et inversible dans Aemaicro}, we have $\Psi \in \mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$ and $u = \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle (\Psi)$. Let us denote:
\[R_{1} := -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}, \quad  R_{2} := -\epsilon ^2  R_{\partial_Y^2}\circ \partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 ,\quad  R_{3} := -\epsilon ^2 k_{1} ^2 R_{\partial_Y^2}, \quad  R_{4} :=\epsilon \. \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} .\]
Thus we have $\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon} =\{R_{1} ,\dots ,R_{4} \}$. \Cref{operateurs R} implies that we have:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\Delta \circ R_{1} =-k_{0} ^2 \, \mathrm{id}$ and $\Delta \circ R_{i} =0$ for~any $i\neq 1$,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 \circ R_{2} =-\epsilon ^2  \partial _{X|\Lambda} ^2 $ and $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 \circ R_{3} =-\epsilon ^2 k_{1} ^2 \, \mathrm{id}$ and $\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ R_{i} =0$ for~any $i\neq 2,3$,
	\item $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ R_{4} =\epsilon \. \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}}$ and $\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \circ R_{i} =0$ for~any $i\neq 4$,
	\item and $\sigma _{d} \circ R_{i} =0$ for~any $i$ and $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.
\end{itemize}
These relations first hold for the original operators on the spaces $\mathcal{A}$, and are then generalized to their extension to $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}$. This implies:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $(\mu _{0} \Delta +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\mu _{0} \Delta \circ ( \mathrm{id}-R_{1} )\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  =\mu _{0} \Delta \circ ( \mathrm{id}-S)\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  =\mu _{0} \Delta $,
	\item $\big(\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  + \epsilon ^2 (\mu _{1} \partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\big)\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  =\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ ( \mathrm{id} -R_{2} -R_{3} )\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2  \circ {( \mathrm{id} -S)}\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 $,
	\item similarly $(\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} - \epsilon \.\mu _{0} \.\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} )\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}}$.
	\item and $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\sigma _{d,p,\ell }$ for any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$, $p\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, \cref{eq: equations de SDA} is equivalent to
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \Psi & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \Psi & 0 &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \Psi_{|Y=0^{-}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d,p,\ell } (\Psi) & s_{d,p,\ell } & \ \forall (d,p,\ell )\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\times \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}
\end{array}\right.\]
Similarly to the proof of \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi}, the only solution of this system in $\mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$ is $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d,p,\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\cdot  s_{d,p,\ell } \,\phi_{d}$, which ends the proof.
<!-- end demo-35 -->
<!-- demo-36: body_md -->
The commutation with the restriction $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Lambda)\rightarrow \mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Gamma )$ is obvious given the definition. As~for $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Omega )\rightarrow \mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Gamma )$, we have for any basis function
\begin{align*}
	\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon\big({\ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ]}\big)_{|\Gamma } &= \sum _{j'=0} ^{j} \binom{j}{j'} \ln ^{\ell +j'\!} \!\epsilon  \cdot  r^{q+k} \,\Im[\alpha ^{q-k} (\ln x-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{j-j'} ]_{|\Gamma } \\
	&= \sum _{j'=0} ^{j} \frac{\ln ^{\ell +j'\!} \!\epsilon }{j'!} \cdot  r^{q+k} \,\Im\!\left[ \alpha ^{q-k} \frac{j!}{(j-j') !} (\ln x-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{j-j'} \right]_{|\Gamma } \\
	&= \sum _{j'=0} ^{j} \frac{\ln ^{\ell +j'\!} \!\epsilon }{j'!} \cdot  r^{q+k} \.\partial _{T} Q(\ln x) \quad \ \text{with }  Q(T) :=\Im[\alpha ^{q-k} (T-\mathrm{i}\Theta )^{j} ] \\
	&= \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon\big({\ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ]}_{|\Gamma } \big)
\end{align*}
Therefore, for any $f \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ]$, we have $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon(f _{|\Omega } )_{|\Gamma } =\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon\big((f _{|\Omega } )_{|\Gamma } \big) =\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon(f _{|\Gamma } )= \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon(f _{|\Lambda} )_{|\Gamma }$. This shows that $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ is well defined on $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Pi )$.
<!-- end demo-36 -->
<!-- demo-37: body_md -->
By~subtraction, it suffices to treat the case $\Psi =0$. Let $(f _{d,p,\ell } )_{d,p,\ell }$ be a family s.t.
\[\Phi  = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 } \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\,f _{d,p,\ell } \]
and $f _{d,p,\ell } \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (D)$ for any $(d,p,\ell )$. For~any $(p,\ell )$, let $f _{p,\ell } := \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \mathbb{R}} f _{d,p,\ell }$, so that we have $\Phi  =\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p} \sum _{\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\,f _{p,\ell }$. Since $\Phi \in \mathcal{A}_\epsilon^{\mathrm{fin}}(D)$, we have $f _{p,\ell } \in \mathcal{A}(D)$. Let $\mathbf{x} \in D$. The map
\[f_{\mathbf{x}} :\epsilon \,\mapsto \, \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}(\Phi )(\mathbf{x}) = \sum _{p,\ell } \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon\, f _{p,\ell } (\mathbf{x})\]
is well-defined because the above sum is finite and we have $f_{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$ (for the variable $\epsilon$ instead of $x$). By~\cref{decomposition de A en sev,rq: base de A couche et Gamma} (which give a basis of $\mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$), we have the equivalence: $f_{\mathbf{x}} =0 \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \forall (p,\ell ),\, f _{p,\ell } (\mathbf{x})=0$. Therefore, we have: $(\forall \epsilon>0,\, \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}(\Phi )=0) \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  (\forall \mathbf{x} \in D,f_{\mathbf{x}} =0) \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  (\forall (p,\ell ),\, f _{p,\ell } =0 )\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \Phi =0$.
<!-- end demo-37 -->
<!-- demo-38: body_md -->
Let us extend $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon$ into an application $\mathcal{A}(D)[\ln \epsilon ] \rightarrow \mathcal{A}(D)[\ln \epsilon ]$ that has degree 0. It is then extended to $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)$ by \cref{def: op à degree dans les SF 2D}. Moreover, let $\tau :\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)\rightarrow \mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)$ be defined by $\tau :(f _{d,p} )_{d,p} \mapsto (f _{d,p-d} )_{d,p}$. By~construction, we have $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon=\tau \circ \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon$. Let us study $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon$ and $\tau $ separately.
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon$ has a degree, so it commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and powers of $\epsilon $ by \cref{les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D}. In addition, it commutes with powers of $\ln \epsilon $ by construction.
	\item It is easy to see that $\tau $ commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$, $\epsilon $ and operators that have a degree (in particular with the multiplication by $\ln ^{\ell } \epsilon $, which has degree 0).
\end{itemize}
<!-- end demo-38 -->
<!-- demo-39: body_md -->
\def\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon{\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon} 
\def\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon} 
Let us define $(\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon,\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon)$ in the same way as $(\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon,\mathcal{H}_\epsilon)$ in \cref{def: Eps}, but replacing \crefrange{eq: def Eps avec preEps}{eq: def preEps dans la couche} by resp.:\vspace{-2pt}
\begin{align*}
	\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\big((f _{d,p} )_{d,p} \big) &:= (\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon(f _{d,p\textcolor{red!93!black}{+}d} ))_{d,p}  \tag{\ref*{eq: def Eps avec preEps}'} \\[0.5ex]
	\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon\big({\ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j} ]}\big) &:= \sum _{j'=0} ^{j} \binom{j}{j'} \textcolor{red!93!black}{(-1)^{j'\!} } \ln ^{\ell +j'\!} \!\epsilon  \cdot  \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log (\alpha z)^{j-j'} ], \tag{\ref*{eq: def preEps dans Omega}'} \\
	\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon(\ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot x^{d} Q(\ln x)) &:= \sum _{j=0} ^{\deg Q} \textcolor{red!93!black}{(-1)^{j} }\. \frac{\ln ^{\ell +j} \!\epsilon }{j!} \cdot x^{d} \,\partial _{T} ^{j} Q(\ln x), \tag{\ref*{eq: def preEps dans Gamma}'} \\
	\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon(\ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot x^{d} Q(\ln x,Y)) &:= \sum _{j=0} ^{\deg Q} \textcolor{red!93!black}{(-1)^{j} }\. \frac{\ln ^{\ell +j} \!\epsilon }{j!} \cdot x^{d} \,\partial _{T} ^{j} Q(\ln x,Y). \tag{\ref*{eq: def preEps dans la couche}'}
\end{align*}
Let us prove that $\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon$ is the inverse of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$. We do it in two steps.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Let $d\in \mathbb{R}$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (D)[\ln \epsilon ]$. It is easy to see that, for~any $\epsilon>0$, we have $\mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}\circ \,\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon (f ) = h_{1/\epsilon} \circ \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}(f )$. By~\cref{eq: relation Eps pEps}, this implies
	\[\mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon (f ) =  h_{\epsilon} \circ  h_{1/\epsilon} \circ \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}(f ) =\mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}(f )\]
	which yields $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon (f ) = f $ by \cref{rigidite des SF 2D en eps}.
	\item Now let $(f _{d,p} )_{(d,p)\in \mathbb{R}^2 } \in \mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)$. Using the commutation of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ (and similarly $\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon$) with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and powers of $\epsilon $ (see \cref{Eps commute avec fsum et eps et lneps}), and then using step 1, we obtain
	\[\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon\bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d,p} \epsilon ^{p} f _{d,p} \bigg) = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d,p} \epsilon ^{p} \.\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon(f _{d,p} ) = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d,p} f _{d,p} .\]
	Similarly, one can show $\mathcal{H}^{\rm inv}_\epsilon\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon = \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end demo-39 -->

The implication $\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}$ can be proven by introducing $\mathrm{eval}_{\rho }$ and then commuting everything we can until we find what we want: $\forall f \in \mathcal{A}(D_{1} ), \forall \rho >0,$
\begin{alignjustif}
	\rho ^{d} \.f\circ h_{\rho } (f ) &= \rho ^{d} \.f\circ h_{\rho } \circ \mathrm{eval}_{\rho } (f ) & \text{because } f \in \mathcal{A}(D_{1} )\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }(f )=f \\
	&= \rho ^{d} \.f\circ \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f ) & \text{by \cref{eq: relation Eps pEps}}  \\
	&= \rho ^{d} \,\mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ f\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f ) & \text{by \cref{def: op à degree dans les SF 2D}} \\
	&= \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }(\epsilon ^{d} \.f\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f )) \\
	&= \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ f(f ) & \text{by assumption} \\
	&= h_{\rho } \circ \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ f(f ) & \text{by \cref{eq: relation Eps pEps}}  \\
	&= h_{\rho } \circ f(f ) & \text{because } f(f )\in \mathcal{A}(D_{2} )\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ f(f )=f(f )
\end{alignjustif}
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
Incidentally, this calculation can be illustrated by the following diagram. The idea is that we already know that the back, sides, top and bottom faces of this cube are commutative diagrams, which implies that the front face is also commutative.
