Now let us prove the implication $\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}} $. To begin, let us prove that, for~any $D\in \{D_{1} ,D_{2} \}$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}$, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: Ad et Ker(pEps-truc)}}
	\mathcal{A}_{q} (D) = \bigcup _{j\in \mathbb{N}} \operatorname{Ker}\!\big[(h_{2|\mathcal{A}(D)} -2^{q} )^{j} \big] =: E_{q} (D) . \vspace{-\jot}
\end{equation}
\begin{sousdemo}
	Let $q\in \mathbb{R}$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)$. By~construction, $f $ is a linear combination of factors $\mathbf{r}^{q} \ln ^{j} \!\mathbf{r}$ (with $j\in \mathbb{N}$) multiplied by a function of $\theta $ for $D_{1} =\Omega $, or $Y$ for $D_{1} =\Lambda$. In addition, for any $P\in \mathbb{C}[T] \setminus \{0\}$, there exists $Q\in \mathbb{C}[T]$ s.t.\ that we have $(2\mathbf{r})^{q} P(\ln (2\mathbf{r}))-2^{q} \mathbf{r}^{q} P(\ln \mathbf{r}) =\mathbf{r}^{q} Q(\ln \mathbf{r})$ and $\deg (Q)=\deg (P)-1$. Hence we have $f \in E_{d} (D)$.\\
	Conversely, let $f \in E_{q} (D)$. By~definition of $\mathcal{A}(D)$, there exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $q_{1} <\cdots <q_{n}$ and $f _{i} \in \mathcal{A}_{q_{i}} (D)$ for each $i\in [\![1,n]\!]$ s.t.\ $f  = \sum_{i=1}^n f _{i}$. We already know that $f _{i} \in E_{q_{i}} (D)$ for~any $i$. Moreover, the $E_{q_{i}} (D)$ are in direct sum, as generalized eigenspaces of $h_{2}$. Thus we have $f _{i} =0$ for~any $i$ s.t.\ $q_{i} \neq i$, which yields $f  \in \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)$.
\end{sousdemo}
Now, let $q\in \mathbb{R}$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}_{q} (D_{1} )$. Let $j\in \mathbb{N}$ be s.t.\ $(h_{2} -2^{q} )^{j} (f )=0$. By~$d$-homogeneity of $f$, we have
\[(h_{2} -2^{q+d} )^{j} \circ f(f )=f\circ (2^{d} h_{2} -2^{q+d} )^{j} (f ) =2^{d\mkern0.5mu j} f\circ (h_{2} -2^{q} )^{j} (f )=0.\]
By~\cref{eq: Ad et Ker(pEps-truc)}, this implies $f(f ) \in \mathcal{A}_{q+d} (D_{2} )$ and that $f$ as degree $d$ (in the sense of \cref{def: degre d'un operateur}).\\
Next, let $q\in \mathbb{R}$, $f \in \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)$ and $\rho >0$. By~the same arguments as the implication $\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}$, we have
\[\mathrm{eval}_{\rho }(\epsilon ^{d} f\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f )) =\rho ^{d} \.f\circ h_{\rho } (f ) \qquad  \text{ and } \qquad  h_{\rho } \circ f(f ) =\mathrm{eval}_{\rho }\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ f(f ).\]
By~$d$-homogeneity of $f$, we deduce $\mathrm{eval}_{\rho } (\epsilon ^{d} f\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f )) = \mathrm{eval}_{\rho }(\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ f(f ))$ for~any $\rho >0$, which implies $\epsilon ^{d} f\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon(f ) = \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ f(f )$ by \cref{rigidite des SF 2D en eps}. Finally, this property can be extended to any element of $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(D)$ similarly to the proof of \cref{Eps inversible}, using the commutation of $f$, $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ and $\epsilon ^{d}$ with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and the powers of $\epsilon $ and $\ln \epsilon $.
<!-- end demo-40 -->
<!-- demo-41: body_md -->
Let us assume \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro bis} and prove \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis}. The operator $\Delta _{|\Omega }$ sends $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Omega )$ to itself by \cref{operateurs de derivation dans A} and is homogeneous of order $-2$. So by \cref{commutation Eps avec op homogene} we have $\mu _{0} \Delta  \Psi +\epsilon ^2 \omega ^2 \rho _{0} \Psi = \epsilon ^2 \.\mathcal{H}_\epsilon(\mu _{0} \Delta  \Psi +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \Psi)=0$. Using the homogeneity of the other involved differential operators, one can prove the rest of \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis}. Likewise for \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis}${} \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  {}$\cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro bis}.
<!-- end demo-41 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-7: body_md -->
\label{ansatz sur Aeps} 
In this section, we assume
\[\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \!\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } \.\in \. \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P}} \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \mathbb{P}-p} \epsilon ^{p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ] \quad \ \text{ and } \quad  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \!\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot S^\infty_{p,\ell } \.\in \. \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P}} \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in p-\mathbb{P}} \epsilon ^{p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ].\]
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-7 -->
<!-- demo-42: body_md -->
We only prove \cref{eq: champ lointain total}, as \cref{eq: champ de coin total} is similar. By~\cref{ansatz: existence de bfuDApl et SDApl}, we have for~any $(p,\ell )\in \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}$ :
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } & -(\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\mathbf{u}^0_{p-2,\ell } &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } & \mu _{0} \,\partial _{y|y=0^{+}} \mathbf{u}^0_{p-1,\ell } &\text{ on }\Gamma 
\end{array}\right.\]
Let $\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } :=\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\,\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell }$. By~multiplying the above equations by $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$, summing over $(p,\ell )$ and using the commutation of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$ with operators that have a degree (see \cref{les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D}), one easily obtains:
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } + \epsilon ^2 (\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } &0&\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} \mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } - \epsilon \,\mu _{0} \,\partial _{y|y=0^{+}} \mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } &0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
\end{array}\right.\]
Finally, we have $\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon } \in \mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$ thanks to \cref{ansatz sur Aeps}. So we can apply \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro}, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end demo-42 -->
<!-- demo-43: body_md -->
Let us prove only \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro}. By~\cref{champs totaux en fct de sigma}, the matching assumption of \cref{def: raccord algebrique} is equivalent to:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: raccord algebrique presque prouve}}
\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle \bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\, \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\phi_{d} \bigg) = \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  \bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\, \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\phi_{d} \bigg)\end{equation}
Moreover, \cref{operateurs R} implies: $\forall R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon},\; \pi_\sigma\circ R=0$. Since $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle $ is a sum of the identity and non-trivial products of elements of $\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}$, we have $\pi_\sigma\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle =\pi_\sigma\circ  \mathrm{id}=\pi_\sigma$. Thus applying $\pi_\sigma$ to \cref{eq: raccord algebrique presque prouve} gives \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro}.\\
It remains to show conversely that \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro} implies \cref{eq: raccord algebrique presque prouve}. Let us denote $\Phi _{1}$ and $\Phi _{2}$ the two sides of \cref{eq: raccord algebrique presque prouve}. Let us show that they satisfy 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid preuve}}
	\forall i\in \{1,2\}, \quad \ \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
		\mu _{0} \Delta  \Phi _{i} +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \Phi _{i} & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
		\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \Phi _{i} + \epsilon ^2 (\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\Phi _{i} &0&\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
		\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} \Phi _{i} - \epsilon \,\mu _{0} \,\partial _{y|y=0^{+}} \Phi _{i} &0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
For $\Phi _{1}$ this is a direct consequence of \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro} (which can be applied thanks to \cref{ansatz sur Aeps}). As~for $\Phi _{2}$, \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro} shows that $\widetilde{\Phi }_{2} := \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  \big(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon\, \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\phi_{d} \big) \in \mathcal{A}^-_\epsilon(\Pi )$ is a solution of the rescaled Helmholtz problem \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis}, so $\Phi _{2} =\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \widetilde{\Phi }_{2} )$ satisfies \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid preuve} by \cref{action de Eps sur Helmholtz dans Aemaicro}. Moreover, we have shown that \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro} is equivalent to $\pi_\sigma(\Phi _{1} )=\pi_\sigma(\Phi _{2} )$. Hence for any $(d,p,\ell )\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\times \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}$, we have $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } (\Phi _{1} )= \sigma _{d,p,\ell } (\Phi _{2} )$ ; let us denote $s_{d,p,\ell }$ this common quantity. \Cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro} states the problem \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid preuve} with the additional condition $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } (\Phi _{i} )=s_{d,p,\ell }$ for any $(d,p,\ell )$ has a unique solution in $\mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$. This proves $\Phi _{1} =\Phi _{2}$, i.e.\ \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro}.
<!-- end demo-43 -->
<!-- demo-44: body_md -->
We will only prove point 1, as point 2 is similar. We can rewrite \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro} as
\[\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \,\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap (\mathbb{P}-p)} \!\! \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\,\phi_{d} = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p\in \mathbb{P},\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \,\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap (\mathbb{P}-p)} \!\! \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot \sigma _{d} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } ) \cdot  \pi_\sigma \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d} )\]
This is possible thanks to the many commutation properties of \cref{chap: SF,chap: raccord algebrique}:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle $ commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ on $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ by \cref{fsum et le crochet commutent en 2D} and with $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$ by \cref{rq: eps et le crochet commutent,sec: SF 2D de singularites de coin},
	\item $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1}$ commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$ by \cref{Eps commute avec fsum et eps et lneps},
	\item it~is easy to see that $\pi_\sigma$ has degree 0, so it commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ and $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$ by \cref{les op a degre commutent avec fsum et eps dans les SF 2D,sec: SF 2D de singularites de coin},
	\item $\epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon$ commutes with $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ by \cref{fsum et eps commutent,sec: SF 2D de singularites de coin}.
\end{itemize}
Next, let $(d,p,\ell )\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\times \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}$. Applying $\sigma _{d,p,\ell }$ and using \cref{def: sigma et fsum commutent dans Aemaicro} gives:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pre conditions de raccord preuve 2}}
	\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) = \sum _{p'\in \mathbb{P},\ell '\in \mathbb{N}} \,\sum _{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap (\mathbb{P}-p')} \!\! \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{p'} \ln ^{\ell '\!} \!\epsilon  \cdot  \pi_\sigma \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big) \cdot \sigma _{d'} (S^\infty_{p',\ell '} )
\end{equation}
where the above sums are finite. Conversely, since both sides of \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro} belong to the range of $\pi_\sigma$, having \cref{eq: pre conditions de raccord preuve 2} for any $(d,p,\ell )$ is equivalent to \cref{eq: hyp raccord projetee sur les phid pt de vue macro}, and thus to the matching assumption by \cref{hyp raccord projetee sur les phid}.\\
Now, we clearly have, for any $\Phi \in \mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Pi )$, $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{p'} \ln ^{\ell '\!} \!\epsilon  \,\Phi \big) = \sigma _{d,p-p',\ell -\ell '} (\Phi )$ if $\ell \geqslant \ell '$ and $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{p'} \ln ^{\ell '\!} \!\epsilon  \,\Phi \big) =0$ otherwise. Thus, \cref{eq: pre conditions de raccord preuve 2} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pre conditions de raccord preuve 3}}
	\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) = \sum _{p'\in \mathbb{P}} \sum _{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap (\mathbb{P}-p')} \sum _{\ell '=0} ^{\ell } c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p-p',\ell -\ell '} \cdot  \sigma _{d'} (S^\infty_{p',\ell '} )
\end{equation}
because $\sigma _{d,p-p',\ell -\ell '} \circ \pi_\sigma = \sigma _{d,p-p',\ell -\ell '}$. Moreover, for~any $R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}$, we have $\deg _{\epsilon } \!R \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\deg _{\epsilon } \!R+\deg _{\mathcal{A}} \!R\in \mathbb{N}$ (see \cref{fig: degres des elements de Rmacro et Rmicro}). So for $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p-p',\ell -\ell '}$ to be non-zero, we need $p-p'+d'\in \mathbb{N}$ and $(p-p'+d')+d-d'\in \mathbb{N}$. Therefore, \cref{eq: pre conditions de raccord preuve 3} is equivalent to the desired formula of $\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )$.
<!-- end demo-44 -->
<!-- demo-45: body_md -->
Let $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}$ be the set of families of complex numbers $(\mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell } )_{p\in \mathbb{P},d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\cap (\mathbb{P}-p),\ell \in \mathbb{N}}$ s.t.\ for~any $(p,d)$ only a finite number of the $\mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell }$ are non-zero. We define $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}$ similarly by replacing ``$d\in \mathbb{P}-p$'' with ``$d\in p-\mathbb{P}$''. We define the following linear maps:\vspace{-1mm}
\[\mathtt{P} : \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}} \rightarrow  \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}},\ (\mathtt{S}_{p,d,\ell } )_{p,d,\ell } \ \mapsto \ \bigg( \sum _{p'\in [\![0,p+d]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}} \sum _{\substack{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ p'-d'\in [\![0,p]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}}} \!\sum _{\ell '=0} ^{\ell } c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p-p',\ell -\ell '} \cdot  \mathtt{S}_{p',d',\ell '} \bigg)_{\!p,d,\ell } \vspace{-4mm}\]
\[\mathtt{Q} : \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}} \rightarrow  \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}},\ (\mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell } )_{p,d,\ell } \ \mapsto \ \bigg( \sum _{p'\in [\![0,p-d]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}} \sum _{\substack{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ p'+d'\in [\![0,p]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}}} \!\sum _{\ell '=0} ^{\ell } c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p-p',\ell -\ell '} \cdot  \mathtt{u}_{p',d',\ell '} \bigg)_{\!p,d,\ell }\]
These sums have a finite number of terms, so they are well-defined. Next, we define the subspaces $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_{\pm} = \{\mathtt{u} \in \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}} \mid \forall (p,d,\ell ),\; \mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell } \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \pm d>0\}$ and likewise $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}_{\pm}$. So we have $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}} = \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_{+} \oplus  \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_{-}$ and similarly for $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}$. In addition, we decompose $\mathtt{P}$ and $\mathtt{Q}$ on those subspaces, which gives in block matrix notation:\vspace{-1mm}
\begingroup
\def\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex}{\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex}}
\def\rule{0pt}{2.2ex}{\rule{0pt}{2.2ex}}
\[\mathtt{P} \,=\, \raisebox{-2.2ex}{$\begin{array}{@{}c@{}c}
	\left(\begin{array}{c}
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{P}^{}_{+} \\ \hline
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{P}^{}_{-}
	\end{array}\right)
	\! & \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}
		\left. \rule{0pt}{2.2ex} \right\} \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_+ \\[1ex]
		\left. \rule{0pt}{2.2ex} \right\} \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_-
	\end{array}\\[-1.9ex]
	\underbrace{\rule{5.5ex}{0pt}}_{\textstyle\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}} & 
\end{array}$}
\qquad \text{ and } \qquad 
\mathtt{Q} \,=\, \raisebox{-2.2ex}{$\begin{array}{@{}c@{}c@{}c}
	\left(\begin{array}{c}
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{Q}^{}_{+} \\ \hline
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{Q}^{}_{-}
	\end{array}\right) 
	\;=\;& \left(\begin{array}{c|c}
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+} & \mathtt{Q}^{-}_{+} \\ \hline
		\rule[-1.5ex]{0pt}{4ex} \mathtt{Q}^{+}_{-} & \mathtt{Q}^{-}_{-}
	\end{array}\right)
	\! & \begin{array}{@{}c@{}}
		\left. \rule{0pt}{2.2ex} \right\} \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}_+ \\[1ex]
		\left. \rule{0pt}{2.2ex} \right\} \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}_-
	\end{array}\\[-1.9ex]
	& \underbrace{\rule{5ex}{0pt}}_{\textstyle\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_+} \underbrace{\rule{5ex}{0pt}}_{\textstyle\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_-} & 
\end{array}$} \vspace{-1mm}\]
\endgroup
Finally, we denote $\sigma(\mathbf{u}) := (\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}_{p,\ell } ))_{p,d,\ell }$, $\sigma(S) := (\sigma _{d} (S_{p,\ell } ))_{p,d,\ell }$ and $\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{\pm}$, $\sigma(S)_{\pm}$ their components on $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_{\pm}$ and $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}_{\pm}$. With these notations, the two conditions of \cref{pre conditions de raccord} rewrite as $\sigma(\mathbf{u}) =\mathtt{P}\,\sigma(S)$ and $\sigma(S) =\mathtt{Q}\,\sigma(\mathbf{u})$, while the condition of the present theorem is:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: condition de raccord preuve}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}l}
	\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{-} & \mathtt{P}^{}_{-} \,\sigma(S) \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma(S)_{+} & \mathtt{Q}^{}_{+} \,\sigma(\mathbf{u})
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
Let us show that \cref{eq: condition de raccord preuve} implies one of the two conditions of \cref{pre conditions de raccord}, e.g.\ $\sigma(\mathbf{u}) =\mathtt{P}\,\sigma(S)$.\\
Note that by \cref{pre conditions de raccord} we have for~any $\mathtt{u} \in \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}$ and $\mathtt{S} \in \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}$: $\mathtt{u}=\mathtt{P}\mathtt{S} \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \mathtt{S}=\mathtt{Q}\mathtt{u}$. So $\mathtt{P}$ and $\mathtt{Q}$ are inverses of each other. Hence we have $\mathtt{Q}(\sigma(\mathbf{u})-\mathtt{P}\,\sigma(S)) = \mathtt{Q}\,\sigma(\mathbf{u})-\sigma(S)$. Projecting this onto $\mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{S}}_{+}$, we deduce:
\[\mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+}(\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{+} -\mathtt{P}^{}_{+}\,\sigma(S)) + \mathtt{Q}^{-}_{+}(\underbrace{\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{-} -\mathtt{P}^{}_{-}\,\sigma(S)}_{=0} ) = \underbrace{\mathtt{Q}^{}_{+}\,\sigma(\mathbf{u})-\sigma(S)_{+} }_{=0} .\vspace{-5mm}\]
Let us show that $\mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+}$ is injective.
\begin{sousdemo}
	Let $\mathtt{u} \in \mathtt{V}^{\mathtt{u}}_{+} \setminus \{0\}$ and let us show that $\mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+} \mathtt{u} \neq 0$. Let $(p,d,\ell )$ be the smallest triplet for lexicographic order s.t.\ $\mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell } \neq 0$. The term of $\mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+} \mathtt{u}$ of index $(p+d,d,\ell )$ is :\vspace{-2mm}
	\[\sum _{p'\in [\![0,p]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}} \sum _{\substack{d'\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*\\ p'+d'\in [\![0,p+d]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}}}} \!\sum _{\ell '=0} ^{\ell } c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p+d-p',\ell -\ell '} \cdot  \mathtt{u}_{p',d',\ell '} \,=\, c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d,d,0} \cdot  \mathtt{u}_{p,d,\ell } .\vspace{-1mm}\]
	We claim that it~is non-zero because $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d,d,0} =1$. Indeed, in the sum \vspace{-2mm}
	\[\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  := \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty \sum _{(R_{1} ,\dots ,R_{n} )\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}^{n} } R_{1} \circ R_{2} \circ \dots \circ R_{n} \]
	the only term of degree $(0,0)$ is the identity, which appears for $n=0$. So the component of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d} )$ in $\epsilon ^{d} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ]$ is $\epsilon ^{d} \phi_{d}$. Thus we have $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d,d,0} = \sigma _{d,d,0} \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d} ) = \sigma _{d} (\phi_{d} ) =1$. So~$\mathtt{Q}^{+}_{+} \mathtt{u} \neq 0$.
\end{sousdemo}
We have proven that $\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{+} =\mathtt{P}^{}_{+}\.\sigma(S)$. Given that $\sigma(\mathbf{u})_{-} = \mathtt{P}^{}_{-} \.\sigma(S)$, we deduce $\sigma(\mathbf{u}) =\mathtt{P}\,\sigma(S)$.
<!-- end demo-45 -->
<!-- demo-46: body_md -->
We prove only the case $d>0$. The difference of the left and right-hand sides is equal to:
\begin{align*}
	T_{\leqslant q} \big( \langle \mathcal{F}\rangle (\Phi )\big) - T_{\leqslant q} \circ  \sum _{n=0} ^{N} \bigg(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f\bigg)^{n} \!\circ T_{\leqslant q} (\Phi )
	=  T_{\leqslant q} \circ \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty \bigg(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f\bigg)^{n} (\Phi ) -  T_{\leqslant q} \circ \sum _{n=0} ^{N} \bigg(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f\bigg)^{n} \!\circ T_{\leqslant q} (\Phi ) &\\
	= T_{\leqslant q} \circ  \underbrace{\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=N+1} ^{\infty } \bigg(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f\bigg)^{n} (\Phi )}_{=:A} {}+ T_{\leqslant q} \circ  \underbrace{\sum _{n=0} ^{N} \bigg(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f\bigg)^{n} \!\circ T_{>q} (\Phi ) }_{=:B} &
\end{align*}
In addition, for any $\Psi  \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(D)$, we have $\operatorname{supp}\big(\sum _{f\in \mathcal{F}} f(\Psi )\big) \subset \operatorname{supp}(\Psi )+d$. Hence, denoting $m:=\min  \operatorname{supp}\Phi $, we have $\operatorname{supp}(A) \subset \bigcup _{n>N} [m+nd,\infty )=[m+(N+1)d,\infty )$ by \cref{les SF sont stables par fsum}. By~construction of $N$, we have $m+(N+1)d>q$, so $T_{\leqslant q} (A)=0$. Moreover, we have $\operatorname{supp}(B)\subset \bigcup _{n=0} ^{N} (q+nd,\infty )=(q,\infty )$ so $T_{\leqslant q} (B)=0$.
<!-- end demo-46 -->
<!-- demo-47: body_md -->
We only prove the first case. Let $(d,d',p,\ell ) \in (\@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*)^2 \times \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}$. For~any $N\in \mathbb{N}$, we have
\[A_{N} \.:=\, c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } - \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ \sum _{n=0} ^{N} \bigg(\sum _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} R\bigg)^{n} (\phi_{d'} ) \,=\, \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ \underbrace{\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=N+1} ^{\infty } \bigg(\sum _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} R\bigg)^{n} (\phi_{d'} )}_{:=\Phi _{N}} .\]
$A_{N}$ depends only on the component of $\Phi _{N}$ in $\epsilon ^{p+d} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon ]$. Let us find a value of $N$ s.t.\ this component vanishes.\\
Let $v:=(-2,3)$. For~any $\Phi \in \mathcal{A}^-_\epsilon(\Pi )$, we denote $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi ):=\{v\cdot (d,p) \mid (d,p)\in \operatorname{supp} \Phi \}$. We have $\min _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} v\cdot \deg R = 2$ (see \cref{fig: degres des elements de Rmacro et Rmicro}), so, for any $\Phi \in \mathcal{A}^-_\epsilon(\Pi )$ and $M\in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.\ $\operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi )\subset [M,\infty )$, we have $\operatorname{supp}_{v} \big(\sum _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} R(\Phi )\big) \subset  [M+2,\infty )$. This implies:
\[\operatorname{supp}_{v} (\Phi _{N} ) \subset  \bigcup _{N+1} ^{\infty } \operatorname{supp}_{v} \!\Bigg[ \bigg(\sum _{R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} R\bigg)^{n} (\phi_{d'} ) \Bigg] \subset  [-2d'+2(N+1),\infty ).\]
Thus, to have $A_{N} =0$, it suffices that $-2d'+2(N+1)$ is greater than $v\cdot (d,p+d)=-2d+3(p+d)$, i.e.\ $N+1>(3p+d+2d')/2$. Hence, for $N:=\lfloor {(3p+d+2d')/2}\rfloor $, we have $A_{N} =0$.
<!-- end demo-47 -->
<!-- demo-48: body_md -->
There exists an increasing sequence $(p_{m} )$ s.t.\ $\mathbb{P}=\{p_{m} \mid m\in \mathbb{N}\}$. So we can prove the result by induction on $p\in \mathbb{P}$. For $p=0$, \cref{eq: eq vol champs de couche} states: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\partial _{Y} ^2  U_{0,\ell } & 0 &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\partial _{Y} U_{0,\ell } & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	U_{0,\ell } & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Lambda
\end{array}\right.\] so $U_{0,\ell } =0$ for~any $\ell $. It~is coherent with \cref{eq: expression de Upl} (which is a sum of zeros in this case).\\
Next, for the inductive step, we assume that \cref{eq: expression de Upl} holds for ranks smaller that $p$. \cref{eq: eq vol champs de couche} gives: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{}l@{}l@{\,}l}
	\partial _{Y} ^2  U_{p,\ell } &\;=\; -(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )U_{p-2,\ell }
	&\;=\; -\sum_{n=0}^\infty  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n+1} \partial _{y} u_{(p-2)-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{n} (Y) & \\[0.5mm]
	&&\;=\; -\sum_{n=1}^\infty  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{n}} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{\textcolor{red!93!black}{n-1}} (Y) &\text{ in }\Lambda \\
	\partial _{Y} U_{p,\ell } &\;=\; \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,\partial _{y} u_{p-1,\ell } &&\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	U_{p,\ell } &\;=\; 0 &&\text{ on }\Sigma_\Lambda
\end{array}\right.\] It~is easy to see that $\sum_{n=0}^\infty  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{n} (Y)$ is the only solution of this.
<!-- end demo-48 -->
<!-- demo-49: body_md -->
Let $j\in [\![1,n]\!]$ be s.t.\ $(d_{j} ,\ell _{j} )$ is maximal for the lexicographic order. Let $I\subset [a,b]$ be a non-trivial interval on which $|f_{j} |$ is greater than a positive constant. Since $\sum _{i\neq j} r^{d_{i}} \ln ^{\ell _{i}} \! r\cdot  f_{i} (\theta ) =o(r^{d_{j}} \ln ^{\ell _{j}} r)$, we have when $r\rightarrow \infty $ and $\theta \in I$: $|f (r,\theta )| \gtrsim  r^{d_{j}} \ln ^{\ell _{j}} r \gtrsim  r^{d_{j}}$. And we can similarly treat the vicinity of 0.
<!-- end demo-49 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-8: body_md -->
For~any $D\in \{\Pi ,\Omega ,\Gamma ,\Lambda\}$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}(D)$, we denote $\operatorname{deg_{min}} f :=\sup \{d\in \mathbb{R} \mid f \in \sum _{q\geqslant d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)\}$ and $\operatorname{deg_{max}} f :=\inf \{d\in \mathbb{R} \mid f \in \sum _{q\leqslant d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)\}$.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-8 -->
<!-- demo-50: body_md -->
The inclusion $\supset$ is easy to check, so we focus on $\subset $. Let $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega ) \setminus \{0\}$ be s.t.\ $\chi_0 f \in H^{1} (\Omega )$. There exist $d\in \mathbb{R}$, $f _{1} \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \setminus \{0\}$ and $f _{2} \in \sum _{q>d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$ s.t.\ $f =f _{1} +f _{2}$. If $\partial _{\theta } f _{1}$ were null everywhere, then would so too $f _{1}$ because $f _{1|\Sigma_\Omega} =0$. But we assumed the contrary, so $\partial _{\theta } f _{1} \neq 0$. Thus \cref{croissance des fcts de A} implies that there exists a non-trivial interval $I\subset [0,\Theta ]$ s.t.\ $|\partial _{\theta } f _{1} (r,\theta )| \gtrsim  r^{d}$ when $r\rightarrow 0$ and $\theta \in I$. Finally $r^{-1} \partial _{\theta } (\chi_0 f ) \in L^2 (\Omega )$ implies that $d>0$.
<!-- end demo-50 -->
<!-- demo-51: body_md -->
Let us show the existence first, and then the uniqueness.\\
\underline{Existence:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $\tilde{g} \in H^{1/2} _{00} (\Gamma )$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$ be s.t.\ $g= \tilde{g} +\chi_0 f $. We look for the solution in the form $u= \tilde{u}+\chi_0 \psi $ with $\tilde{u} \in H^{1} (\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$. Let
\[\psi ^{+} := \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0}^\infty (-k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}})^{n} \bigg(R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}(f )+\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*} s_{d} \, \phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} \bigg) \;\in \;\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )\]
where we recall that $\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} :=\phi_{d|\Omega }$, and let $\psi :=T_{\leqslant 2} (\psi ^{+} )$. \Cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Omega} shows that we have
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	(\mu _{0} \Delta  +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )\psi ^{+} & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.4mm]
	\psi ^{+} & f  &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.4mm]
	\psi ^{+} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega\\[0.4mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\psi ^{+} )& s_{d} & \ \forall d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*
\end{array}\right.\]
Using $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$, $\psi  = \psi ^{+} -(T_{>2} )(\psi ^{+} )$ and $\deg \Delta =-2$ (see \cref{operateurs de derivation dans A}), this implies
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{}l}
	(\mu _{0} \Delta  +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )\psi  &{}\in  \mathcal{A}(\Omega )\cap  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{d>0} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) = \sum\limits _{d>0} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \\[0.5mm]
	\psi _{|\Gamma } -f  &{}\in  \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )\cap  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{d>2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Gamma ) = \sum\limits _{d>2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Gamma ) \\
	\psi _{|\Sigma_\Omega} &{}= 0 \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\psi  )&{}= s_{d} \;\ \forall d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*
\end{array}\right.\]
Therefore $(\mu _{0} \Delta  +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )(\chi_0 \psi )\in L^2 (\Omega )$ and $\chi_0 \,(\psi _{|\Gamma } -f )\in H^{1/2} _{00} (\Gamma )$. Finally, thanks to \cref{pb de Helmholtz variationnel}, we can take $\tilde{u}$ as the unique solution in $H^{1} (\Omega )$ of: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \tilde{u} +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \tilde{u} & f - (\mu _{0} \Delta +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )(\chi_0 \psi ) &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\tilde{u} & \tilde{g} -\chi_0 \,(\psi -f )  &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	\tilde{u} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega
\end{array}\right.\]

\underline{Uniqueness:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $u$ be a homogeneous solution. There exist $\tilde{u} \in H^{1} (\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ s.t.\ $u= \tilde{u}+\chi_0 \psi $. Let $f :=\Delta \psi +k_{0} ^2 \psi $. By~\cref{operateurs de derivation dans A}, $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$. Let us show that $\operatorname{deg_{min}} f >-2$.
\begin{sousdemo}
	We denote $d:=\operatorname{deg_{min}} f $ and $\widetilde{f } :=(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )(\chi_0 \psi )$. By~\cref{croissance des fcts de A}, there exists a non-trivial interval $I\subset [0,\Theta ]$ s.t.\ when $r\rightarrow 0$ and $\theta \in I$: $\widetilde{f }(r,\theta ) =f (r,\theta )\gtrsim  r^{d}$. Besides, $\widetilde{f } = -(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 ) \tilde{u} \,\in  (H^{1} _{0} (\Omega ))'$. Let us test it with $\zeta _{q} :(r,\theta ) \mapsto  \widetilde{f } (r,\theta )\cdot r^{q-2d-2} \,\big(1-\chi_0(2^{1/q} r)\big)\,\chi (\theta )$ where $q>0$ and $\chi \in \mathcal{D}(0,\Theta ) \setminus \{0\}$ is everywhere non negative. Since $\zeta _{q} \in \mathcal{D}(\Omega )$:
	\[\langle  \widetilde{f }, \zeta _{q} \rangle  := \int _{0} ^{\infty } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \widetilde{f } \cdot \zeta _{q} \cdot r\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}r \,\lesssim \, \|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega )} \qquad  \forall q>0\]
	Let us assume by contradiction that $d\leqslant -2$. It~is~not difficult to check that when $q\rightarrow 0^{+}$:
	\[\langle  \widetilde{f }, \zeta _{q} \rangle  \gtrsim  \int _{c_{1} 2^{- \frac{1}{q} }} ^{c_{2}} r^{d} \,r^{q-d-2} \,r\mathrm{d}r \gtrsim  \frac{1}{q} \quad  \text{ and } \quad  \|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1}} \lesssim  \|\nabla  \zeta _{q} \|_{L^2 }  \lesssim  \bigg(\int _{c_{3} 2^{- \frac{1}{q} }} ^{c_{4}} r^{2(q-d-3)} \,r\mathrm{d}r \!\bigg)^{ \frac{1}{2} } \!\lesssim  \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}}\]
	with some constants $c_{i}$ and Poincaré's inequality. But it contradicts $\langle  \widetilde{f }, \zeta _{q} \rangle  \lesssim  \|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1}}$. So $d>-2$.		
\end{sousdemo}
Now let us show that $\operatorname{deg_{min}} \psi >0$.
\begin{sousdemo}
	Let us assume the contrary. Then there exist $d\leqslant 0$, $\psi _{1} \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \setminus \{0\}$ and $\psi _{2} \in \sum _{q>d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$ s.t.\ $\psi =\psi _{1} +\psi _{2}$. \Cref{operateurs de derivation dans A} states that $\deg  \Delta =-2$, so $\Delta \psi _{1} \in \mathcal{A}_{d-2} (\Omega )$ and $\Delta \psi _{2} \in \sum _{q>d-2} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$. In addition, $f  \in \sum _{q>-2} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$ and $\mathcal{A}(\Omega ) = \bigoplus_{q\in \mathbb{R}} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$ according to \cref{decomposition de A en sev}. So~identifying the coordinate of $\Delta \psi +k_{0} ^2 \psi  =f $ in $\mathcal{A}_{d-2} (\Omega )$ gives $\Delta \psi _{1} =0$.\\
	Moreover, $\psi _{|\Gamma } = - \tilde{u}_{|\Gamma } \in H^{1/2} (\Gamma )$, so $\psi _{|\Gamma } \in \sum _{q>0} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Gamma )$. Hence: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
		\Delta  \psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega \\[0.5mm]
		\psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega \cup \Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.\]
	By~\cref{pb de Laplace homogene dans A}, it implies $d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$ and $\psi _{1} =\sigma _{d} (\psi _{1} )\,\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d}$. However, $\sigma _{d} (\psi _{1} )=\sigma _{d} (\psi )=\sigma _{d} (u)=0$, which contradicts $\psi _{1} \neq 0$.
\end{sousdemo}
Finally, \cref{H1 inter A} implies $\chi_0 \psi \in H^{1} (\Omega )$, so $u\in H^{1} (\Omega )$. This means that $u=0$ by \cref{pb de Helmholtz variationnel}.
<!-- end demo-51 -->
<!-- demo-52: body_md -->
We denote $A :=\Lambda \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}$ and $B:=B(0,R_{\mathrm{c}})$, and we recall that $R_{\mathrm{c}}>0$ is s.t.\ $\Omega _{1} \setminus B=\Pi  \setminus B$.\\
Poincaré's inequality gives for a.e. $X>R_{\mathrm{c}}$: $\|v(X,\cdot )\|_{L^2 (-1,0)} \; \lesssim  \; \|\partial _{Y} v(X,\cdot )\|_{L^2 (-1,0)}$. Integrating w.r.t.\ $X$ the square of this then gives: $\|v\|_{L^2 (A)} \lesssim  \|\partial _{Y} v\|_{L^2 (A)} \leqslant  \|v\|_{V}$. So~$\|v\|_{H^{1} (A)} \lesssim  \|v\|_{V}$.\\
Next, a generalized Poincaré inequality on circular slices of $\Omega  \setminus B$ gives for a.e. $r>R_{\mathrm{c}}$: $\|v(r,\cdot )\|_{L^2 (0,\pi )} \lesssim  \|\partial _{\theta } v(r,\cdot )\|_{L^2 (0,\pi )} + |v(r,\theta =0)|$. Then integrating w.r.t.\ $r$ the square of this times $ \frac{1}{1+r}$ gives:\vspace{-2mm}
\[\int _{\Omega  \setminus B} \frac{v^2 }{(1+r)r} \,r\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}r \;\lesssim \; \int _{\Omega  \setminus B} \frac{(\partial _{\theta } v)^2 }{(1+r)r} \,r\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}r + \int _{\Gamma  \setminus B} \frac{v^2 }{1+r} \mathrm{d}r.\]
Therefore $\| \frac{v}{1+r} \|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus B)} ^2  \lesssim  \|\nabla  v\|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus B)} ^2 + \|v\|_{L^2 (\Gamma  \setminus B)} ^2 $. But we know that $\|v\|_{L^2 (\Gamma  \setminus B)} \lesssim  \|v\|_{H^{1} (A)} \lesssim  \|v\|_{V}$, so $\| \frac{v}{1+r} \|_{L^2 (\Pi  \setminus B)} \lesssim \|v\|_{V}$. Finally Poincaré's inequality in $B$ also gives $\| \frac{v}{1+r} \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{1} \cap  B)} \lesssim \|v\|_{V}$.
<!-- end demo-52 -->
<!-- demo-53: body_md -->
The variational formulation of this problem is: \[ \forall v\in V,\qquad  \int _{\Omega _{1}} \mu  \nabla S\cdot \nabla v = -\int _{\Omega _{1}} Fv+ \int _{\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}} gv.\]
The left-hand side is coercive by~definition of $V$. \Cref{inegalite de Hardy dans Omega1} ensures that the right-hand side is continuous. Moreover it~is easy to see that $V$ is complete. So we can conclude using the Lax-Milgram theorem.
<!-- end demo-53 -->
<!-- demo-54: body_md -->
The inclusion $\supset$ is easy to check, so we focus on $\subset $. Let $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$ be s.t.\ $\chi_\infty f \in V$. The same method as \cref{H1 inter A} shows that $\operatorname{deg_{max}} f _{|\Omega } <0$. And using that $\partial _{Y} (\chi_\infty f ) \in L^2 (\Lambda)$ we likewise get $\operatorname{deg_{max}}(f _{|\Lambda} )<- \frac{1}{2}$.
<!-- end demo-54 -->
<!-- demo-55: body_md -->
This proof is similar to \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}. Let us show the existence first, and then the uniqueness.\\
\underline{Existence:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} We look for the solution in the form $S= \tilde{S}+\chi_\infty \psi $ with $\tilde{S} \in V$ and $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$. More precisely we denote (using notation $\langle .\rangle $ from \cref{def: serie geometrique d'op 1D})
\[f ^{-} := \left\langle -R_{\partial_Y^2}\circ \partial _{X|\Lambda} ^2 ,\; \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} \right\rangle  \bigg( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} R_{\Delta} (f _{|\Omega } )+ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2} (f _{|\Lambda} ) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} s_{d} \,\phi_{d} \bigg) \,\in \, \mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )\]
and $\psi :=T_{\geqslant -2} (f ^{-} )$. By~\cref{pb de Poisson dans A Pi}, we have
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  f ^{-} & f  &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \Delta  f ^{-} & f  &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	[f ^{-} ]_{\Gamma } & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma \\[0.5mm]
	[\mu \partial _{Y} f ^{-} ]_{\Gamma } & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[0.5mm]
	f ^{-} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega \cup \Sigma_\Lambda\\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (f ^{-} ) & s_{d} & \ \forall d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*
\end{array}\right.\]
Similarly to the proof of \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}, one can check that it implies
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{}l}
	(\mu _{0} \Delta  \psi  -f )_{|\Omega } &{}\in  \mathcal{A}(\Omega )\cap  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{d<-4} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) = \sum\limits _{d<-4} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \\[0.5mm]
	(\mu _{1} \Delta  \psi  -f )_{|\Lambda} &{}\in  \mathcal{A}(\Lambda)\cap  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{d<-2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Lambda) = \sum\limits _{d<-2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Lambda) \\[-0.5mm]
	[\psi ]_{\Gamma } &{}= 0\\[0.5mm]
	[\mu \partial _{Y} \psi ]_{\Gamma } &{}\in  \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )\cap  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{d<-2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Gamma ) = \sum\limits _{d<-2} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Gamma ) \\[-0.5mm]
	\psi _{|\Sigma_\Omega \cup \Sigma_\Lambda} &{}= 0 \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{d} (\psi )&{}= s_{d} \;\ \forall d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*
\end{array}\right.\]
where $[{\dots }]_{\Gamma }$ stands for the jump on $\Gamma $. Therefore we have $(1+r)\,\big[\!\operatorname{div}\!\big(\mu  \nabla  (\chi_\infty \psi )\big)-\chi_\infty f \big] \in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$ and $[\mu \partial _{Y} (\chi_\infty \psi )]_{\Gamma } \in L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\})$. Finally, thanks to \cref{pb variationnel de Poisson dans Omega1}, we take $\tilde{S}$ as the unique solution in $V$ of: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  \tilde{S}) & F+\chi_\infty f - \operatorname{div}\!\big(\mu  \nabla  (\chi_\infty \psi )\big)&\text{ in }\Omega _{1} \setminus (\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}) \\[0.5mm]
	\tilde{S} &0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega _{1} \\[0.5mm]
	[\mu \partial _{Y} \tilde{S}]_{\Gamma } & -[\mu \partial _{Y} (\chi_\infty \psi )]_{\Gamma } &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\} 
\end{array}\right.\]

\underline{Uniqueness:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $S$ be a homogeneous solution and let us show that $S=0$. There exist $\tilde{S} \in V$ and $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ s.t.\ $S= \tilde{S}+\chi_\infty \psi $. The proof decomposes into the following steps, all proven by contradiction.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item \underline{$\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\Delta \psi _{|\Omega } )<-2$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Like in step 1 of the uniqueness proof of \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}, we test the inequality:
	\[\int _{\Omega } \Delta (\chi_\infty \psi )\cdot \zeta  =-\int _{\Omega } \Delta  \tilde{S} \cdot \zeta  =\int _{\Omega } \nabla  \tilde{S} \cdot \nabla  \zeta  \lesssim  \|\zeta \|_{V} \qquad  \forall \zeta  \in \mathcal{D}(\Omega )\]
	with $\zeta _{q} :(r,\theta ) \mapsto  \Delta (\chi_\infty \psi )(r,\theta )\cdot r^{-q-2d-2} \,\chi_0(2^{-1/q} r)\,\chi (\theta )$ when $q\rightarrow 0^{+}$, where $d:=\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\Delta \psi _{|\Omega } )$ and $\chi \in \mathcal{D}(0,\Theta ) \setminus \{0\}$ is everywhere non negative.
	\item \underline{$\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\Delta \psi _{|\Lambda} )<- \frac{1}{2}$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} This step works like the previous one.
	\item \underline{$\operatorname{deg_{max}} [\mu \partial _{Y} \psi ]_{\Gamma } <- \frac{1}{2}$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $d:= \operatorname{deg_{max}}  [\mu \partial _{Y} \psi ]_{\Gamma }$ and $f := [\mu \partial _{Y} (\chi_\infty \psi )]_{\Gamma }$.	We have $\nabla  \tilde{S} \in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$ and, by steps 1 and 2, $\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  \tilde{S}) =-\operatorname{div}\!\big(\mu  \nabla  (\chi_\infty \psi )\big) \in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$. Thus $f  =-[\mu \partial _{Y} \tilde{S}]_{\Gamma } \in H^{-1/2} (\Gamma )$. Like previously, we test it with $\zeta _{q} :x \mapsto  f (x) \cdot x^{-q-2d-1} \,\chi_0(2^{-1/q} x)$ when $q\rightarrow 0^{+}$. If $d\geqslant  - \frac{1}{2}$, we get $\langle  f , \zeta _{q} \rangle _{\Gamma } \gtrsim  \frac{1}{q}$ and $\|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1/2} (\Gamma )} \lesssim  \|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1} (\Gamma )} \lesssim  \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}}$, which contradicts $\langle  f , \zeta _{q} \rangle _{\Gamma } \lesssim  \|\zeta _{q} \|_{H^{1/2} (\Gamma )}$.
	\item \underline{$\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\psi _{|\Lambda} )<- \frac{1}{2}$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $d:=\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\psi _{|\Lambda} )$. There exist $\psi _{1} \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Lambda) \setminus \{0\}$ and $\psi _{2} \in \sum _{q<d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Lambda)$ s.t.\ $\psi _{|\Lambda} =\psi _{1} +\psi _{2}$. By~\cref{operateurs de derivation dans A}, $\deg (\partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 )=-2$, $\deg (\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} )=-1$ and $\deg (\partial _{Y|\Lambda} ^2 )=\deg (\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} )=0$. In addition, \cref{decomposition de A en sev} states that $\mathcal{A}(D) = \bigoplus_{q\in \mathbb{R}} \mathcal{A}_{q} (D)$ for~any $D\in \{\Lambda,\Gamma \}$. So by~taking the coordinates of $\Delta \psi _{|\Lambda}$ in $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Lambda)$ and of $[\mu \partial _{Y} \psi ]_{\Gamma }$ in $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Gamma )$, we get if $d\geqslant  - \frac{1}{2}$: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
		\partial _{Y} ^2  \psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
		\partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{-}} \psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.\]
	But since $\psi _{|\Sigma_\Lambda} =0$, it implies $\psi _{1} =0$, which is contradictory.
	\item \underline{$\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\psi _{|\Omega } )<0$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} We denote $d:=\operatorname{deg_{max}}(\psi _{|\Omega } )$. There exist $\psi _{1} \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \setminus \{0\}$ and $\psi _{2} \in \sum _{q<d} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Omega )$ s.t.\ $\psi _{|\Omega } =\psi _{1} +\psi _{2}$. Since $\deg (\Delta _{|\Omega } )=-2$, taking the coordinate of $\Delta \psi _{|\Omega }$ in $\mathcal{A}_{d-2} (\Omega )$ and of $\psi _{|\Gamma }$ in $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Lambda)$ gives if $d\geqslant 0$: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
		\Delta  \psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
		\psi _{1} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.\]
	By~\cref{pb de Laplace homogene dans A}, it implies $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$ and $\psi _{1} =\sigma _{d} (\psi _{1} )\phi_{d}$. But $\sigma _{d} (\psi _{1} )=\sigma _{d} (\psi )=\sigma _{d} (S)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
Finally, \cref{V inter A} implies $\chi_\infty \psi \in V$, so $S\in V$. So the uniqueness in \cref{pb variationnel de Poisson dans Omega1} implies $S=0$.
<!-- end demo-55 -->
<!-- demo-56: body_md -->
Let us focus on the first point. By~\cref{operateurs de derivation dans A}, $\delta $ maps $\mathcal{A}(D)$ to $\mathcal{A}(D')$ for some $D'\in \{\Omega ,\Gamma ,\Lambda\}$ and has a degree (see \cref{def: degre d'un operateur}). Hence $\delta (f^{0} )$ is well-defined in $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(D')$ and the claimed statement makes sense. Let $d:=\deg  \delta $. It is easy to see that $\delta $ is a linear combination of terms of the form $r^{i} \partial _{r} ^{j} \partial _{\theta } ^{k}$ if $D=\Omega $, and $x^{i} \partial _{x} ^{j} \partial _{Y} ^{k}$ if $D\in \{\Gamma ,\Lambda\}$, with $(i,j,k)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}^2 $ and $i-j=d$. Thus for~any $q\in \mathbb{R}$, we have $\delta (f)=\delta (T_{\leqslant q} (f))+o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{q-d} ) = T_{\leqslant q-d} (\delta (f))+o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{q-d} )$.
<!-- end demo-56 -->
<!-- demo-57: body_md -->
Let us prove only the first point. We assume by contradiction $f^{0} _{1} \neq f^{0} _{2} $. Then $d:=\min  \operatorname{supp}(f^{0} _{1} -f^{0} _{2} )$ is well-defined by construction of $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(D)$ and we have $f := T_{\leqslant d} (f^{0} _{1} -f^{0} _{2} )\in \mathcal{A}_{d} (D) \setminus \{0\}$. Subtracting $f =T_{\leqslant d} (f^{0} _{i} )+o (\mathbf{r}^{d} )$ for $i=1,2$, we get $f =o(\mathbf{r}^{d} )$. In addition, by \cref{croissance des fcts de A}, there exist $r_{0} >0$ and $C>0$ s.t.\ (if $D=\Omega $ e.g., but it~is similar in the other cases): $\forall r>r_{0} ,\,\forall \theta ,\, |f (r,\theta )| \geqslant C\,r^{d}$. This contradicts $f  = o(\mathbf{r}^{d} )$ and ends the proof.
<!-- end demo-57 -->
<!-- demo-58: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$. An easy calculation gives that any element of $\operatorname{Ker} A(\lambda )$ must be proportional to $\theta  \in [-1,\Theta ] \mapsto  \mathbf{1}_{[0,\Theta ]} (\theta ) \cdot \sin (\lambda \theta )$. This function belongs to $\mathcal{H}^{m} \setminus \{0\}$ iff $\lambda \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$. Therefore $\operatorname{Ker} A(\lambda ) \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \lambda \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.\\
	Moreover, it~is easy to see that, for~any $(f,g,a)\in \mathcal{H}^{m}_\times$, \cref{eq: EDO en theta a resoudre} with $\lambda :=0$ has a unique solution in $\mathcal{H}^{m+2}$. Thus $A(0):\mathcal{H}^{m+2} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^{m}_\times$ is invertible. Now, for~any $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, we have $A(\lambda )=A(0)+\lambda ^2 B$ with $B:u\mapsto (u_{|(0,\Theta )} ,0,0)$. $B$ is a compact operator from $\mathcal{H}^{m+2}$ to $\mathcal{H}^{m}_\times$, so the Fredholm alternative holds for $A(\lambda )$. Therefore $A(\lambda ):\mathcal{H}^{m+2} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^{m}_\times$ is invertible iff $\lambda \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$.

	\item Since $\lambda \mapsto A(\lambda )$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$, so too is $\lambda \mapsto A(\lambda )^{-1}$. Let us describe its behavior near the points $q\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$ using \cite[Theorem~5.1.1, p.\,147]{KozMazRos97}. It depends on the ``Jordan chains'' of $A(q)$, which are the sequences $(u_{0} ,\dots ,u_{n} )\in (\mathcal{H}^{m} )^{n+1}$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, s.t.\ 
	\begin{equation}{\label{eq: chaine de Jordan}}
	\forall k\in [\![0,n]\!],\qquad  \sum _{j=0} ^{k} \frac{1}{j!} \frac{\mathrm{d}^{j} A}{\mathrm{d}\lambda ^{j}} \Big|_{\lambda =q} (u_{k-j} )= 0 \end{equation}
	Let us compute these chains. Taking $k:=0$ in \cref{eq: chaine de Jordan} gives $A(q)(u_{0} )=0$, so $u_{0}$ is proportional to $\theta \mapsto  \mathbf{1}_{[0,\Theta ]} (\theta ) \cdot \sin (q\theta )$ by step 1. In addition, if $n\geqslant 1$, taking $k:=1$ gives $A(q)(u_{1} )+ \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}\lambda } (q) (u_{0} )=0$. This implies on one hand $u_{1} '' +q^2 u_{1} +2qu_{0} =0$ in $(0,\Theta )$. On the other we get $u_{1|(-1,0)} '' =0$ and $u_{1} '(0^{-})=0$, so $u_{1|(-1,0)} =0$, which gives $u_{1} (0)=u_{1} (\Theta )=0$. Therefore
	\[0 \neq \int _{0} ^{\Theta } 2q|u_{0} |^2  = \int _{0} ^{\Theta } -(u_{1} ''+q^2 u_{1} ) \cdot  \overline{u_{0} }= \int _{0} ^{\Theta } -u_{1} \cdot (\underbrace{\overline{u_{0} ''+q^2 u_{0} }}_{=0} ) =0. \vspace{-2mm}\]
	This is absurd, so we must have $n=0$ for~any Jordan chain of $A(q)$. Therefore, \cite[Theorem~5.1.1, p.\,147]{KozMazRos97} states that $A(\lambda )^{-1}$ has a simple pole at $q$, and $\operatorname{Im}(\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda =q} A(\lambda )^{-1} )=\mathbb{C}u_{0}$.
	
	\item Let $(f,g,a)\in \mathcal{H}^{m}_\times$ and $u:=A(\lambda )^{-1} (f,g,a)\in \mathcal{H}^{m+2}$. We will write $\lesssim $ for inequalities valid up to a constant that depends on $(m,\beta _{1} ,\beta _{2} )$ but not on $(\lambda ,f,g,a)$. By~Poincaré's inequality and integration by parts, we have\vspace{-2mm}
	\[\|u\|_{H^{1} (-1,0)} ^2  \lesssim  \int _{-1} ^{0} |u'|^2  = - \int _{0} ^{-1} g \bar{u}+ a\, \bar{u}(0)\lesssim  (\|g\|_{L^2 (-1,0)} +|a|) \cdot  \|u\|_{H^{1} (-1,0)}\]
	thus $\|u\|_{H^{1} (-1,0)} \lesssim  \|g\|_{L^2 (-1,0)} +|a|$. Since $u''_{|(-1,0)} =g$, we deduce $\|u\|_{H^{m+2} (-1,0)} \lesssim  \|g\|_{H^{m}} +|a|$.\\
	Then, let $u_{1} :\theta  \in [0,\Theta ] \mapsto u(0) \big(1- \frac{\theta }{\Theta } \big)$, $v:=u-u_{1}$ and $f_{\lambda } :=f-\lambda ^2 u_{1}$. We have $v(0)=v(\Theta )=0$ and $v''+\lambda ^2 v=f_{\lambda }$, so
	\[\int _{0} ^{\Theta } (-|v'|^2 +\lambda ^2 |v|^2 )=\int _{0} ^{\Theta } f_{\lambda } \bar{v}\]
	Dividing by $\lambda $ and taking the absolute value of the imaginary part, we get:
	\[\frac{|\Im(\lambda )|}{|\lambda |^2 } \|v'\|_{L^2 } ^2  + |\Im(\lambda )|\, \|v\|_{L^2 } ^2  \leqslant  \frac{1}{|\lambda |} \|f_{\lambda } \|_{L^2 } \|v\|_{L^2 } .\]
	Now we assume $|\Im(\lambda )|>1$ and $\beta _{1} <\Re(\lambda )<\beta _{2}$, so $|\lambda |\lesssim |\Im(\lambda )|$. Thus $\|v'\|_{L^2 } ^2  + |\lambda |^2  \|v\|_{L^2 } ^2  \leqslant  \|f_{\lambda } \|_{L^2 } \|v\|_{L^2 }$, which yields $\|v\|_{L^2 } \lesssim  |\lambda |^{-2} \|f_{\lambda } \|_{L^2 }$ and then $\|v'\|_{L^2 } \lesssim  |\lambda |^{-1} \|f_{\lambda } \|_{L^2 }$. Now from $v''=f_{\lambda } -\lambda ^2 v$, one can easily derive by induction on $m$ that $\|v\|_{H^{m+2}}  \lesssim  |\lambda |^{m} \|f_{\lambda } \|_{H^{m}}$. This implies $\|u\|_{H^{m+2} (0,\Theta )} \lesssim  |\lambda |^{m} \|f\|_{H^{m}} +|\lambda |^{m+2} |u(0)|$, with $|u(0)|\lesssim  \|u\|_{H^{m+2} (-1,0)}$.\\
	So finally $\|u\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m+2}} \lesssim  |\Im(\lambda )|^{m+2} \|(f,g,a)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}_\times}$.
\end{enumerate}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-1ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
<!-- end demo-58 -->
<!-- demo-59: body_md -->
For~any $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, let $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>\beta } :=\{\lambda \in \mathbb{C} \mid \Re(\lambda )>\beta \}$. The Laplace transform of $s$ is well-defined and holomorphic from $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>d}$ to $\mathcal{H}^{m}$. We will show that $\hat{s}$ has a meromorphic extension on $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>d-1}$, with poles belonging in $\mathfrak{P}:=\@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\cap (d-1,d]$, then we will apply the residue theorem on a rectangle surrounding these poles. The functions $\phi_{q}$ will appear in the residues.\medskip

\underline{Step 1 :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} $\hat{s}$ satisfies in $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>d}$:
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{}ll}
	\mu _{0} (\partial _{\theta } ^2 +\lambda ^2 ) \hat{s}(\lambda ,\theta ) &\;=\; \hat{f}(\lambda ,\theta ) & \text{if}  \ \theta \in (0,\Theta )\\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{\theta } ^2  \hat{s}(\lambda ,\theta ) &\;=\; \hat{g}(\lambda ,\theta ) -\mu _{1} \,\big[(\lambda +2)^2 -(\lambda +2)\big] \, \hat{s}(\lambda +2,\theta ) := \tilde{g}(\lambda ,\theta ) & \text{if}  \ \theta \in (-1,0)\\[0.5mm]
	\hat{s}(\lambda ,0^{+} ) - \hat{s}(\lambda ,0^{-}) &\;=\; 0& \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{\theta } \hat{s}(\lambda ,0^{-}) &\;=\; \hat{h}(\lambda ) +\mu _{0} \partial _{\theta } \hat{s}(\lambda +1,0^{+} ) := \tilde{h}(\lambda ) & \\[0.5mm]
	\hat{s}(\lambda ,\Theta ) = \hat{s}(\lambda ,-1) &\;=\; 0 &
\end{array}\right.\] For~any $\lambda \in  \mathbb{C}_{\Re>d-1} \setminus \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$, let $\tilde{s} (\lambda ) := A(\lambda )^{-1} \big( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} \hat{f}(\lambda ), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{g}(\lambda ), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{h}(\lambda )\big)$. Then $\tilde{s}$ is also solution of the above system, so $\tilde{s}$ and $\hat{s}$ coincide on $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>d} \setminus \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$ by \cref{resolution de l'EDO en theta}. Hence $\tilde{s}$ is an extension of $\hat{s}$ on $\mathbb{C}_{\Re>d-1} \setminus \mathfrak{P}$, that we will still denote $\hat{s}$. \Cref{resolution de l'EDO en theta} implies that this extension is meromorphic with simple poles and: $\forall q\in \mathfrak{P},\; \operatorname{Res}_{q} \hat{s} =(\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda =q} A(\lambda )^{-1} ) \big( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} \hat{f}(q), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{g}(q), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{h}(q)\big)$.\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 2 :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $b\in (d-1,d_{\mathrm{\min }} )$ and $k\in \mathbb{R}_+^*$. The residue theorem applied to $\lambda  \mapsto  e^{\lambda t} \hat{s}(\lambda )$ on the rectangle $[b,d+1]\times [-k,k] \subset \mathbb{C}$ gives the following equality in $\mathcal{H}^{m}$. \begin{eqnarray*}
	2\mathrm{i}\pi  \sum _{q\in \mathfrak{P}} \operatorname{Res}_{q} (\lambda \mapsto e^{\lambda t} \hat{s}(\lambda )) &=& \int _{-k} ^{k} e^{(d+1+\mathrm{i}\gamma )t} \hat{s}(d+1+\mathrm{i}\gamma )\,\mathrm{d}\gamma  - \int _{-k} ^{k} e^{(b+\mathrm{i}\gamma )t} \hat{s}(b+\mathrm{i}\gamma )\,\mathrm{d}\gamma  \\[-1mm]
	&& + \int _{b} ^{d+1} e^{(\beta -\mathrm{i}k)t} \hat{s}(\beta -\mathrm{i}k)\,\mathrm{d}\beta  - \int _{b} ^{d+1} e^{(\beta +\mathrm{i}k)t} \hat{s}(\beta +\mathrm{i}k)\,\mathrm{d}\beta 
\end{eqnarray*}
Note that when $k\rightarrow \infty $ the first integral tends to the inverse Laplace transform of $s$ (up to a constant). We will show that the last two integrals tend to 0, by proving the following: 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: etape de base du DA des champs de coin preuve}}
\forall n\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad  \sup _{\beta \in [b,d+1]} \int _{\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1]} \gamma ^{n} \| \hat{s}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} \,\mathrm{d}\gamma  < \infty  \vspace{-2mm}\end{equation}
\begin{sousdemo}
	Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and $\beta \in [b,d+1]$. \cref{eq: normes des operateurs resolvants R1 R2 et R3} and the expressions of $\tilde{g}$ and $\tilde{h}$ yield
	\begin{align*}
		\int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1]} \gamma ^{n} \,\| \hat{s}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} \,\mathrm{d}\gamma 
		&\leqslant  \int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1]} \gamma ^{n} \,\|A(\lambda )^{-1} \|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}^{m-2}_\times,\mathcal{H}^{m} )} \\
		& \qquad  \qquad  \quad  {}\times \Big\|\big({\textstyle  \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} \hat{f}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma ), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{g}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma ), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{h}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )}\big)\Big\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m-2}_\times} \,\mathrm{d}\gamma  \hspace{-20mm} \\
		&\lesssim  \int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1]} \! \gamma ^{n+m+2} \,\Big( \| \hat{f} (\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{H^{m-2}} +\| \hat{g} (\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{H^{m-2}} +| \hat{h}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )| \\[-2mm]
		& \qquad  \qquad  \quad  \ {} + \| \hat{s}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma +1)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} + \gamma ^2 \| \hat{s}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma +2)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} \Big) \,\mathrm{d}\gamma  
	\end{align*}
	Let us treat the term with $f$, given that the others are similar.
	\begin{eqnarray*}
		\int _{\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1]} \gamma ^{n+m+2} \| \hat{f} (\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{H^{m-2}} \,\mathrm{d}\gamma  
		&\underset{\mathcal{\text{C.S.}}}{\leqslant }& \|\gamma ^{-1} \|_{L^2 (\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1])} \cdot  \Big\| \gamma ^{n+m+3} \| \hat{f}(\beta +\mathrm{i}\gamma )\|_{H^{m-2}} \Big\|_{L^2 (\mathbb{R} \setminus [-1,1])} \\[-0.5mm]
		&\lesssim & \|e^{-\beta t} \partial _{t} ^{n+m+3} f\|_{L^2 (\mathbb{R},H^{m-2} (0,\Theta ))} \\
		&\lesssim & \max _{\beta '\in \{b,d+1\}} \|e^{-\beta 't} \partial _{t} ^{n+m+3} f\|_{L^2 (\mathbb{R},H^{m-2} (0,\Theta ))} \\
		&=& \max _{\beta '\in \{b,d+1\}} \|f\|_{K^{n+m+3} _{\beta '} (\mathbb{R},H^{m-2} (0,\Theta ))}
	\end{eqnarray*}
	thanks to an interpolation between $b$ and $d+1$. We have majorized by a finite constant independent of $\beta $, so the supremum on $\beta $ is finite. Thus \cref{eq: etape de base du DA des champs de coin preuve} is proven.
\end{sousdemo}
Therefore: $\displaystyle \int _{1} ^{\infty } \bigg\| \int _{b} ^{d+1} e^{(\beta \pm \mathrm{i}k)t} \hat{s}(\beta \pm \mathrm{i}k) \,\mathrm{d}\beta \,\bigg\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} \mathrm{d}k \lesssim  \int _{1} ^{\infty } \! \int _{b} ^{d+1} \| \hat{s}(\beta \pm \mathrm{i}k)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{m}} \,\mathrm{d}\beta \,\mathrm{d}k < +\infty $.\\
So by~taking arbitrarily large $k$, we can make the terms $\int _{b} ^{d+1} e^{(\beta \pm \mathrm{i}\gamma )t} \hat{s}(\beta \pm \mathrm{i}k) \,\mathrm{d}\beta $ tend to 0 in $\mathcal{H}^{m}$. Hence:
\[\sum _{q\in \mathfrak{P}} \operatorname{Res}_{q} (\lambda \mapsto e^{\lambda t} \hat{s}(\lambda )) = \frac{1}{2\mathrm{i}\pi } \int _{\mathbb{R}} e^{(d+1+\mathrm{i}\gamma )t} \hat{s}(d+1+\mathrm{i}\gamma ) \,\mathrm{d}\gamma   - \frac{1}{2\mathrm{i}\pi } \int _{\mathbb{R}} e^{(b+\mathrm{i}\gamma )t} \hat{s}(b+\mathrm{i}\gamma ) \,\mathrm{d}\gamma .\]
Now, since $\hat{s}$ has only simple poles, the terms of the sum are equal to 
\[e^{qt} \operatorname{Res}_{q} \hat{s} = e^{qt} (\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda =q} A(\lambda )^{-1} )\big({\textstyle \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} \hat{f}(q), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{g}(q), \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} \tilde{h}(q)}\big) = e^{qt} c_{q} \mathbf{1}_{[0,\Theta ]} (\theta ) \sin (q\theta ) = c_{q} \,\mathchoice{
	\def2mu{3mu} \def-0.05ex{0.2ex} \def-0.05ex{-0.05ex}
	\mkern2mu{\overbracket[0.2pt][0pt]{
	\raisebox{0pt}[\height+-0.05ex]{$\overbracket[0.2pt][0pt]{\mkern-2mu
	\raisebox{0pt}[\height+-0.05ex]{$\textstyle \phi_{q} $}
	\mkern-2mu}$}}}\mkern2mu}{
	\def2mu{3mu} \def-0.05ex{0.2ex} \def-0.05ex{-0.05ex}
	\mkern2mu{\overbracket[0.2pt][0pt]{
	\raisebox{0pt}[\height+-0.05ex]{$\overbracket[0.2pt][0pt]{\mkern-2mu

for some constant $c_{q} \in \mathbb{C}$ by point 2 of \cref{resolution de l'EDO en theta}. The first integral is equal to $s(t)$ by inverse Laplace transform (because $s\in K_{d+1} ^{\infty } (\mathbb{R},\mathcal{H}^{m} )$). We define $s_{\mathrm{r}} (t)$ to be equal to the last integral. Thus we get the desired formula, and \cref{eq: etape de base du DA des champs de coin preuve} shows that $s_{\mathrm{r}} \in K^{\infty } _{b} (\mathbb{R},\mathcal{H}^{m} )$.

We consider any $d\in \mathbb{R}_-$ and we will fix it later. The proof has three steps: showing that $S^{V} \in V$, showing that $S^{V}$ is regular w.r.t $t$, and deducing that it~is regular w.r.t.\ $\theta $. For~any $r_{1} ,r_{2} \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.\ $R_{\mathrm{c}}<r_{1} <r_{2}$, we will denote $\chi \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty } (\mathbb{R}^2 )$ a radial function equal to 0 on $B(0,r_{1} )$ and 1 on $\mathbb{R}^2  \setminus B(0,r_{2} )$ ($r_{1} ,r_{2} $ are implicit in this~notation).\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $f :\Pi \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be equal to $T_{\leqslant d} (F^{\infty } _{D} )$ on $D$ for~any $D\in \{\Omega ,\Lambda\}$, and $F_{\mathrm{v}} = F-\chi_\infty f $. If $d<-2$ then $(1+r)F_{\mathrm{v}} \in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$. So the same construction than in \cref{cadre fonctionnel pour les champs de coin} shows that for $d$ small enough, the problem 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: pb verifie par S V}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  S^{V} ) & f_{1} := F_{\mathrm{v}} + \chi_\infty f  - \operatorname{div}\!\big(\mu  \nabla  (\chi_\infty \cdot S^{\mathcal{A}} )\big)&\text{ in }\Omega _{1} \setminus (\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\})  \\[0.5mm]
[\mu  \partial _{Y} S^{V} ]_{\Gamma } & g_{1} := -[\mu \partial _{Y} (\chi_\infty S^{\mathcal{A}} )]_{\Gamma } &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\} \\[0.5mm]
S^{V} &0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega _{1}
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
has a unique solution in $V$ and that $S = S^{V} + \chi_\infty S^{\mathcal{A}}$. In addition, it also gives that $(\mu  \Delta  S^{\mathcal{A}} - f )_{|D} \in  \sum _{d'<d} \mathcal{A}_{d'} (D)$ for~any $D\in \{\Omega ,\Lambda\}$, and $[\mu \partial _{Y} S^{\mathcal{A}} ]_{\Gamma } \in  \sum _{d'<d} \mathcal{A}_{d'} (\Gamma )$. And we have $F_{\mathrm{v}} =o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{d} )$ by hypothesis, so for $d$ small enough and up to increasing $R_{\mathrm{c}}$ (without loss of generality):

	\chi  S^{V} &0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega \cup \Sigma_\Lambda
\end{array}\right.\]

We consider any $d\in \mathbb{R}_+$ and we will fix it later. The proof has five steps: writing the equations satisfied by $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}}$, and then showing that $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}}$ is regular in the layer, that it~is $H^{1}$ in $\Omega $, that it~is regular in $\Omega $ w.r.t $t$, and that it~is regular in $\Omega $ w.r.t.\ $\theta $. For~any $r_{1} ,r_{2} \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.\ $r_{1} <r_{2} <r_{f}$, we denote $\chi \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty } (\mathbb{R}^2 )$ a radial function equal to 1 on $B(0,r_{1} )$ and 0 on $\mathbb{R}^2  \setminus B(0,r_{2} )$ ($r_{1} ,r_{2} $ are implicit in this~notation).\\

\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Similarly to the proofs of \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains,cadre fonctionnel pour les champs de coin,regularite de S variationnel}, one can show that:
\[\left\{\begin{array}{@{\,}r@{\;=\;}l@{\,}l@{}}

	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2 \mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} & g_{1} :=g-\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2 (\chi_f \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} ) &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|y=0^{+}} - \mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|y=0^{-}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[1mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} \mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|Y=0^{-}} & h_{1} :=h-\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} (\chi_f \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} ) &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[1mm]
	\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega \cup \Sigma_\Lambda
\end{array}\right.\]
with
\[\left\{\begin{array}{@{}r@{\;\in \;}l@{}}
	(\mu _{0} \Delta  +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} )\mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} & \sum\limits _{d'>d} \! \mathcal{A}_{d'} (\Omega ) \\[0.5mm]
	\partial _{Y} ^2 \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} _{|\Lambda} - T_{\leqslant d} (g^{0} ) & \sum\limits _{d'>d} \! \mathcal{A}_{d'} (\Lambda)  \\[0.5mm]
	\partial _{Y} \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} _{|Y=0^{-}} - T_{\leqslant d} (h^{0} ) & \sum\limits _{d'>d} \! \mathcal{A}_{d'} (\Gamma )
\end{array}\right.\]

So the following system has a solution in $H^{1} (\Omega )$ by \cref{pb de Helmholtz variationnel}: \[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  u^{\mathrm{v}} +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} u^{\mathrm{v}} & f_{1} &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	u^{\mathrm{v}} _{|y=0^{+}} & \mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|y=0^{-}} &\text{ on }\Gamma  \\[1mm]
	u^{\mathrm{v}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Sigma_\Omega
\end{array}\right.\]
But $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}}$ also satisfies these equations, so $u^{\mathrm{v}} +\chi_f \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} _{|\Omega }$ satisfies the same problem as $\mathbf{u}_{|\Omega }$, and they both belong to $H^{1} (\Omega )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$. Then by uniqueness in \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}, $u^{\mathrm{v}} +\chi_f \mathbf{u}^{\mathcal{A}} _{|\Omega } =\mathbf{u}_{|\Omega }$, i.e.\ $u^{\mathrm{v}} = \mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|\Omega }$. Thus, $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{v}} _{|\Omega } \in H^{1} (\Omega )$.\\

Let us show by induction on $p$ that for~any $\ell $:
\begin{itemize}[itemindent=5mm]
	\item[(H1)] $u_{p,\ell }$, $U_{p,\ell }$ and $S_{p,\ell }$ exist and are unique,
	\item[(H2)] $\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell }$ and $S^\infty_{p,\ell }$ exist, are the asymptotic expansions w.r.t.\ $\mathbf{r}$ of $\mathbf{u}_{p,\ell }$ and $S_{p,\ell }$ and satisfy \cref{eq: bfuDA SDA},
	\item[(H3)] $\forall j\in \{0,1\}, \forall m\in \mathbb{N},\; \partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} ^{j} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \in  H^{1} _{0} (\Gamma )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$.
\end{itemize}
Since all fields vanish for $p<0$, the initial case is trivial and only the inductive step remains to prove. Let $p\in \mathbb{P}$. Let us assume (H1)--(H3) at any rank $p'<p$ and prove it at rank $p$.\medskip

\underline{Existence and uniqueness of the fields:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \underline{$U_{p,\ell }$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} By~(H3), the $\partial _{y} u_{p',\ell |\Gamma }$ with $p' <p$ are all in $H^{m} _{\mathrm{loc}} (\Gamma )$ for~any $m\in \mathbb{N}$. So the functions $(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell |\Gamma }$ are continuous and Formula \cref{eq: definition des champs de couche} is well-defined at any point of $\Lambda$.
	\item \underline{$u_{p,\ell }$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} By~(H2), $S^\infty_{p',\ell '}$ exists for~any $p'<p$ and $\ell '$, so the coefficients $\sigma _{d'} (S^\infty_{p',\ell '} )$ are well-defined. Thus, \cref{eq: definition des champs lointains} defines well $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$. And we have: $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } ) \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  [\![0,p+d]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}} \neq  \varnothing  \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  d\geqslant -p$, so $(\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } ))_{d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*}$ has finite support. Next, we apply \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}. Its hypotheses are satisfied, because (H3) implies:\vspace{-1mm}
	\[U_{p,\ell |\Gamma } = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{n} (0) \,\in \,H^{1} _{0} (\Gamma )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Gamma ) \,\subset \, H^{1/2} _{00} (\Gamma )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Gamma ) \vspace{-1mm}\] 
	\item \underline{$S_{p,\ell }$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Similarly, (H2) implies that $(\sigma _{d} (S_{p,\ell } ))_{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*}$ is well defined and has finite support. Next, we apply \cref{DA des champs de coin}. We need to check its hypotheses, i.e.\ there exist $f:\Omega _{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and $f :\Pi \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ s.t.\ $\omega ^2 \rho \,S_{p-2,\ell } = F+\chi_\infty f $, $(1+r)F\in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$, $f _{|\Omega } \in \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ and $f _{|\Lambda} \in \mathcal{A}(\Lambda)$. By~(H2), there exists $\psi \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$ s.t.\ $S_{p-2,\ell } =\psi  +o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{-4} )$. So it suffices to set $f :=\omega ^2 \rho  \psi $ and $F:=\omega ^2 \rho  \,S_{p-2,\ell } -\chi_\infty f $.
\end{itemize}\medskip

\underline{Asymptotic expansions:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex}
\begin{itemize}
	\item \underline{$\mathbf{u}_{p,\ell }$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} We use \cref{DA des champs lointains concatenes}. To do so, we must check that there exist $g_{\Gamma } \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Gamma )$ and $g_{\Lambda} \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Lambda)$ s.t.:\vspace{-2mm}
	\[\forall d\in \mathbb{R}, \qquad  \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
		\partial _{Y} ^2  U_{p,\ell } & T_{\leqslant d} (g_{\Lambda} )+o_{\partial } (x^{d} ) &\text{ in }\Lambda\\[0.5mm]
		\partial _{Y} U_{p,\ell |Y=0^{-}} & T_{\leqslant d} (g_{\Gamma } )+o_{\partial } (x^{d} ) &\text{ on }\Gamma 
	\end{array}\right.\]
	Given the definition of $U_{p,\ell }$ in \cref{eq: definition des champs de couche} and using \cref{derivation des DA dans Amaicro}, it suffices to show that, for~any $p'<p$ there exists $h\in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Gamma )$ s.t.: $\forall d\in \mathbb{R},\; \partial _{n} u_{p'\!,\ell |\Gamma } = T_{\leqslant d} (h)+o_{\partial } (x^{d} )$. But it derives from (H2).
	\item \underline{$S_{p,\ell }$\,:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Similarly, we use \cref{DA des champs de coin} thanks to (H2).
\end{itemize}\medskip

\underline{Regularity on $\Gamma $:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $j\in \{0,1\}$ and $m\in \mathbb{N}$. The asymptotic expansion of $\mathbf{u}_{p,\ell }$ implies: $\exists h\in \mathcal{A}(\Gamma ),\allowbreak\;\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} ^{j} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } = h+o_{\partial } (x^{1} )$. So there exists $x_{0} \in \mathbb{R}_+^*$ s.t.\ $\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} ^{j} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } -h$ is $H^{1}$ on $\Gamma \cap \{x<x_{0} \}=(0,x_{0} )\times \{0\}$ and it vanishes at 0. To prove (H3) at rank $p$, it remains to show that $\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} ^{j} u_{p,\ell } \in H^{1} ((\frac{x_{0} }{2} ,\infty )\times \{0\})$. To do so, it suffices to get $u \in H^{m+3} ((\frac{x_{0} }{2} ,\infty )\times (0, \frac{\delta }{2} ))$ with $\delta  :=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}(f),\Gamma )$. But it follows from classical elliptic regularity because on one side $\mu _{0} \Delta u_{p,\ell } +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} u_{p,\ell } =0$ on $(\frac{x_{0} }{4} ,\infty )\times (0,\delta )$, and on the other $u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } =U_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \in H^{m+3} ((\frac{x_{0} }{4} ,\infty )\times \{0\})$ by \cref{eq: definition des champs de couche} and (H3).
<!-- end demo-63 -->
<!-- demo-64: body_md -->
We have $u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant 1} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )_{|\Omega } = o_{\partial } (r^{1} )$, so $\chi_0 \cdot (u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant 1} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )_{|\Omega } )\in H^{1} (\Omega )$. By~\cref{def: sigma dans H1 + khi A}, this implies $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )=\sigma _{d} \big(T_{\leqslant 1} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )_{|\Omega } \big) =\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )$. Likewise for $S_{p,\ell }$.
