Let $(d,d',p)\in (\@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*)^2 \times \mathbb{P}$. Let us show that there exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ that depends only on $(d,d',p,\Theta )$ s.t.: $\forall \ell >n,\; c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } =0$.
\begin{sousdemo}
	\let\n=k 
	By~definition, we have $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ with $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\in \mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$.	So, by construction of $\mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$, there exists $n$ (that may depend on $\mu _{0} ,\mu _{1} ,\rho _{0} ,\rho _{1} ,\omega $) s.t.: $\forall \ell >n,\; c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } =0$. It remains to show that $n$ can be taken independent of $(\mu _{0} ,\mu _{1} ,\rho _{0} ,\rho _{1} ,\omega )$.\\
	By~construction, $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell }$ depends only on the coordinate of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ in $\epsilon^{p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon]$                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
	, which in turn depends on the coordinate of $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ in $\epsilon^{p+d} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon]$.  
	Moreover, we have 
	\[\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) :=\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\n=0} ^{\infty } \bigg(\sum _{R\in \smash\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}} \bigg)^{\!\n} (\phi_{d'} ) =\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\n=0} ^{\infty } \sum _{(R_{1} ,\dots ,R_{k} )\in \smash{\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}^{\n} }} R_{1} \circ \cdots \circ R_{\n} (\phi_{d'} )\]
	with $R_{1} \circ \cdots \circ R_{\n} (\phi_{d'} ) \in \epsilon^{\Sigma _{i} \deg _{\epsilon} \!R_{i} } \mathcal{A}_{d'+\Sigma _{i} \deg _{\mathcal{A}} \!R_{i} }(\Pi )$ for any term in the above sum. Let $f:(x,y)\in \mathbb{R}^2 \mapsto  2x-y$. Since, we~have $f(\deg _{\mathcal{A}} R,\deg _{\epsilon} R )\geqslant 1$ for any $R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}$, there exists $\n_{0} \in \mathbb{N}$ that depends only on $(d,d',p)$ s.t.:
	\[\forall \n>\n_{0} ,\; \forall (R_{i} )\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}^{\n} ,\qquad  f\bigg(d'+\sum _{i=1} ^{\n} \deg _{\mathcal{A}} R_{i} ,\sum _{i=1} ^{\n} \deg _{\epsilon} R_{i} \bigg) > f(d,p+d).\]
	Hence we have
	\[\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) :=\sum _{\n=0} ^{\textcolor{red!93!black}{\n_{0} }} \sum _{(R_{1} ,\dots ,R_{n} )\in \smash{\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}^{\n} }} R_{1} \circ \cdots \circ R_{\n} (\phi_{d'} ).\]
	Now, the construction of the operators $R_{\Delta}$, $R_{\partial_Y^2}$ and $R_{\mathrm{N}}$ in \cref{operateurs R dans Omega,operateurs R} shows that applying any of these operators increases the degree in $\log (\alpha z)$ and $\ln r$ by at most one, so the same holds for the elements of $\@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}$. Moreover, the construction of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ in \cref{def: Eps} shows that, for~any $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$, the degree in $\ln \epsilon$ of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{\pm 1} (f )$ is less or equal to the degree in $\log (\alpha z)$ and $\ln r$ of $f $. Thus, taking $n:=\n_{0}$, we have: $\forall \ell >n,\; c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } =0$.
\end{sousdemo}
The same property is true for the coefficients $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell }$. Finally the result follows by induction from \cref{def: construction des termes}.

\Cref{borne sur l} shows that the degree in $\ln \epsilon$ is finite for~any $p$. So, to prove \cref{ansatz sur Aeps} it suffices to check that, for~any $(p,\ell )$, $\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } \in \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \mathbb{P}-p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )$ and $S^\infty_{p,\ell } \in \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in p-\mathbb{P}} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )$. Let us show it for $\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell }$ only, as it~is similar for $S^\infty_{p,\ell }$. We proceed by induction.\vspace{1mm}
\begin{sousdemo}
	Since all fields vanish for $p<0$, only the inductive step is non-trivial.                                                      
	\cref{eq: bfuDApl} states that
	\[\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } =\sum_{n=0}^\infty  (-k_{0} ^2 \,R_{\Delta})^{n} \bigg(\underbrace{R_{\partial_Y^2}\circ (\partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )(\mathbf{u}^0_{p-2,\ell } ) + {\textstyle \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} }R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p-1,\ell } )}_{:=A} + \!\! \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \!\!\! \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) \,\phi_{d} \bigg). \vspace{-1mm}\]
	Since $\deg  R_{\Delta} \in \mathbb{N}$, it suffices to show that the big brackets belong to $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \mathbb{P}-p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )$. This is true for $A$ using the induction hypothesis and $\deg R_{\partial_Y^2}=0$, $\deg (\partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 )=-2$ and $\deg (R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} )=-1$ (see \cref{operateurs R,operateurs de derivation dans A}). It remains to show that $\forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\!,\; \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}} d\in \mathbb{P}-p$. This last assertion holds because on one hand $\tau\mathbb{N}^*\subset \mathbb{P}-p$, and on the other hand \cref{coincidence des sigma singuliers} and \cref{eq: definition des champs lointains} imply: $\forall d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*,\; \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  \sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } ) \neq 0\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  [\![0,p+d]\!]_{\mathbb{P}\!,\mathbb{N}} \neq  \varnothing  \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  d\in \mathbb{P}-p$.
\end{sousdemo}
Hence the assumptions of \cref{sec: raccordement algebrique}, which were \cref{ansatz: existence de bfuDApl et SDApl,ansatz sur Aeps}, are satisfied. So we can apply \cref{condition de raccord}. \Cref{eq: definition des champs lointains,eq: definition des champs de coin,coincidence des sigma singuliers} show that the matching conditions \cref{eq: condition de raccord 1,eq: condition de raccord 2} are satisfied. Thus \cref{condition de raccord} states that the matching assumption of \cref{def: raccord algebrique} is satisfied.

<!-- demo-67: body_md -->
If $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } \neq 0$, then the sum \cref{eq: def cfinal} contains at least one term, of indexes denoted $(p_{1,} p_{2} ,d_{1} ,d_{2} ,\ell _{1} ,\ell _{2} )$. The conditions on the sum indexes imply
\begin{itemize}
	\item $p=(p_{1} +d)+2n+(p_{2} -d_{2} )-d+d_{2} \in \mathbb{N}+\tau\mathbb{N}^*+\tau\mathbb{N}^* \subset \mathbb{P}+ 2\tau $
	\item and $p+d-d'=(p_{1} +d)+2n+(p_{2} -d')\in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end demo-67 -->
<!-- demo-68: body_md -->
Uniqueness follows from the uniqueness in \cref{cadre fonctionnel des champs lointains}. So it suffices to prove that the far fields satisfy the equations above.\medskip

\underline{Boundary condition:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} By~\cref{eq: definition des champs de couche} and \cref{eq: definition des champs lointains}, we have
\[u_{p,\ell } (x,0) =U_{p,\ell } (x,0) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{n} (0).\]
So we need to calculate $\mathcal{U}_{n} (0)$. Let $\mathrm{U} :(Y,t) \mapsto  \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \mathcal{U}_{n} (Y)\, t^{2n+1}$. The definition of $(\mathcal{U}_{n} )$ (reminded in \cref{eq: construction directe des upl eq1} below) formally implies a differential equation on $\mathrm{U}$ given in \cref{eq: construction directe des upl eq2}.\par
\vspace{2.5mm}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c@{}c@{}}
\begin{minipage}{0.5\linewidth}
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: construction directe des upl eq1}}
\forall n\in \mathbb{N},\ \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mathcal{U}_{n} '' & -\mathcal{U}_{n-1} \\[0.5mm]
	\mathcal{U}_{n} ' (0) & \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \delta _{n,0} \\[0.5mm]
	\mathcal{U}_{n} (-1) & 0 
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
\end{minipage}
&
\begin{minipage}{0.5\linewidth}
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: construction directe des upl eq2}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
\partial _{Y} ^2 \text{U}  & -t^2 \text{U}  \\[0.5mm]
\partial _{Y} \text{U}  _{|Y=0} & \mathcal{U}_{0} '(0)\cdot t = \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} t \\[0.5mm]
\text{U}  _{|Y=-1} & 0 
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
\end{minipage}
\end{tabular}\par
\vspace{2.5mm}
Thus $\mathrm{U} (Y,t) = \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \frac{\sin (t(Y+1))}{\cos (t)} =:f (Y,t)$. This is formal, as we do~not know whether the series $\mathrm{U}$ converges. However, there exists a sequence of polynomial functions $(\Phi _{n} )$ s.t., for~any $(Y,t)\in (-1,0)\times (- \frac{\pi }{2} , \frac{\pi }{2} )$, $f (Y,t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \Phi _{n} (Y)\, t^{2n+1}$ (because $f $ is odd w.r.t.\ $t$). Since $f $ satisfies \cref{eq: construction directe des upl eq2}, $(\Phi _{n} )$ is a solution of \cref{eq: construction directe des upl eq1}. But this solution is unique, so $(\Phi _{n} )=(\mathcal{U}_{n} )$ and $\mathrm{U} =f $. Hence $\forall t\in (- \frac{\pi }{2} , \frac{\pi }{2} ),\; \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \mathcal{U}_{n} (0)\, t^{2n+1} = \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \tan (t)$. That is to say $\forall n\in \mathbb{N},\; \mathcal{U}_{n} (0) = \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{n}$.\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Corner condition:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} For~any $(d,p,\ell )\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*\times \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}$, let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}} ^{\infty } _{d,p,\ell } := \omega ^{p} \mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,p/2}$ if $\frac{p}{2} \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\ell =0$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}} ^{\infty } _{d,p,\ell } :=0$ otherwise. For~any family $(x_{p,\ell } )$, we denote $x_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} :=(x_{p,\ell } )$ the family itself. We also denote $*$ the convolution product w.r.t.\ $(p,\ell )$. Let $d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$. We have
\begin{align*}
	\sigma _{d} (u_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} ) &= \sum _{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sigma _{d_{1}} (S^\infty_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} ) 
	\tag*{by \cref{eq: definition des champs lointains}}\\
	&= \sum _{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sum _{d_{2} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sigma _{d_{1}} ( \widetilde{\mathcal{S}} ^{\infty } _{d_{2} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )*\sigma _{d_{2}} (S_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} ) \tag*{by \cref{eq: expression de Spl avec les correcteurs}} \\
	&= \sum _{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sum _{d_{2} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sigma _{d_{1}} ( \widetilde{\mathcal{S}} ^{\infty } _{d_{2} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )*\sum _{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d'\!,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sigma _{d'} (\mathbf{u}^0_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )
	\tag*{by \cref{eq: definition des champs de coin}}\\
	&= \sum _{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \bigg(\sum _{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sum _{d_{2} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sigma _{d_{1}} ( \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{d_{2} ,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )* c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d'\!,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} \bigg)* \sigma _{d'} (u^0_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )\\
	&= \sum _{d'\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \tilde{c}^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d'\!,\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} * \sigma _{d'} (u^0_{\text{\tiny $\bullet$},\text{\tiny $\bullet$}} )
\end{align*}
with $\displaystyle \tilde{c}^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \sum _{\substack{(p_{1} ,p_{2} ),n\in \mathbb{N}\\ p_{1} +p_{2} +2n=p}} \sum _{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sum _{d_{2} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sum _{\substack{(\ell _{1} ,\ell _{2} )\in \mathbb{N}^2 \\ \ell _{1} +\ell _{2} =\ell }} c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,p_{1} ,\ell _{1} }\cdot \omega ^{2n} \sigma _{d_{1}} (\mathcal{S} ^{\infty } _{d_{2} ,n} )\cdot c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d'\!,p_{2} ,\ell _{2} }$.\\[1mm]
Moreover, for~any $R\in \mathcal{R}^\pm_\epsilon$, we have $\deg _{\epsilon } \!R \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\deg _{\epsilon } \!R \pm  \deg _{\mathcal{A}} \!R\in \mathbb{N}$ (see \cref{fig: degres des elements de Rmacro et Rmicro}). So by~definition of the coefficients $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{\dots }$ and $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{\dots }$:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,p_{1} ,\ell _{1} } \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  p_{1} +d\in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } p_{1} +d_{1} \in \mathbb{N}$,
	\item $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d',p_{2} ,\ell _{2} } \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  p_{2} -d_{2} \in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } p_{2} -d'\in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{itemize}
This implies that $\tilde{c}^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } =c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell }$ for~any $(d,d',p,\ell )$. Thus by \cref{coefs cfinal non nuls}, if $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } \neq 0$ then $p\in \mathbb{P}+ 2\tau$ and $p+d-d'\in \mathbb{N}$. This and the property $(\sigma _{d'} (u_{p',\ell '} ) \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  p'\in \mathbb{P} \text{ and } p'+d'\in \mathbb{P})$ explain the sum indexes of the formula given for $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$ in \cref{construction directe des upl}.
<!-- end demo-68 -->
<!-- demo-69: body_md -->
Let us prove it by induction on $p$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item First, let $p=0$. For~any $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and $d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$, $\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )$ is equal to $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$ by \cref{coincidence des sigma singuliers}, and $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$ vanishes by \cref{construction directe des upl}. Thus \cref{validation construction et DA des champs} shows
	\[\mathbf{u}^0_{0,\ell } =\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}\rangle \bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{0,\ell } ) \,\phi_{d} \bigg).\]
	Hence we have $\mathbf{u}^0_{0,\ell } \in  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{q\in \mathbb{N}+\tau\mathbb{N}^*} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Pi ) = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{q\in \mathbb{P}+\tau} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Pi )$.
	\item Now we assume $p>0$. Let $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and $d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$ be s.t.\ $\sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}_{p,\ell } ) \neq 0$. Then the expression of $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$ given by \cref{construction directe des upl} has at least one non-zero term $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p-p',\ell -\ell '} \cdot \sigma _{d'} (u^0_{p',\ell '} )$. This term satisfies $p+d-(p'+d')\in \mathbb{N}$ by the conditions on the sum indexes, and $d'\in \mathbb{P}-p'+\tau$ by induction hypothesis. Hence we have $d+p=[p+d-(p'+d')] + (p'+d') \in \mathbb{N} + (\mathbb{P}+\tau) \subset  \mathbb{P}+\tau$. Thus, by \cref{validation construction et DA des champs}, we have
	\[\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } = \big\langle  {-k_{0} ^2 \,R_{\Delta}} \big\rangle  \bigg(\displaystyle \underbrace{ {-R_{\partial_Y^2}}\circ (\partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )}_{=:R_{2} } (\mathbf{u}^0_{p-2,\ell } ) + \underbrace{\frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} }_{=:R_{1} } (\mathbf{u}^0_{p-1,\ell } )+ \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ \mathclap{d\in \mathbb{P}-p+\tau}}} \sigma _{d} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) \,\phi_{d} \bigg).\]
	For~any $i\in \{1,2\}$, $R_{i}$ has degree $i$, so $R_{i} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p-i,\ell } )\in  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{q\in \mathbb{P}-i+\tau+i} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Pi )$ by induction hypotheses. Thus $\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } \in \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{q\in \mathbb{P}-p+\tau} \mathcal{A}_{q} (\Pi )$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end demo-69 -->
<!-- demo-70: body_md -->
We will compare $\mathbf{u}^\epsilon_{p,\ell }$ and $S_{p,\ell }$ in $C_\eta$ to their asymptotic expansions at 0, resp $\infty $. Let us denote:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, \mathbf{u}^\epsilon_{p,\ell } $ in $\Pi _{\epsilon }$
	\item $S_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, S_{p,\ell } ({\textstyle \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } })$ in $\Omega _{\epsilon }$
	\item $\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \left\{\begin{array}{@{}l@{}l}
		T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )(x,y) &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
		T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )(x,{\textstyle \frac{y}{\epsilon } }) &\text{ in }\Lambda_{\epsilon } 
	\end{array}\right.$
	\item $S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )({\textstyle \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } })$ in $\Pi _{\epsilon }$.
\end{itemize}
(see \cref{def: troncature de SF} for $T_{\bullet}$). We split the estimate into three parts that we will bound separately:
\[\|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -S_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} \leqslant  \|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} + \|\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} + \|S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} -S_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} .\]
In addition, we will split some of the norms $\|{\dots }\|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}$ into $\|{\dots }\|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)} +\|{\dots }\|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item \underline{$\|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)}$ :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} By~\cref{validation construction et DA des champs}, for~any $(p,\ell )$ we have $u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0 _{p,\ell } )=o_{\partial } (r^{P-p} )$ in $\Omega $ when $r\rightarrow 0$. By~\cref{def: petit o derivable} of $o_{\partial }$, it implies $u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )=O(r^{P-p} )=O(r^{P-p-1} )$ and $\nabla \big[u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(r^{P-p-1} )$ uniformly in $\theta $. Thus:\vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*}
		\|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)}
		&\leqslant  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \|u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \left( \int _{B(0,\eta )} r^{2(P-p-1)} \,\mathrm{d}r\,r\mathrm{d}\theta  \right)^{1/2} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot \eta ^{P-p} \\
		&\lesssim \; \eta ^{P-2} \qquad  \quad  \text{because }  \epsilon ^{p} \lesssim  \eta ^{p} \text{ and } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \lesssim \eta ^{-2}
	\end{align*}
	
	\item \underline{$\|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}$ :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Similarly, $U_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )=o_{\partial } (x^{P-p} )$ in $\Lambda$ when $x\rightarrow \infty $. Thus
	\newlength{\widthGauche} 
	\settowidth{\widthGauche}{$\partial _{x} \big[U_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(x^{P-p-1} )$\,} 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \parbox{\widthGauche}{$U_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )=O(x^{P-p} )$} so $U_{p,\ell } (x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } ) -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )(x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } )=O(x^{P-p} )$
		\item \parbox{\widthGauche}{$\partial _{x} \big[U_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(x^{P-p-1} )$} so $\partial _{x} \big[U_{p,\ell } (x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } ) -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )(x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } )\big] =O(\epsilon ^{-1} x^{P-p-1} )$
		\item \parbox{\widthGauche}{$\partial _{Y} \big[U_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(x^{P-p} )$} so $\partial _{Y} \big[U_{p,\ell } (x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } ) -T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )(x, \frac{y}{\epsilon } )\big]=O(\epsilon ^{-1} x^{P-p} )$ 
	\end{itemize}
	which are all $O(\epsilon ^{-1} x^{P-p-1} )$ (uniformly in $Y$). Hence:\vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*}
		\|\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \epsilon ^{-1} \,\left( \int _{[0,\eta ]\times [-\epsilon ,0]} x^{2(P-p-1)} \,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \right)^{1/2} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \epsilon ^{-1} \cdot \epsilon ^{ \frac{1}{2} } \eta ^{P-p- \frac{1}{2} } \\
		&\lesssim \; \eta ^{P-2} \qquad  \quad  \text{because }  \epsilon =\eta ^2  \text{ and } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \lesssim \eta ^{- \frac{1}{2} }
	\end{align*}
	
	\item \underline{$\|S_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)}$ :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Similarly $S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty _{p,\ell } )=o_{\partial } (r^{p-P} )$ in $\Omega $ when $r\rightarrow \infty $, so $S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )=O(r^{p-P} ) \text{ and } \nabla \!_{(X,Y)}\big[S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(r^{p-P-1} )=O(r^{p-P} )$ uniformly in $\theta $. Since $\nabla \!_{(x,y)} =\epsilon ^{-1} \nabla \!_{(X,Y)}$, we deduce: \vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*}
		\|S_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)}
		&\leqslant  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \Big\|\big[S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big]({\textstyle \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } })\Big\|_{H^{1} (\Omega \cap C_\eta)} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot  \epsilon ^{-1} \left( \int _{\mathbb{R}^2  \setminus B(0,\eta /2)} \left( \frac{r}{\epsilon } \right)^{2(p-P)} \,\mathrm{d}r\,r\mathrm{d}\theta  \right)^{1/2} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot \epsilon ^{P-p-1} \cdot \eta ^{p-P+1} \\
		&\lesssim \; \eta ^{P-2} \qquad  \quad  \text{because }  \epsilon =\eta ^2  \text{ and } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \lesssim \eta ^{-1}
	\end{align*}
	
	\item \underline{$\|S_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}$ :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} $S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty _{p,\ell } )=o_{\partial } (X^{p-P} )$ in $\Lambda$ when $x\rightarrow 0$, so:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )=O(X^{p-P} )$ 
		\item $\partial _{X} \big[S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(X^{p-P-1} )=O(X^{p-P} )$
		\item $\partial _{Y} \big[S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big]=O(X^{p-P} )$ 
	\end{itemize}
	uniformly in $Y$. Hence:\vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*}
		\|S_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}
		&\leqslant  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, \Big\|\big[S_{p,\ell } -T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big]({\textstyle \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } })\Big\|_{H^{1} (\Lambda_{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \epsilon ^{-1} \,\left( \int _{[\eta /2,\infty [\times [-\epsilon ,0]} \left( \frac{x}{\epsilon } \right)^{2(p-P)} \,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \right)^{1/2} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot  \epsilon ^{P-p-1} \cdot \epsilon ^{ \frac{1}{2} } \eta ^{p-P+ \frac{1}{2} } \\
		&\lesssim \; \eta ^{P-2} \qquad  \quad  \text{because }  \epsilon =\eta ^2  \text{ and } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \lesssim \eta ^{- \frac{3}{2} }
	\end{align*}
	
	\item \underline{$\|\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} -S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)}$ :\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex}  
	\def\tilde{\mathbf{u}}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}} 
	\def\tilde{S}{\tilde{S}} 
	Let us show that this norm vanishes. We recall that the physical scaling by $\epsilon $, denoted $h_{\epsilon }$, is defined at page~\pageref{page: def pEps} while the formal scaling by $\epsilon$, denoted $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ in introduced in \cref{def: Eps}. Here $\epsilon$ is the formal indeterminate of $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Pi )$, see \cref{sec: SF 2D de singularites de coin}. In addition, $\mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}$ maps any element of $\mathcal{A}_\epsilon(\Pi )$ with finite support to the element of $\mathcal{A}(\Pi )$ obtained by replacing $\epsilon$ with $\epsilon $, see \cref{eq: def evaleps}. By~\cref{eq: relation Eps pEps}, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )&= \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}\bigg(\sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) \bigg) \\
		\text{and }  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^p \ln^\ell \!\epsilon \cdot h_{\epsilon } ^{-1} \big(T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } )\big) &= \mathrm{eval}_{\epsilon}\circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \bigg(\sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } ) \bigg). \quad 
	\end{align*}
	The above functions are equal to $\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P}$, resp.\ $S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P}$, up to a scaling w.r.t.\ $y$ in the layer. Hence, to prove $\mathbf{u}^0_{\epsilon ,P} =S^\infty_{\epsilon ,P}$, it suffices to show the following equality in $\mathcal{A}^+_\epsilon(\Pi )$:
	\begin{equation}{\label{eq: exactitude du raccord algebrique tronque}}
	\sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\leqslant P-p} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) = \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \bigg(\sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot T_{\geqslant p-P} (S^\infty_{p,\ell } ) \bigg) \end{equation}
	For~any $(p,d)$ let $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d}$ be the coordinate of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon\, \mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell }$ in $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon]$ and $\tilde{S}_{p,d}$ be the one of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{p,\ell } \epsilon^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon\, S^\infty_{p,\ell }$. Moreover, for~any $d$ and $f \in \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon]$, let $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} (f ):= \epsilon^{d} \.\mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} (f )$. By~\cref{def: Eps}, $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon$ maps $\mathcal{A}_{d} (\Pi )[\ln \epsilon]$ to itself. Then we have:
	\def\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Smallleftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Smallrightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\,{\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Leftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\,}                                          
	\begin{align*}
		\text{\cref{eq: exactitude du raccord algebrique tronque}}  &\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Smallleftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Smallrightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\, \sum _{p\leqslant P} \sum _{d\leqslant P-p} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \bigg(\sum _{p\leqslant P} \sum _{d\geqslant p-P} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{S}_{p,d} \bigg)\\
		&\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Smallleftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Smallrightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\, \sum _{p\leqslant P} \sum _{p+d\leqslant P} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \sum _{p\leqslant P} \sum _{p-d\leqslant P} \epsilon^{p-d} \.\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \tilde{S}_{p,d} )\\
		&\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Smallleftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Smallrightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\, \sum _{p\leqslant P} \sum _{p+d\leqslant P} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \sum _{p+d\leqslant P} \sum _{p\leqslant P} \epsilon^{p} \.\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \tilde{S}_{p+d,d} )\\
		&\relax\,\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\mathrel{\mbox{$\Smallleftarrow\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6.5pt}=$}}\hspace{-6pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Smallrightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}\, \forall (p,d) \text{ s.t.\ }  p\leqslant P \text{ and } p+d\leqslant P, \quad  \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \tilde{S}_{p+d,d} ) \stepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq: exactitude du raccord algebrique tronque bis}
	\end{align*}
	because two formal series coincide iff their coordinates coincide one by one.\\
	But \cref{confimation de l'hyp de raccord} shows the matching assumption
	\[ \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{p,d} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \bigg(\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{p,d} \epsilon^{p} \tilde{S}_{p,d} \bigg) =\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}\limits_{p,d} \epsilon^{p} \.\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \tilde{S}_{p+d,d} ),\]
	which is equivalent to: $\forall (p,d),\;\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{p,d} = \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_\epsilon^{-1} ( \tilde{S}_{p+d,d} )$. Thus we get \cref{eq: exactitude du raccord algebrique tronque bis}, and then \cref{eq: exactitude du raccord algebrique tronque}.
	                                                                                                                                                                                                     
\end{enumerate}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-1ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}

Let $r_{\epsilon ,P} := u_{\epsilon ,P} -u_{\epsilon }$. It satisfies, for some functions $f_{\epsilon }$ and $g_{\epsilon }$,
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\operatorname{div}(\mu _{\epsilon } \nabla  r_{\epsilon ,P} ) +\omega ^2 \rho _{\epsilon } r_{\epsilon ,P} & f_{\epsilon } &\text{ in }\Omega _{\epsilon } \\[0.5mm]
	r_{\epsilon ,P} & 0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega _{\epsilon } \\[0.5mm]
	r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{+}} - r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{-}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\}\\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{0} \partial _{y} r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{+}} - \mu _{1} \partial _{y} r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{-}} & g_{\epsilon } &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\}
\end{array}\right.\]
As for \cref{eq: uniforme coercivite}, this problem is well-posed with a stability constant independent of $\epsilon $:
\[\|r_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} \lesssim  \|f_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} + \|g_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\})} .\]
To get our error estimate, it suffices to show that $\|f_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 } +\|g_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 } \lesssim  \epsilon ^{ \frac{P}{2} -2} =\eta ^{P-4}$.

\medskip\underline{Estimate of $\|f_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 }$:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} We denote:
\begin{itemize}
	\item $\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, \mathbf{u}^\epsilon_{p,\ell } $ in $\Pi _{\epsilon }$
	\item $S_{\epsilon ,P} := \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, S_{p,\ell } ({\textstyle \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } })$ in $\Omega _{\epsilon }$
	\item and $\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } :u\mapsto  \operatorname{div}(\mu _{\epsilon } \nabla  u) +\omega ^2 \rho _{\epsilon } u$ the differential operator of Helmholtz's equation.
\end{itemize}
Since $\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } u_{\epsilon } =f$ by~definition of $u_{\epsilon }$, we have \begin{align*}
	f_{\epsilon } &= \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } r_{\epsilon ,P} \\
	&= \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \big((1-\chi _{\eta } )\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} + \chi _{\eta } S_{\epsilon ,P} -u_{\epsilon } \big) \\
	&= \big((1-\chi _{\eta } ) \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -f\big)+ \chi _{\eta } \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } S_{\epsilon ,P} +[\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } ,\chi _{\eta } ](S_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} )
\end{align*}
where $[.,.]$ is the commutator. Let us estimate these terms one by one.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item For $\epsilon $ small enough, $1-\chi _{\eta }$ is equal to 0 in $B(0,\epsilon R_{\mathrm{c}})$ and 1 in $\operatorname{supp}(f)$, so $(1-\chi _{\eta } ) \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P|\Omega } = (1-\chi _{\eta } )(\mu _{0} \Delta +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} ) \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P|\Omega } = (1-\chi _{\eta } )f=f$.\\
	Moreover, using that $\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  U_{p,\ell } = -(\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )U_{p-2,\ell }$ for~any $(p,\ell )$, we get in $\Lambda_{\epsilon } \setminus B(0,\epsilon R_{\mathrm{c}})$:
	\begin{align*}
		\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} &= (\mu _{1} \Delta +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} \\
		&= \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \,(\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} ) U_{p,\ell } \\
		&= \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p+ \frac{1}{2} } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \sum _{n\in \mathbb{N}} \mu _{1} \,(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n+1} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } (x,0) \cdot  \mathcal{U}_{n} ({\textstyle \frac{y}{\epsilon } }) \tag*{by \cref{eq: definition des champs de couche}}
	\end{align*}
	Since $\mathcal{U}_{n} \in L^{\infty } (-1,0)$ for~any $n$ (see \cref{eq: correcteurs de couche}), we deduce:
	\[\|(1-\chi _{\eta } ) \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{L^2 (\Lambda_{\epsilon } )} \lesssim  \!\! \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {(p-1)/2}\rfloor }  \epsilon ^{p+ \frac{1}{2} } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot \big\|(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n+1} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } \big\|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\})} .\]
	Let us show that, for~any $p,\ell ,m$, $\|\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\})} \lesssim  \eta ^{-p-m-1}$ \refstepcounter{equation}\textup{\tagform@{\theequation}}\label{eq: estimation de derivees de upl sur Gamma}.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \Cref{validation construction et DA des champs} states that $\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } \in H^{1} _{0} (\Gamma )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$ for~any $p,\ell ,m$. So $\|\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>1\})} <\infty $.
		\item By~\cref{validation construction et DA des champs}, $\partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } = \partial _{y} T_{\leqslant -p- \frac{1}{2} } (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } ) +o_{\partial } (x^{-p- \frac{3}{2} })$ when $x\rightarrow 0$, and \cref{ansatz sur Aeps} is satisfied, thus $T_{\leqslant -p- \frac{1}{2} } (\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell } )=0$. So: $\forall m\in \mathbb{N},\; \partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } =O(x^{-p- \frac{3}{2} -m})$ when $x\rightarrow 0$. It implies $\|\partial _{x} ^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{\eta /2<x<1\})} \lesssim  \eta ^{-p-m-1}$.
	\end{itemize}
	Hence:\vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*}
		\|(1-\chi _{\eta } ) \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{L^2 (\Lambda_{\epsilon } )}
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p+ \frac{1}{2} } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {(p-1)/2}\rfloor }  \eta ^{-(p-1-2n)-2(n+1)-1} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p+ \frac{1}{2} } \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot \eta ^{-p-2} \\
		&\lesssim  \eta ^{P-4} \qquad  \quad  \text{because }  \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \lesssim \eta ^{-1}
	\end{align*}
	So $\|(1-\chi _{\eta } )\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} -f\|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} \lesssim  \eta ^{P-4}$.
	
	\item For the second term of $f_{\epsilon }$, \cref{eq: definition des champs de coin} implies that $\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } S_{\epsilon ,P} = \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \,\omega ^2 \rho  S_{p,\ell }$. But by \cref{validation construction et DA des champs,ansatz sur Aeps}: $\forall (p,\ell ),\; S_{p,\ell } =O(r^{p} )$. Thus, using that $\rho $ is bounded and $\|S_{p,\ell } ( \frac{x}{\epsilon } , \frac{y}{\epsilon } ) \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap B(0,\eta ))} = \epsilon \, \|S_{p,\ell } \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{1} \cap B(0,\eta /\epsilon ))}$, we get \begin{align*}
		\|\chi _{\eta } \mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } S_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} &\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \cdot \epsilon \, \|S_{p,\ell } \|_{L^2 (\Omega _{1} \cap B(0,\eta /\epsilon ))} \\
		&\lesssim  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-2,P]} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{n_{p}}  \epsilon ^{p+1} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \Big( \frac{\eta }{\epsilon } \Big)^{p+1} \\
		&\lesssim  \eta ^{P-4} \qquad  \qquad  \text{because }  \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \lesssim \eta ^{-3}
	\end{align*}
	
	\item Using that $\|\Delta  \chi _{\eta } \|_{L^2 } +\|\nabla  \chi _{\eta } \|_{L^2 } =O(\eta ^{-2} )$, the last term of $f_{\epsilon }$ satisfies \begin{align*}
		\|[\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon } ,\chi _{\eta } ](S_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} )\|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } )}
		&\lesssim  \|\Delta  \chi _{\eta } \cdot (S_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} ) + 2 \nabla  \chi _{\eta } \cdot \nabla (S_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} )\|_{L^2 (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} \\
		&\lesssim  \eta ^{-2} \|S_{\epsilon ,P} -\mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } \cap C_\eta)} \\
		&\lesssim  \eta ^{P-4} \qquad  \qquad  \text{by \cref{erreur de raccord}.} 
	\end{align*}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-2.3ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
\end{enumerate}

\underline{Estimate of $\|g_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 }$:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Without loss of generality, we assume $\partial _{y} \chi _{\eta |\Gamma } =0$. \cref{eq: definition des champs de coin} implies that $\mu _{0} \partial _{Y} S_{p,\ell |Y=0^{+}} = \mu _{1} \partial _{Y} S_{p,\ell |Y=0^{-}}$ on $\Gamma \cap \{X>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}$ for~any $(p,\ell )$. Thus we have on $\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\}$: \begin{align*}
		g_{\epsilon } &= \mu _{0} \partial _{y} r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{+}} - \mu _{1} \partial _{y} r_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{-}} \\
		&= (1-\chi _{\eta } ) \cdot \big(\mu _{0} \partial _{y} \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{+}} - \mu _{1} \partial _{y} \mathbf{u}_{\epsilon ,P|y=0^{-}} \big) \\
		&= (1-\chi _{\eta } ) \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap (P-1,P]} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \cdot \mu _{0} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |y=0^{+}} 
	\end{align*}
	By~\cref{eq: estimation de derivees de upl sur Gamma}, we have that $\|\partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\})} \lesssim  \eta ^{-p-1}$. So $\|g_{\epsilon } \|_{L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>\eta /2\})} \lesssim  \eta ^{P-4}$ since $\ln ^{\ell } \epsilon \lesssim \eta ^{-2}$.
<!-- end demo-71 -->
<!-- demo-72: body_md -->
\def\Omega^\delta{\Omega^\delta} 
Let $\Omega^\delta:=\Omega  \setminus \overline{B}(0,\delta )$. We will use the symbol $\lesssim $ for inequalities that hold up to a constant independent of $\epsilon $ and $\delta $. To begin, let us show that, for any $(p,\ell )\in \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}$, we have $\|u_{p,\ell } \|_{H^{1} (\Omega^\delta)} \lesssim  \delta ^{-p}$.
\begin{sousdemo}
	\Cref{validation construction et DA des champs} shows $u_{p,\ell } = T_{\leqslant 1} (u^0_{p,\ell } )+o_{\partial } (r)$, so there exists $r_{0} >0$ s.t.\ we have on $\Omega \cap  B(0,r_{0} )$:
	\[|u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant 1} (u^0_{p,\ell } )|\lesssim  r \text{ and } |\nabla  (u_{p,\ell } -T_{\leqslant 1} (u^0_{p,\ell } ))|\lesssim  1.\]
	Moreover \cref{precision de l'ansatz sur uDA} yields $T_{\leqslant 1} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) \in \sum _{d\geqslant -p+\tau} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega ) \subset \sum _{d>-p} \mathcal{A}_{d} (\Omega )$. Thus, we have on $\Omega \cap  B(0,r_{0} )$: $|u_{p,\ell } |\lesssim  r^{-p}$ and $|\nabla  u_{p,\ell } |\lesssim  r^{-p-1}$. Finally, we have $u_{p,\ell } \in H^{1} (\Omega )+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ by construction, so $u_{p,\ell }$ is also $H^{1}$ on $\Omega  \setminus \overline{B}(0,r_{0} )$. The bound on $\|u_{p,\ell } \|_{H^{1} (\Omega^\delta)}$ follows by integration.
\end{sousdemo}
Next, let us use \cref{estimation d'erreur globale} at order $P' := 2P+4$. It gives $\|u_{\epsilon } -u_{\epsilon ,P'} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} =o(\epsilon ^{P} )$, thus:
\begin{align*}
\bigg\|u_{\epsilon } - \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P} \cap [0,P)} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, u_{p,\ell } \bigg\|_{H^{1} (\Omega^\delta)} &\lesssim  \|u_{\epsilon } -u_{\epsilon ,P'} \|_{H^{1} (\Omega _{\epsilon } )} +  \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [P,P']} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon  \,\|u_{p,\ell } \|_{H^{1} (\Omega^\delta)} \\
&\lesssim  \epsilon ^{P} + \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P}\cap [P,P']} \sum _{\ell =0} ^{\ell _{p}} \epsilon ^{p} \.|{\ln \epsilon }|^{\ell _{p}} \cdot  \delta ^{-p} 
\end{align*}
where we denoted $\ell _{p} :=\max \{\ell \in \mathbb{N} \mid u_{p,\ell } \neq 0\}$, similarly to $\ell _{P}$. For~any $a>0$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\epsilon ^{a} |{\ln \epsilon }|^{\ell } \.\delta ^{-a} \lesssim  \epsilon ^{a/2} \.\delta ^{-a} \leqslant  1$ by assumption. Applying this to $a:=p-P$ when $p>P$, we obtain
\[\bigg\|u_{\epsilon } - \sum _{p\in \mathbb{P} \cap [0,P)} \sum _{\ell \in \mathbb{N}} \epsilon ^{p} \ln ^{\ell } \!\epsilon \, u_{p,\ell } \bigg\|_{H^{1} (\Omega^\delta)} \lesssim \; \epsilon ^{P} + \sum _{\ell =0} ^{\ell _{P}} \epsilon ^{P} \.|{\ln \epsilon }|^{\ell _{P}} \delta ^{-P} + \epsilon ^{P} \delta ^{-P} 
\;\lesssim \; \delta ^{-P} \epsilon ^{P} (1+|{\ln \epsilon }|)^{\ell _{P}} .\]
<!-- end demo-72 -->
<!-- demo-73: body_md -->
It suffices to apply \cref{DA de SE avec CL et delta variable} with a truncation order $P'>P$ s.t.\ $\mathbb{P} \cap [0,P')=\mathbb{P} \cap [0,P]$.
<!-- end demo-73 -->
<!-- demo-74: body_md -->
First, let us note that $\lim \mathcal{J}_{a} =(r\mapsto  J_{a} (k_{0} r))$ and $\lim\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{a} = \big[(r,\theta )\mapsto  J_{a} (k_{0} r)\sin (a(\theta -\Theta ))\big]$ satisfy the above equalities.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*')]
    \item It~is well known that $J_{a}$ satisfies $x^2 J_{a} ''(x)+xJ_{a} '(x)+(x^2 -a^2 )J_{a} (x) =0$ (see \cite{Leb72}), which yields $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )[J_{a} (k_{0} r)\sin (a(\theta -\Theta ))] = 0$ thanks to the expression of the laplacian in polar coordinates.
    \item $J_{a} (k_{0} r)\sin (a(\theta -\Theta ))|_{\theta =0} = -\sin (a\Theta ) J_{a} (k_{0} r)$
    \item We have, for~any $z$, $ \frac{2a}{z} J_{a} (z) = J_{a-1} (z)+J_{a+1} (z)$ \cite{Leb72}. Therefore $\partial _{y} [J_{a} (k_{0} r)\sin (a(\theta -\Theta ))]_{|\Gamma } = \frac{1}{r} J_{a} (k_{0} r) \cdot  a \cos (a\Theta )= \frac{k_{0} }{2} \cos (a\Theta ) (J_{a-1} (k_{0} r)+J_{a+1} (k_{0} r))$.
    \item We have $2 J_{a} '(z) = J_{a-1} (z)-J_{a+1} (z)$ \cite{Leb72}. Therefore $\partial _{x} [J_{a} (k_{0} x)] = \frac{k_{0} }{2} (J_{a-1} (k_{0} x)-J_{a+1} (k_{0} x))$.
    \item When $a\in \mathbb{Z}$, \cite{Leb72} states $J_{-a} =(-1)^{a} J_{a}$. Hence $J_{-a} (k_{0} r)= (-1)^{a} J_{a} (k_{0} r)$ and $J_{-a} (k_{0} r)\sin (-a(\theta -\Theta ))= -(-1)^{a} J_{a} (k_{0} r)\sin (a(\theta -\Theta ))$ for~any $(r,\theta )$.
\end{enumerate}
Now $r^{-a+1} J_{a} (k_{0} r)$, $r^{-a+1} J_{a-1} (k_{0} r)$ and $r^{-a+1} J_{a+1} (k_{0} r)$ are power series of $r$ (with infinite convergence radius), so we can identify the powers of $r$ in equalities (1')--(4'). This gives exactly the desired properties.
<!-- end demo-74 -->
<!-- demo-75: body_md -->
By~definition of $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{a}$ and commutation of $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$ with $\sigma _{d}$ (see \cref{def: sigma et fsum commutent dans Aemaicro}), it suffices to prove $\sigma _{d} \big(\Im[(\alpha z)^{a+k} \.\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) = \delta _{d,a} \,\delta _{k,0}$ for~any $k\in \mathbb{N}$. Since $a\not\in -\mathbb{N}^*$, there are three possible cases:
\begin{itemize}
    \item either $a=0$, in which case both $\Im[(\alpha z)^{a+k} \.\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]$ and $\delta _{d,a}$ vanish,
    \item or $a\in \mathbb{N}^*$, which implies $a+k>k$,
    \item or $a\not\in \mathbb{Z}$, which implies $a+k\not\in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{itemize}
In the two last cases, $\Im[(\alpha z)^{a+k} \.\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]$ belongs to the basis of $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$ used to define $\sigma _{d}$, so we have $\sigma _{d} \big(\Im[(\alpha z)^{a+k} \.\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) = \delta _{d,a+2k} \,\delta _{k,0} = \delta _{d,a} \,\delta _{k,0}$  by \cref{def: sigma}.
<!-- end demo-75 -->
<!-- demo-76: body_md -->
\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$. First, note that $\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle (\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} )$ is a solution in $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$ of 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve expression sing homog CL}}
    \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;}ll}
    \Delta u + k_{0} ^2 u &= 0 &\text{ in }\Omega \\
    u &= 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma \\
    \sigma _{q} (u) &= \delta _{q,d} & \ \forall q\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*
    \end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
while $\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}\rangle (\phi_{d} ) \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ solves
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;}ll}
\Delta u + k_{0} ^2 u &= 0 &\text{ in }\Omega \\
\partial _{Y} ^2 u &= 0 &\text{ in }\Lambda\\
\partial _{Y} u_{|Y=0^{-}} &= 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma \\
\sigma _{q} (u) &= \delta _{q,d} & \ \forall q\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*
\end{array}\right.\]
In~particular, $\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}\rangle (\phi_{d} )_{|\Omega } \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$ is also solution of \cref{eq: preuve expression sing homog CL}. Since \cref{eq: preuve expression sing homog CL} has a unique solution in $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$ by \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Omega}, we have $\langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta}\rangle (\phi_{d} )_{|\Omega } = \langle -k_{0} ^2  R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle (\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} )$.\\
Now let us assume $d\not\in -\mathbb{N}^*$. By~\cref{relations sur BesselGamma/Omega,sigma de BesselOmega}, $\Gamma (d+1) ( \frac{2}{k_{0}} )^{d} \mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d}$ is also a solution of \cref{eq: preuve expression sing homog CL}. Therefore it~is equal to $\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle (\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} )$. Moreover we have $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d} \longrightarrow  J_{a} (k_{0} r) \sin (d(\theta -\Theta )) = (-1)^{d\Theta /\pi } J_{a} (k_{0} r) \sin (d\theta )$, which explains the presence of $(-1)^{d\Theta /\pi }$.
<!-- end demo-76 -->
<!-- demo-77: body_md -->
\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us show that, for any $p\in \mathbb{P}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, we have:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: expression uDA avec mcl preuve 1}}
    \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
    (\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )u^0_{p,\ell } & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\
    u^0_{p,\ell } & \sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{n} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u^0_{p-1-2n,\ell } &\text{ on }\Gamma 
    \end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
On the one hand, by~\cref{validation construction et DA des champs,pb de Helmholtz dans A Pi}, we have $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )u^0_{p,\ell } =(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )\mathbf{u}^0_{p,\ell |\Omega } =0$. On the other hand, \cref{construction directe des upl} states that we have
\[u_{p,\ell } = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{n} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2n,\ell } \quad \text{ on }\Gamma .\]
In addition, by \cref{validation construction et DA des champs}, we have $\mathbf{u}_{p',\ell } = T_{\leqslant q} (\mathbf{u}^0_{p',\ell } )+o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{q} )$ for~any $p'\in \mathbb{P}$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}$ ($\mathbf{r}$ is defined in \cref{eq: def bfu bfr} and the truncation operator $T_{\leqslant q}$ in introduced in \cref{def: troncature de SF}). Restricting this to $\Omega $ gives $u_{p',\ell } = T_{\leqslant q} (u^0_{p',\ell } )+o_{\partial } (r^{q} )$. Thus by \cref{derivation des DA dans Amaicro}, we deduce
\[\forall q\in \mathbb{R}, \qquad  u_{p,\ell } = T_{\leqslant q} \bigg(\sum_{n=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{n} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y|\Gamma } u^0_{p-1-2n,\ell } \bigg) +o_{\partial } (r^{q} ).\]
By~uniqueness of the asymptotic expansion in $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$, see \cref{unicité du DA}, we deduce the second line of \cref{eq: expression uDA avec mcl preuve 1}.\smallbreak

\underline{Step 2:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us prove \cref{expression uDA avec mcl} by induction on $p$. We can initialize for $p<0$, which is trivial because by convention $u_{p,\ell }$ vanishes for~any $p<0$. Now let us assume that the property holds for~any $p'<p$ and let us show it at rank $p$. By~\cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Omega}, \cref{eq: expression uDA avec mcl preuve 1} implies
\begin{align*}
u^0_{p,\ell } &= \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle  \Bigg( R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}} \bigg( \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} u^0_{p-1-2m,\ell |\Gamma } \bigg)+ \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\phi^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Omega$}}_{d} \Bigg) \\
&= \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle  \circ  R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}} \bigg( \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} u^0_{p-1-2m,\ell |\Gamma } \bigg) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^0_{d,0}
\end{align*}
Then the induction hypothesis yields:
\begin{align*}
u^0_{p,\ell } &= \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle  \circ  R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}} \bigg(\sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-1-2m-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^0_{d,n|\Gamma } \bigg) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^0_{d,0} \\
&= \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle  \circ  R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}} \bigg(\sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \sum _{N=1} ^{\infty } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-N,\ell } ) \,\Phi^0_{d,N-1-2m|\Gamma } \bigg) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^0_{d,0} \\
& \qquad  \text{with }  N:=1+2m+n\\
&= \sum _{N=1} ^{\infty } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*}  \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-N,\ell } ) \cdot \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle  \circ  R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}} \bigg( \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,N-1-2m|\Gamma } \bigg) + \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^0_{d,0} \\
&= \sum _{N=1} ^{\infty } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}}

Let us prove it by induction on $n$. The case $n=0$ follows from \cref{expression sing homog CL}. Let $n\geqslant 1$ and let us assume that the property is true at the ranks $n'<n$.\\
For~any $(a_{m} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $s\in \{-1,1\}$, we say that $(a_{m} )$ is $s$-symmetric iff: $\forall m\in \mathbb{Z},\; a_{-m} = s\,a_{m}$. Let $\iota : (a_{m} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}} \mapsto  (a_{-m} )$ and $\tau : (a_{m} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}} \mapsto  (a_{m+1} )$. We have $\iota  \tau =\tau ^{-1} \iota $ and $\iota  \tau ^{-1} =\tau  \iota $, so $\iota (\tau +\tau ^{-1} )=(\tau +\tau ^{-1} )\iota $ and $\iota (\tau ^2 -2+\tau ^{-2} )=(\tau ^2 -2+\tau ^{-2} )\iota $. Therefore, for~any $s\in \{-1,1\}$ and $a\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}}$, if $a$ is $s$-symmetric, then so are $(\tau +\tau ^{-1} )(a)$ and $(\tau ^2 -2+\tau ^{-2} )(a)$.\\
Now, \cref{relations sur BesselGamma/Omega} shows that for~any $(a_{m} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ with finite support, we have:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\partial _{y} \big( \sum _{m} a_{m} \mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m} \big)_{|\Gamma } = \sum _{m} b_{m} \mathcal{J}_{d+m}$ with $(b_{m} ) := (-1)^{d\Theta /\pi } \frac{k_{0} }{2} (\tau +\tau ^{-1} )\big((\cos (m\Theta )a_{m} )_{m} \big)$
    \item $\partial _{x} ^2  \big( \sum _{m} a_{m} \mathcal{J}_{d+m} \big) = \sum _{m} b'_{m} \mathcal{J}_{d+m}$ with $(b'_{m} ) := \big( \frac{k_{0} }{2} \big)^2  (\tau -\tau ^{-1} )^2 \big((a_{m} )_{m} \big) = \big( \frac{k_{0} }{2} \big)^2  (\tau ^2 -2+\tau ^{-2} )\big((a_{m} ) \big)$
\end{itemize}
If $(a_{m} )$ is $s$-symmetric, then so are $(b_{m} )$ and $(b'_{m} )$. Thus, the induction hypothesis shows that there exists a $(-1)^{n-1}$-symmetric sequence $(c_{n,m} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\mathbb{Z}}$, independent of $d$, s.t.\ \[\Phi^0_{d,n|\Gamma } := \sum_{j=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{j} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{j} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2j|\Gamma } = \Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} (-1)^{d\Theta /\pi } \sum _{m} c_{n,m} \,\mathcal{J}_{d+m} .\]
Moreover,                                                       
the support of $(c_{n,m} )$ is included in $[\![-n,n]\!]$ (because applying $\partial _{y|\Gamma }$, resp.\ $\partial _{x} ^2 $, makes the support 1 step larger, resp.\ 2) and we have: $\forall m,\; c_{n,m} \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  m\equiv n\,[2]$ (because applying $\partial _{y|\Gamma }$ moves the support from even integers to odd and conversely, while $\partial _{x} ^2 $ does~not change the parity of the support). Now let
\[a_{n,0} :=0 \quad  \text{ and } \quad  \forall m\in \mathbb{Z}^*,\,\ a_{n,m} :=- \frac{c_{n,m} }{\sin (m\Theta )} \qquad  \text{ and } \qquad  f := \Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} \sum _{m=-n} ^{n} a_{n,m} \,\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m} .\]
If $\tau \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ or $(\tau \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ and } n\in [\![0,b-1]\!])$, then none of the above sinus vanishes, so $(a_{n,m} )$ and $f $ are well defined. Let us show that $f =\Phi^0_{d,n}$. First, note that $c_{n,0} =0$ (by $(-1)$-symmetry of $(c_{m} )$ if $n$ is even, and by oddness of the support of $(c_{n,m} )$ if $n$ is odd). In addition, $(a_{n,m} )$ is independent of $d$ and $(-1)^{n}$-symmetric and $(\forall m,\; a_{n,m} \neq 0 \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}}  m\equiv n\,[2])$ by properties of $(c_{n,m} )$. Finally, let us show that $f $ is a solution of \cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n>0}, the problem solved by $\Phi^0_{d,n}$. Since this problem has a unique solution (see \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Omega}), it will imply that $\Phi^0_{d,n} =f $.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )f  = 0$ by \cref{relations sur BesselGamma/Omega}.
    \item \Cref{relations sur BesselGamma/Omega} shows $f _{|\Gamma } = \Gamma (d+1) ( \frac{2}{k_{0}} )^{d} \sum\limits _{m=-n} ^{n} a_{n,m} \,\sin ((d+m)\Theta )\,\mathcal{J}_{d+m}$. So, using $c_{n,0} =0$, we deduce
    \[f _{|\Gamma } = \Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} (-1)^{d\Theta /\pi } \sum\limits _{m\in \mathbb{Z}} c_{n,m} \,\mathcal{J}_{d+m} =\Phi^0_{d,n|\Gamma } .\]
    \item Let $q\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$ and let us show that $\sigma _{q} (f ) = 0$. $f $ is a linear combination of the $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m}$ with $m\in [\![-n,n]\!] \setminus \{0\}$ (because $a_{n,0} =0$), so it suffices to prove $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m} )=0$ for~any such $m$. Let $m\in [\![-n,n]\!] \setminus \{0\}$. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $\tau \not\in \mathbb{Q}$, then $\mathbb{Z}\cap \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}=\{0\}$, so $m\not\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$.
        \item Otherwise, $\tau \in \mathbb{Q}$ and it~is easy to check that $\mathbb{Z}\cap \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}} =b\mathbb{Z}$. By~assumption $n<b$, so $0<|m|<b$, which yields $m\not\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$.
    \end{itemize}
    In both cases, we obtain $m\not\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$, which yields $d+m\not\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$. Now if $d+m \not\in -\mathbb{N}^*$, we can apply \cref{sigma de BesselOmega}, which gives $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{J}_{d+m} )=0$ because $d+m\neq q$. Otherwise, $d+m\in -\mathbb{N}^*$, so $\mathcal{J}_{d+m} =(-1)^{d+m} \mathcal{J}_{-d-m}$ by \cref{relations sur BesselGamma/Omega}, item 5. In this case, \cref{sigma de BesselOmega} gives again $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{J}_{-d-m} )=0$.
\end{itemize}

Let $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$ and $\Phi _{\epsilon } :=\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle (\phi_{d} )$. For~any $R\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}$, we have $\deg _{\epsilon } R \in \mathbb{N}$, so there exists $(\Phi _{n} )_{n} \in \mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )^{\mathbb{N}}$ s.t.\ $\Phi _{\epsilon } = \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0} ^{\infty } \epsilon ^{n} \.\Phi _{n}$. By~\cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro}, we have 
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \Phi _{\epsilon } +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \Phi _{\epsilon } & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \Phi _{\epsilon } + \epsilon ^2 (\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\Phi _{\epsilon } &0&\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} \Phi _{\epsilon } - \epsilon \,\mu _{0} \,\partial _{y|y=0^{+}} \Phi _{\epsilon } &0 &\text{ on }\Gamma 
\end{array}\right.\]
Identifying each power of $\epsilon $ gives for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$ (denoting $\Phi _{-1} :=\Phi _{-2} :=0$):
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\mu _{0} \Delta  \Phi _{n} +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} \Phi _{n} & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y} ^2  \Phi _{n} & -(\mu _{1} \partial _{x} ^2 +\omega ^2 \rho _{1} )\Phi _{n-2} &\text{ in }\Lambda \\[0.5mm]
	\mu _{1} \partial _{Y|Y=0^{-}} \Phi _{n} & \mu _{0} \,\partial _{y|y=0^{+}} \Phi _{n-1} &\text{ on }\Gamma 
\end{array}\right.\]
This system has the same structure as the equations satisfied by $\mathbf{u}_{n,0}$. Thus, similarly to \cref{expression de Upl} one can express $\Phi _{n|\Lambda}$ in terms of the $\partial _{y} \Phi _{n'|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}}$ with $n'<n$ and deduce:
\[\forall n\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad  \Phi _{n} = \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|y=0^{+}} \quad \text{ on }\Gamma .\]
Moreover, by \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro}, we have $\sigma _{q} (\Phi _{n} )=\sigma _{q,n,0} (\Phi _{\epsilon } ) =\delta _{d,q} \,\delta _{n,0}$ for~any $q\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$. Hence, $(\Phi _{n|\Omega } )$ satisfies the same equations \cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n=0}--\cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n>0} as $(\Phi^0_{d,n} )$. Since these equations have unique solution according to \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans A Omega}, we deduce: $\forall n\in \mathbb{N},\; \Phi _{n} =\Phi^0_{d,n}$.

\underline{Step 1:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us first treat $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell }$. We have $c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$, where $ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) =\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{n=0} ^{\infty } \epsilon ^{n} \Phi^0_{d',n} $ by~\cref{expression de Rmacro phi avec les mcl}. Thanks to \cref{expression sing heterog CL} and the fact that $\tau$ is irrational, we know that, for~any $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $\Phi^0_{d',n}$ is a linear combination of the $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{a}$, $a\in \mathbb{R}$. So, by \cref{eq: def BesselOmega}, $\Phi^0_{d',n}$ is a formal series of terms of the form $c\,\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]$ with $c\in \mathbb{C}$. In other words, $\Phi^0_{d',n}$ does~not involve $\log (\alpha z)$. Now, by~definition of $\mathcal{H}_\epsilon$ in \cref{def: Eps}, we have for~any $(q,k,n)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}^2 $:
\[\mathcal{H}_\epsilon\big(\epsilon ^{n} \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) = \epsilon ^{n+q+k} \,\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ].\]
By~definition of $\sigma _{d,p,\ell }$ in \cref{def: sigma sur Aeps}, this implies:
\[\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ \mathcal{H}_\epsilon\big(\epsilon ^{n} \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) = \delta _{d,q+k} \,\delta _{p,n+q+k} \,\delta _{\ell ,0} \cdot \sigma _{d} \big(\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) = \sigma _{d,p-d,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{n} \Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]\big) .\]
As we have seen, $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ is a formal series of terms of the form $c\,\epsilon ^{n} \.\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} ]$ with $c\in \mathbb{C}$. So we deduce
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel preuve EpsRmacro}}
    c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) =\sigma _{d,p-d,\ell } \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) = \sigma _{d,p-d,\ell } (\phi_{d'} ) =\delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p,d} \,\delta _{\ell ,0}
\end{equation}
because we have $\sigma _{d} \circ R=0$ for any $R\in \{R_{\Delta},R_{\mathrm{N}},R_{\partial_Y^2}\}$, so $\sigma _{d,p-d,\ell } \circ R' =0$ for~any $R'\in \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}$, see \cref{operateurs R,eq: def Rmaicro}.\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 2:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us treat $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } :=\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \circ  \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$. By~\cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel preuve EpsRmacro}, we have $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{-d'} \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big)= \sigma _{d,p+d',\ell } \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) = \delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p+d',0} \,\delta _{\ell ,0} = \delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p,-d} \,\delta _{\ell ,0}$. Hence, if we show
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel eq Aemacro}}
    \mathcal{H}_\epsilon^{-1} \circ  \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) = \epsilon ^{-d'} \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ),
\end{equation}
then this implies $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d',p,\ell } = \delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p,-d} \,\delta _{\ell ,0}$ and concludes this step. Proving \cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel eq Aemacro} is equivalent to proving
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel eq Aemicro}}
    \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ) = \epsilon ^{-d'} \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} ).
\end{equation}
Let us apply \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro} (which shows the uniqueness of the solution of a scaled Helmholtz problem in $\mathcal{A}^-_\epsilon(\Pi )$).
\begin{itemize}
    \item First, both sides of \cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel eq Aemicro} belong to $\mathcal{A}^-_\epsilon(\Pi )$ by \cref{Rmaicro defini et inversible dans Aemaicro,rq: def Eps}.
    \item Secondly, $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ is a solution of the scaled Helmholtz problem \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis} by \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro}. In addition, $\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ is solution of the non-scaled Helmholtz problem \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro bis} by \cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemacro}, so $\epsilon ^{-d'} \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )$ is also solution of \cref{eq: pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro bis} by \cref{action de Eps sur Helmholtz dans Aemaicro}.
    \item Thirdly, for any $(d,p,\ell ) \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\times \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}$, we have $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big) =\sigma _{d,p,\ell } (\phi_{d'} ) =\delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p,0} \, \delta _{\ell ,0}$ (similarly to \cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel preuve EpsRmacro}) and $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{-d'} \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big) =\delta _{d,d'} \,\delta _{p,0} \, \delta _{\ell ,0}$ by \cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel preuve EpsRmacro}. So $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^-_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big)$ and $\sigma _{d,p,\ell } \big(\epsilon ^{-d'} \mathcal{H}_\epsilon \circ \langle \@ifnextchar^{(\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon)}{\mathcal{R}^+_\epsilon}\rangle  (\phi_{d'} )\big)$ coincide.
\end{itemize}
By~\cref{pb de Helmholtz dans Aemicro}, we deduce that \cref{eq: valeur de cfinal cas irrationnel eq Aemicro} holds.\medskip\smallskip

\underline{Step 3:\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex\vrule width 0pt depth 0.25ex} Let us treat $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell }$. We recall that it~is defined only for $d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$ and that:
\[c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \! \sum _{\substack{(p_{1} ,p_{2} )\in (\mathbb{N}-d)\times (\mathbb{N}+d')\\ n\in \mathbb{N},\, p_{1} +p_{2} +2n=p}}
\ \sum _{\substack{d_{1} \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ p_{1} +d_{1} \in \mathbb{N}}} \ \sum _{\substack{d_{2} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*\\ p_{2} -d_{2} \in \mathbb{N}}}
\ \sum _{\substack{(\ell _{1} ,\ell _{2} )\in \mathbb{N}^2 \\ \ell _{1} +\ell _{2} =\ell }}
c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,p_{1} ,\ell _{1} }\cdot \omega ^{2n} \sigma _{d_{1}} (\mathcal{S} ^{\infty } _{d_{2} ,n} )\cdot c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d'\!,p_{2} ,\ell _{2} } .\]
By~steps~1 and 2, the only non-zero terms are obtained for $d_{1} =d$, $d_{2} =d'$, $p_{1} =-d$, $p_{2} =d'$, $\ell _{1} =\ell _{2} =0$ and $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow S}_{d,d_{1} ,p_{1} ,\ell _{1} }=c^{S\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d_{2} ,d'\!,p_{2} ,\ell _{2} }=1$. One can deduce that if $d'<0$ then $c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } =0$, and otherwise the formula reduces to:
\[c^{\mathbf{u}\leftarrow\mathbf{u}}_{d,d',p,\ell } := \delta _{\ell ,0} \! \sum _{\substack{n\in \mathbb{N},\, d'-d+2n=p}}\omega ^{2n} \sigma _{d} (\mathcal{S} ^{\infty } _{d',n} ).\]
Finally, this allows to prove the last result of the lemma.
