<!-- demo-100: body_md -->
Let us prove it by induction on $n$. First, let $n=0$. We have $\|\phi_{d} \|=1$ so, seeing $\phi_{d}$ as an element of $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$, we get $\|\phi_{d} \|_{s} = s^{-d} \,\gamma (d)$. In addition, it~is easy to check that $\phi_{d} \in \@AMprecis0,d\@AMprecis(\Omega )$, which yields $\Phi^0_{d,n} :=\langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle (\phi_{d} ) \in \@AMprecisn,d\@AMprecis(\Omega )$ by \cref{action des op R sur AMprecis}. Then, since $\@AMprecis0,d\@AMprecis(\Omega ) \subset  \@AMprecis0,\delta \@AMprecis(\Omega )$ and $s>s_{\delta ,n}$, \cref{norme de <Rlap>} shows that we have $\|\Phi^0_{d,0} \|_{s} \leqslant  C_{\delta } \;s^{-d} \;\gamma (d)$. Besides, note that 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: comparaison normes sur series formelles}}
    \forall \delta '\in \mathbb{R},\ \forall n'\in \mathbb{N},\ \forall s_{1} \leqslant s_{2} ,\ \forall \Phi \in \@AMprecisn',\delta '\@AMprecis(\Omega ),\quad  \|\Phi \|_{s_{2}} \leqslant  \left( \frac{s_{1} }{s_{2}} \right)^{\delta '} \|\Phi \|_{s_{1}} = C_{\delta ',s_{1} ,s_{2} } \,\|\Phi \|_{s_{1}} .
\end{equation}
This implies that $\|\Phi^0_{d,0} \|_{s'} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,s,s'} \;s^{-d} \;\gamma (d)$.\medskip\smallskip

Secondly, let $n>0$. Let us assume that the property holds for~any $n'<n$ and let us show it at rank $n$. By~induction hypothesis, we have $\Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} \in \@AMprecisn-1-2m,d-n+1+2m\@AMprecis(\Omega )$ for~any $m\in \mathbb{N}$. Hence, using \cref{action des op R sur AMprecis}, we get successively that $\partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \in \@AMprecisn-2m,d-n+2m\@AMprecis(\Omega ) \subset  \@AMprecisn,d-n+2m\@AMprecis(\Omega )$ and $(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \in  \@AMprecisn,d-n\@AMprecis(\Omega )$, and finally by \cref{def: mcl}:
\[\Phi^0_{d,n} := \langle -k_{0} ^2 R_{\Delta}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\rangle \circ R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\bigg( \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \bigg) \in  \@AMprecisn,d-n\@AMprecis(\Omega ).\]
                                                                                                           
Now it only remains to show that $\|\Phi^0_{d,n} \|_{s'} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \;s^{-d} \;\gamma (d)$. Let $M_{n} :=\max \{m\in \mathbb{N} \mid n-1-2m\geqslant 0\}$. Using first \cref{norme de <Rlap>} and $\Phi^0_{d,n} \in \@AMprecisn,d-n\@AMprecis(\Omega ) \subset  \@AMprecisn,\delta -n\@AMprecis(\Omega )$, and then \cref{norme des op R sur series formelles}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \|\Phi^0_{d,n} \|_{s'} &\leqslant  C_{\delta -n,n,s'} \,\bigg\|R_{\mathrm{D}}^{\raisebox{1pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle \Omega$}}\bigg( \sum _{m=0} ^{M_{n}} \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \bigg) \bigg\|_{s'} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s'} \sum _{m=0} ^{M_{n}} \big\| (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \big\|_{s'} 
\end{align*}
\newcommand{s^*}[1]{s_{#1}} 
For~any $k\in [\![0,n]\!]$, let $s^*{k} := \frac{(k+1)s' + (n-k)s}{n+1}$. We have $s<s^*{0} <s^*{1} <\cdots <s^*{n} =s'$. \Cref{norme des op R sur series formelles} and \cref{eq: comparaison normes sur series formelles} imply, for~any $k\in [\![2,n]\!]$ and $\Phi \in \@AMprecisn,\delta -n\@AMprecis(\Gamma )$,
\begin{align*}
    \big\|(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 ) \Phi  \big\|_{s^*{k}} 
    &\leqslant  \big\|\partial _{x} ^2  \Phi  \big\|_{s^*{k}} + |k_{1} ^2 |\,\|\Phi \|_{s^*{k}} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s^*{k},s^*{k-1}} \,\|\partial _{x} \Phi \|_{s^*{k-1}} + |k_{1} ^2 |\,\|\Phi \|_{s^*{k}} \\[1ex]
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s^*{k},s^*{k-1}} \,C_{\delta ,n,s^*{k-1},s^*{k-2}}\,\|\Phi \|_{s^*{k-2}} +C_{\delta ,n,s^*{k},s^*{k-2}} \,\|\Phi \|_{s^*{k-2}} \\[1ex]
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \,\|\Phi \|_{s^*{k-2}} .
\end{align*}
Therefore\vspace{-1ex}
\begin{align*}
    \|\Phi^0_{d,n} \|_{s'} &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \sum _{m=0} ^{M_{n}} \big\|\partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \big\|_{s^*{n-2m}} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \sum _{m=0} ^{M_{n}} \big\|\Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} \big\|_{s^*{n-1-2m}} \qquad  \text{ by \cref{norme des op R sur series formelles}}  \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \;s^{-d} \;\gamma (d)
\end{align*}
where we used in the last line the induction hypothesis, which applies because $s^*{n-1-2m} \geqslant s^*{0} >s$ and $s > s_{\delta ,n} \geqslant  s_{\delta ,n-1-2m}$.
<!-- end demo-100 -->
<!-- demo-101: body_md -->
It suffices to prove the case $\tau\not\in \mathbb{Q}$. According to \cref{expression sing heterog CL}, in this case there exists $(a_{n,m} )_{m} \in \mathbb{C}^{[\![-n,n]\!]}$, that does~not depend on $d$, s.t.\ for~any $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*$, we have
\[\Phi^0_{d,n} = \Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} \sum _{m=-n} ^{n} a_{n,m} \, \mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m} .\]
It~is easy to check that $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{q'} \in \@AMprecis0,q\@AMprecis(\Omega )$ for~any reals $q<q'$ in $\mathbb{Z}+\@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}$, which yields $\Phi^0_{d,n} \in \@AMprecisn,d-n\@AMprecis(\Omega )$. Thus, it only remains to show the following:
\[\forall m\in [\![-n,n]\!], \qquad  A_{m} := \bigg\|\Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} \mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m} \bigg\|_{s'} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \cdot s^{-d} \cdot \gamma (d).\]
By~definition of $\|.\|_{s}$ and $\mathcal{J}^\Omega_{d+m}$, we have 
\begin{align*}
    A_{m} &= |\Gamma (d+1)| \left| \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right|^{d}  \sum_{k=0}^\infty  s'^{-d-m-2k} \gamma (d+m+2k) \bigg\| \frac{(-1)^{k} }{k!\, \Gamma (d+m+k+1)} \left( \frac{k_{0} }{2} \right)^{d+m+2k} \Im[(\alpha z)^{d+m+k} \overline{\alpha z}^{k} ] \bigg\| \\
    &= s'^{-d} \,\gamma (d) \sum_{k=0}^\infty  \underbrace{ \frac{\gamma (d+m+2k)}{\gamma (d)} \cdot  \left| \frac{\Gamma (d+1)}{k!\, \Gamma (d+m+k+1)} \right| }_{=:B_{m,k}} \,\cdot \; \left| \frac{k_{0} }{2s'} \right|^{m+2k}
    \stepcounter{equation}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq: preuve norme SF de mcl cas irrationnel 1}
\end{align*}
Let us estimate $B_{m,k}$. It involves two ratios of factorial-like expressions. Similarly to $j \mapsto  \frac{(j+\ell )!}{j!}$ with $j,\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ for instance, we will see that these ratios have a polynomial behavior. We will then bound this behavior by an exponential, as it~is sufficient for us. However that behavior holds only when the arguments of $\gamma $ and $\Gamma $ are greater than 1, as $\gamma $ is constant on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\Gamma $ has poles in $(-\infty ,1]$. Hence we will need to treat separately the first terms.\\
To begin, note that, for~any $x\in [1,\infty )$ and $k\in \mathbb{N}$, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve norme SF de mcl cas irrationnel 2}}
    \frac{\gamma (x+2k)}{\gamma (x)} = \sqrt{ \frac{\Gamma (x+2k)}{\Gamma (x)} } = \prod _{j=0} ^{2k-1} \sqrt{x+j} = \prod _{j=0} ^{k-1} \sqrt{(x+2j)(x+2j+1)} \leqslant  \prod _{j=0} ^{k-1} (x+2j+1)
\end{equation}
Let us also show that, for~any $a,b\in \mathbb{Z}$ and $s''>1$,
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: majoration de quotients des fonctions gamma}}
    \frac{\gamma (d+b)}{\gamma (d+a)} \leqslant C_{\delta ,a,b,s''} \,s''^{d} \qquad  \text{ and } \qquad  \left| \frac{\Gamma (d+b)}{\Gamma (d+a)} \right| \leqslant C_{\delta ,a,b,s''} \,s''^{d} .
\end{equation}
\begin{itemize}
    \item When $d+a\geqslant 1$ and $d+b\geqslant 1$, \cref{eq: preuve norme SF de mcl cas irrationnel 2} and the properties of the Gamma function imply that there exists $P_{a,b} \in \mathbb{R}[X]$ s.t $\frac{\gamma (d+b)}{\gamma (d+a)}$ and $\frac{\Gamma (d+b)}{\Gamma (d+a)}$ are bounded by $P_{a,b} (d)$. Then, there exists $C_{\delta ,a,b,s''}$ s.t.\ $P_{a,b} (d) \leqslant  C_{\delta ,a,b,s''} \,s''^{d}$ for~any $d\geqslant \delta $.
    \item Otherwise, we have $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\cap [\delta ,1-\min (a,b)]$ by assumption on $d$, so $d$ can take only a finite number of values.
\end{itemize}
Now, let $\ell :=\max (0,\lceil {-\delta +n+1}\rceil )\in \mathbb{N}$. With this choice of $\ell $, we have, for~any $k>\ell $, $d+m+\ell \geqslant 1$ so the arguments of $\gamma $ and $\Gamma $ in the expression of $B_{m,k}$ are greater than 1. Thus, for~any $k>\ell $, we can write:
\begin{alignat*}{2}
    B_{m,k} &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \,s''^{d} \,\frac{\gamma (d+m+2k)}{\gamma (d+m+2\ell )} \, \left| \frac{\Gamma (d+m+\ell +1)}{\Gamma (d+m+k+1)} \right| \, \frac{1}{k!} &\ & \text{ by \cref{eq: majoration de quotients des fonctions gamma}} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \,s''^{d} \times \prod _{j=0} ^{k-\ell -1} (d+m+2\ell +2j+1) \times \prod _{j=\ell } ^{k-1}  \frac{1}{d+m+j} \times \frac{1}{\ell !} \prod _{j=\ell } ^{k-1}  \frac{1}{j+1} && \text{ by \cref{eq: preuve norme SF de mcl cas irrationnel 2}} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \,s''^{d} \times \prod _{j=\ell } ^{k-1} (d+m+2j+1) \times \frac{1}{\ell !} \prod _{j=\ell } ^{k-1}  \frac{1}{d+m+2j} && \text{ using ``$ab\geqslant a+b-1$''}  \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \,s''^{d} \times \prod _{j=\ell } ^{k-1} \left( 1+ \frac{1}{d+m+2j} \right) && \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \,s''^{d} \, 2^{k}                                        
\end{alignat*}
In addition, \cref{eq: majoration de quotients des fonctions gamma} shows that, for~any $k\in [\![0,\ell ]\!]$, we have $B_{m,k} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} s''^{d}$. Combining the estimates of $B_{m,k}$ with \cref{eq: preuve norme SF de mcl cas irrationnel 1}, we obtain:
\[A_{m} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s''} \left( \frac{s''}{s'} \right)^{d} \gamma (d) \left( 1+ \left| \frac{k_{0} }{2s} \right|^{m} \sum _{k>\ell } \left| \frac{k_{0} }{\sqrt{2} s'} \right|^{2k} \right) 
\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s,s''} \left( \frac{s''}{s'} \right)^{d} \gamma (d) \]
provided that $s'> \frac{|k_{0} |}{\sqrt{2}} +1$. Finally, it suffices to take $s'' := \frac{s'}{s}$ and to define $s_{\delta ,n} := \frac{|k_{0} |}{\sqrt{2}} +1 +n$ for this angle $\Theta $ (the ``$+\,n$'' just makes the sequence increasing).
<!-- end demo-101 -->
<!-- demo-102: body_md -->
By~definition of $\|.\|$ on $\@AOprecisd,n,\delta \@AOprecis$, and similarly to the proof of \cref{action des op R sur A precis,norme naive des op R}, it suffices to consider the case where $f =\Im[(\alpha z)^{q} \,\overline{\alpha z}^{k} \log ^{j} \!(\alpha z)]$ with $ (q,k,j)\in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{N}^2 $, $q+k=d$ and $q-k\geqslant \delta $. For~any $r>0$ and $\theta \in [0,\Theta ]$, we have
\begin{align*}
    |f (r,\theta )| &= \big|r^{d} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} (\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} \big]\big|\\
    &\leqslant  C_{j} \,r^{d} \,(1+|{\ln r}|)^{j} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{n} \,r^{d} \,(1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \|f \|
\end{align*}
because $j\leqslant 2n+1$ (by~definition of $\@AOprecisd,n,\delta \@AOprecis$) and $\|f \|=1$. Similarly, we have
\begin{align*}
    |\partial _{r} f (r,\theta )| &= \big|r^{d-1} \Im\big[e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \big[d(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} +j(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j-1} \big]\big]\big|\\
    &\leqslant  C_{n} \,r^{d-1} (1+|d|)\,(1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \|f \|
\end{align*}
with $|d|\leqslant \max (|\delta |,d)$ because $d\geqslant \delta $ (see \cref{rq: lien entre d q k delta}). Likewise:
\begin{align*}
    |r^{-1} \partial _{\theta } f (r,\theta )| &= \big|r^{d-1} \Im\big[\mathrm{i}e^{\mathrm{i}(q-k)(\theta -\Theta )} \big[(q-k)(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j} +j(\ln r+\mathrm{i}(\theta -\Theta ))^{j-1} \big]\big]\big|\\
    &\leqslant  C_{n} \,r^{d-1} (1+|q-k|)\,(1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \|f \|
\end{align*}
with $|q-k|\leqslant \max (|\delta |,d)$ because $q-k\leqslant q+k=d$ and $q-k\geqslant \delta $.
<!-- end demo-102 -->
<!-- demo-103: body_md -->
Let $s'>s>0$, $q'\geqslant q\geqslant \delta $, $0<r\leqslant R$ and $\theta \in [0,\Theta ]$. Let us denote $(f _{d} )_{d\in \mathbb{R}} :=\Phi $ the family of the components of $\Phi $. Since $\Phi \in \@AMprecisn,\delta \@AMprecis(\Omega )$, we have $f _{d} \in \@AOprecisd,n,\delta \@AOprecis$ for~any $d\in \mathbb{R}$. Using \cref{majoration des fonctions de A par leur norme}, we get
\begin{align*}
    |f _{d} (r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  f _{d} (r,\theta )| &\leqslant  C_{n} \,(1+\max (|\delta |,d)) \,r^{d} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \,\|f _{d} \| \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s'/s} \,\Big( \frac{s'r}{s} \Big)^{d} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \,\|f _{d} \| \\[.5ex]
    &= C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'r)^{d} }{\gamma (d)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \cdot  s^{-d} \|f _{d} \|_{\gamma } .
\end{align*}
Let us show that, for~any $d\geqslant q$ we have $\displaystyle \frac{(s'r)^{d} }{\gamma (d)} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,R,s'} \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)}$. There are three possible cases.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Let us assume $d\geqslant q\geqslant 1$. Let $I:=[1,\infty )$ and
    \[g_{r} :d\in I\longmapsto \ln \!\left( \frac{(s'r)^{d} }{\gamma (d)} \right) = d\ln (s'r)- \frac{1}{2} \ln  \Gamma (d).\]
    \defm_r{m_r} 
    Since $d\mapsto \ln \Gamma (d)$ is convex on $I$, $g_{r}$ is concave. In addition, $g_{r} (d)\rightarrow -\infty $ as $d\rightarrow \infty $. Therefore, there exits $m_r \in I$ (that may be equal to 1) s.t.\ $g_{r}$ increases on $[1,m_r]$ and decreases on $[m_r,\infty )$. If $q\geqslant m_r$, then we directly have $(s'r)^{d} /\gamma (d) \leqslant  (s'r)^{q} /\gamma (q)$. Now, let us assume $q<m_r$. In this case, we have $m_r>1$, so
    \[0=g'(m_r)=\ln (s'r)- \frac{1}{2} \psi (m_r) \qquad  \text{which implies}  \qquad  m_r = \psi ^{-1} ( 2\ln (s'r))\]
    because the Digamma function $\psi $ is an increasing bijection from $I$ to $[\psi (1),\infty )$. 
                                                                              
    In~particular, this yields $\ln (s'r)= \frac{1}{2} \psi (m_r)\geqslant  \frac{1}{2} \psi (1)$. Hence
    \begin{align*}
        g_{r} (d)-g_{r} (q) &\leqslant  \max _{I} g_{r} - \min _{[1,m_r]} g_{r} \\
        &= g_{r} (m_r) - g_{r} (1)\\
        &= \psi ^{-1} ( 2\ln (s'r)) \ln (s'r)- \frac{1}{2} \ln  \Gamma (m_r) - \ln (s'r) \\
        &\leqslant  \psi ^{-1} ( 2\ln (s'R)) \ln (s'R)- \frac{1}{2} \ln (\min \nolimits_{I} \Gamma  )- \frac{1}{2} \psi (1) \\
        &= C_{R,s'}
    \end{align*}
    This proves $\frac{(s'r)^{d} }{\gamma (d)} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,R,s'} \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)}$ in this case.
    \item Let us assume $q\leqslant d\leqslant 1$. We have $(s'r)^{d} = (s'r)^{d-q} (s'r)^{q} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,R,s'} (s'r)^{q}$ with $C_{\delta ,R,s'} := 1$ if $s'r<1$ and $C_{\delta ,R,s'} := (s'R)^{1-\delta }$ otherwise (because $q\geqslant \delta $). In addition, we have $\gamma (q)=\gamma (d)=1$ by~definition of $\gamma $.
    \item Otherwise, we have $q\leqslant 1\leqslant d$. Using the two previous cases, we obtain $\frac{(s'r)^{d} }{\gamma (d)} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,R,s'} \frac{(s'r)^{1} }{\gamma (1)} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,R,s'} \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)}$.
\end{enumerate}
Therefore we have shown that, for~any $d\geqslant q$, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve cvg des SF de norme finie 1}}
    |f _{d} (r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  f _{d} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \cdot  s^{-d} \|f _{d} \|_{\gamma } .
\end{equation}
Let $r_{1} \in (0,R)$ and $D:=\{\mathbf{x}\in \Omega  \mid |\mathbf{x}|\in [r_{1} ,R]\}$. If $q\geqslant 0$, \cref{eq: preuve cvg des SF de norme finie 1} implies
\begin{align*}
    \|f _{d} \|_{L^{\infty } (D)} + r_{1} \|\nabla  f _{d} \|_{L^{\infty } (D)} 
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'R)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln R}|)^{2n+1} \cdot  s^{-d} \|f _{d} \|_{\gamma } 
                                                                                                       
\end{align*}
where we used $q\geqslant 0$ to bound $r^{q}$ by $R^{q}$. By~sum, we get
\begin{align*}
    \smash{\sum _{\substack{d\in \operatorname{supp}(\Phi )\\d\geqslant q}}} \|f _{d} \|_{L^{\infty } (D)} + r_{1} \|\nabla  f _{d} \|_{L^{\infty } (D)} &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,r_{1} ,R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'R)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, \sum _{d\geqslant q} s^{-d} \|f _{d} \|_{\gamma } \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,r_{1} ,R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'R)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, \|\Phi \|_{s} \ \underset{q\rightarrow \infty }{\longrightarrow} \; 0 
\end{align*}
This proves that $T_{<q} (\Phi )$ and its~derivatives converge on $D$ as $q\rightarrow \infty $. This convergence is uniform, which ensures that the limit $f$ is $\mathcal{C}^{1}$ and $\nabla  [\lim _{q\rightarrow \infty } T_{<q} (\Phi )] = \lim _{q\rightarrow \infty } \nabla  T_{<q} (\Phi )$. Finally, using
\[\rho_{q'} := f - T_{<q'} (\Phi ) = \sum _{d\in \operatorname{supp}(\Phi ),\,d\geqslant q'} f _{d}\]
and summing \cref{eq: preuve cvg des SF de norme finie 1} over $d\geqslant q'$ proves \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des SF de norme finie}.
<!-- end demo-103 -->
<!-- demo-104: body_md -->
\defs^*{s^*}
Let $s^* := (s+s')/2$. Combining \cref{norme SF de mcl cas general,cvg des SF de norme finie} directly shows that there exists $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \in \mathcal{C}^{1} (\overline{\Omega } \setminus \{0\},\mathbb{C})$ s.t.\ $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )\rightarrow \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ and $\nabla \big[T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )\big]\rightarrow \nabla \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ pointwise. It also gives:
\begin{align*}
    |\rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s^*,s'} \, \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \, \|\Phi^0_{d,n} \|_{s^*} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s^*,s'} \, \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \times C_{\delta ,n,s,s^*} \, s^{-d} \,\gamma (d)
\end{align*}
which proves \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl}. Next, let us prove that the convergence is uniform on every ball $B(0,R )$. For~any $0<r\leqslant R$, \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl} yields
\begin{align*}
    |\rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| + |\nabla  \rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| 
    &\leqslant  \frac{C_{R} }{r} \cdot  \big( |\rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| \big) \\
    &\leqslant  \frac{C_{R} }{r} \cdot  C_{\textcolor{red!93!black}{d},n,s,s'} \, \frac{(s'r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{d,n,s,s',R} \, \frac{(s'r)^{q-2} }{\gamma (q)} \cdot  r \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{d,n,s,s',R} \, \frac{(s'R)^{q-2} }{\gamma (q)} \quad\qquad  \text{if }  q\geqslant 2
\end{align*}
because $r\mapsto  r\,(1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} $ is bounded on $(0,R]$.  Therefore the convergence of $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )$ and its gradient is uniform on $(\overline{\Omega } \setminus \{0\}) \cap  B(0,R )$ for~any $R>0$. Thus it remains only to prove \cref{eq: pb verifie par lim mcl}.\smallskip\medskip

Since $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )\rightarrow \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ locally uniformly, this convergence also holds in $\mathcal{D}'(\Omega )$. Moreover, we have $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )\Phi^0_{d,n} =0$ by \cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n=0}--\cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n>0}, and $\Delta $ has degrees $-2$ as an operator on $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$. Therefore we have
\[0= T_{<q} \big[(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )\Phi^0_{d,n} \big] = \Delta \big[T_{<q+2} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )\big]+k_{0} ^2  T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) \xrightarrow[{q\rightarrow \infty }]{} \Delta \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} + k_{0} ^2  \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}\]
with convergence in $\mathcal{D}'(\Omega )$. Hence, $(\Delta + k_{0} ^2 )\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} =0$.\\
Similarly, for~any $m\in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\partial _{y} \big[T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} )\big]_{|\Gamma } \rightarrow  \partial _{y} \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma }$ locally uniformly, so also in $\mathcal{D}'(\Gamma )$. Thus, using that $\partial _{x}$ and $\partial _{y|\Gamma ,y=0^{+}} $ have degre $-1$ as operators in the spaces $\mathcal{A}$, we get for~any $j\in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve pb verifie par lim mcl}}
    T_{<q} \big[ \partial _{x} ^{j} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} \big]_{|\Gamma } 
    = \partial _{x} ^{j} \partial _{y} \big[T_{<q+j+1} (\Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} )\big]_{|\Gamma } \xrightarrow[q\rightarrow \infty ]{\mathcal{D}'(\Gamma )} \partial _{x} ^{j} \partial _{y} \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma }
\end{equation}
Finally, we deduce the following limit calculation in $\mathcal{D}'(\Gamma )$ (note that the sums in $m$ below have only a~finite number of non zero terms)
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n-1-2m} 
    &= \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  \lim _{q\rightarrow \infty } T_{<q} \big[ (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m} \big] \qquad  \text{by \cref{eq: preuve pb verifie par lim mcl}} \\[-0.5ex]
    &= \lim _{q\rightarrow \infty } T_{<q} \bigg( \sum_{m=0}^\infty  \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} \,T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1}  ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^0_{d,n-1-2m|\Gamma } \bigg) \\
    &= \lim _{q\rightarrow \infty } T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) 
    \setbox0=\hbox{by \cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n=0}--\cref{eq: pb verifie par mcl qd n>0}}
    \hspace{73mm-\wd0} \box0  \\
    &= \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n|\Gamma }    
\end{align*}
Note that here $T_{<q}$ denotes a truncation operator $\mathcal{A}^+\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Gamma )\rightarrow \mathcal{A}(\Gamma )$ whereas $T_{m}$ denotes the Taylor coefficients of the tangent.
<!-- end demo-104 -->
<!-- demo-105: body_md -->
Let us apply \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl} with $q:=d-n$. In this case, we have $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )=0$ so the remainder of $\Phi^0_{d,n}$ at order $q$ is equal to $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$. Hence, \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl} states
\[|\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} (r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{\delta ',n,R,s',s''} \, \frac{\gamma (d)}{\gamma (d-n)} \,s'^{-d} \,(s'' r)^{d-n} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \]
with $\delta ':=\delta -n$ (so that $q\geqslant \delta '$), $s':=s_{\delta ,n}+1$ and $s'':=s' \sqrt{s}$. Thanks to \cref{eq: majoration de quotients des fonctions gamma} from the proof of \cref{norme SF de mcl cas general}, we have $\frac{\gamma (d)}{\gamma (d-n)} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,s} \sqrt{s}^{d}$. Thus we get
\[|\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} (r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,R,s} \,\Big( \sqrt{s} \, \frac{s''r}{s'} \Big)^{d-n} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,R,s} \,(s r)^{d-n} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} .\]
<!-- end demo-105 -->
<!-- demo-106: body_md -->
By~elliptic regularity, $u$ is $H^2 $ in $\Omega \cap \{r_{1} <r<r_{2} \}$ for~any $0<r_{1} <r_{2} <R$. Using Fourier series w.r.t.\ $\theta $, it~is easy to deduce that 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 1}}
    u(r,\theta ) = \sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} c_{d} (r) \sin (d\theta )
\end{equation}
where $c_{d} (r) := \frac{2}{\Theta } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } u(r,\theta )\,\sin (d\theta )\,\mathrm{d}\theta $, with convergence in $L^2 (\Omega \cap \partial B(0,r))$ for~any $r\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. This implies
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 2}}
    \forall r\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}}),\qquad  \|u(r,\cdot )\|_{L^2 (0,\Theta )} ^2  = \frac{\Theta }{2} \sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} |c_{d} (r)|^2 .
\end{equation}
Integrating this relation over $r$ shows that $c_{d} \in L^2 (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ for~any $d$. Hence \cref{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 1} holds also with convergence in $L^2 (\Omega \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}}))$, so in $\mathcal{D}'(\Omega \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}}))$ as well. Thus we can differentiate \cref{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 1}. Using the equation $\Delta u + k_{0} ^2 u = 0$, we get $(r \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r} )^2 c_{d} + (k_{0} ^2 r^2 -d^2 )c_{d} =0$. The properties of the Bessel functions then show that there exist coefficients $a_{d} \in \mathbb{C}$
\[\forall d\in {\textstyle\tau\mathbb{N}^*},\ \forall r\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}}), \quad  c_{d} (r) = a_{d} Z_{d} (k_{0} r) + a_{-d} Z_{-d} (k_{0} r) \quad \text{ with }\quad  Z_{d} := \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
    Y_{d} & \text{if } d\in -\mathbb{N}^* \\
    J_{d} & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.\]
Now, according to \cite{Leb72}, for~any $q\in \mathbb{R}^*$, there exists $b_{q} \in \mathbb{C}^*$ s.t.\ $Z_{q} (r) \sim b_{q} r^{q}$ when $q\rightarrow \infty $. Since $d\geqslant \tau> \frac{1}{2}$ and $c_{d} \in L^2 $, it yields $a_{-d} =0$ for~any $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$.                                                        
Using \cref{expression sing homog CL}, we deduce
\[u(r,\theta ) = \sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} a_{d} \,J_{d} (k_{0} r) \sin (d\theta ) = \sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} s_{d} \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} (r,\theta ) \qquad \text{ with }\qquad  s_{d} := a_{d} \frac{(-1)^{d\pi /\Theta } }{\Gamma (d+1)} \left( \frac{k_{0} }{2} \right)^{d} \]
Moreover, \cite[p.\,44]{Wat95} states:
\[\forall q\in \mathbb{R}_+,\ \forall z\in \mathbb{C}^*, \qquad  \left| \Gamma (q+1) \left( \frac{2}{z} \right)^{q} J_{q} (z) - 1 \right| \leqslant  \exp \!\left( \frac{|z|^2 }{4(q+1)} \right) -1.\]
Let $C>0$ be s.t.\ $\exp (t^2 /4)-1< \frac{1}{2}$ for~any $t\in [0,C]$. We deduce:
                                                                                                                                                                                                              
\[\forall q\in \mathbb{R}_+,\ \forall z\in \mathbb{C}^*, \quad  \ |z|< C \sqrt{q+1} \ \mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\mathrel{\mbox{$=\hspace{-6.5pt}\Rightarrow$}}$}}$}}$}} \ \left| \Gamma (q+1) \left( \frac{2}{z} \right)^{q} J_{q} (z) \right| \geqslant  \frac{1}{2} .\]
Combined with \cref{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 2}, it yields, for~any $r\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ and $d_{0} \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$ s.t.\ $C\sqrt{d_{0} +1} >|k_{0} |R_{\mathrm{s}}$,
\[\infty > \sum _{d\geqslant d_{0}} |c_{d} (r)|^2  = \sum _{d\geqslant d_{0}} |a_{d} J_{d} (k_{0} r)|^2  = \sum _{d\geqslant d_{0}} \bigg|s_{d} \,\Gamma (d+1) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{d} J_{d} (k_{0} r)\bigg|^2  \geqslant  \sum _{d\geqslant d_{0}} \frac{1}{4} |s_{d} r^{d} |^2  \]
so $s_{d} = O(r^{-d} )$ when $d\rightarrow \infty $. Finally it implies that \cref{eq: preuve majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog 1} converges locally uniformly.
<!-- end demo-106 -->
<!-- demo-107: body_md -->
Let $0<r_{1} \leqslant r_{2} \leqslant R<R_{\mathrm{s}}$ and $D':=\overline{\Omega }\cap  \{r_{1} \leqslant r\leqslant r_{2} \}$. Let $s>1$ (to be chosen later). \Cref{estimation des mcl} implies that, for~any $d\geqslant \delta $, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: convergence des series de mcl preuve 1}}
    \|\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \|_{L^{\infty } (D')} + r_{1} \|\nabla  \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \|_{L^{\infty } (D')} \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,R,s} \,(s r_{2} )^{d-n\,} (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln r_{2} }|)^{2n+1} 
\end{equation}
provide that $d-n\geqslant 0$ or $r_{1} =r_{2}$, so that $r^{d-n}$ can be bounded by $r_{2} ^{d-n}$ for~any $r\in [r_{1} ,r_{2} ]$. Let $R'=(R+R_{\mathrm{s}})/2$ and $N\in \mathbb{N}$. By~assumption on $(s_{d} )$, we have $|s_{d} |\leqslant C_{(s_{d} ),R'} \,R'^{-d}$ for~any $d$. Moreover, let us assume that either $(N+1)\tau-n\geqslant 0$ or $r_{1} =r_{2}$. Using \cref{eq: convergence des series de mcl preuve 1} and the bound on $|s_{d} |$, we get:
\begin{multline*}
    A:= \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ \mathclap{d\geqslant (N+1)\tau}}} |s_{d} |\,\Big(\|\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \|_{L^{\infty } (D')} + r_{1} \|\nabla  \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \|_{L^{\infty } (D')} \Big) \\[-4ex]
    \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,(s_{d} ),R,R_{\mathrm{s}},s} \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ \mathclap{d\geqslant (N+1)\tau}}} \Big(\frac{s r_{2} }{R'} \Big)^{d-n} \, (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln r_{2} }|)^{2n+1} .
\end{multline*}
Let us take $s:= \frac{R'}{R''}$ with $R'' := \frac{R+R'}{2} \in (R,R')$. Thus $s>1$ and $\displaystyle \frac{s r_{2} }{R'} = \frac{r_{2} }{R''} \leqslant  \frac{R}{R''} <1$. Therefore, we~have:\vspace{-0.5ex}
\begin{multline*}
    A \leqslant  C_{\delta ,n,(s_{d} ),R,R_{\mathrm{s}}} \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ \mathclap{d\geqslant (N+1)\tau}}} \left( \frac{r_{2} }{R''} \right)^{d-n} \, (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln r_{2} }|)^{2n+1} \\[-4ex]
    \begin{array}{r}
        =\displaystyle C_{\delta ,n,(s_{d} ),R,R_{\mathrm{s}}} \; \frac{1}{1-\left( \frac{r_{2} }{R''} \right)^{\pi/\Theta} }  \left( \frac{r_{2} }{R''} \right)^{(N+1)\tau-n} \, (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln r_{2} }|)^{2n+1} \\[3ex]
        \leqslant \displaystyle C_{\delta ,n,(s_{d} ),R,R_{\mathrm{s}}} \left( \frac{r_{2} }{R} \right)^{(N+1)\tau-n} \, (1+|{\ln r_{1} }|+|{\ln r_{2} }|)^{2n+1}  .
    \end{array}
\end{multline*}
Taking $r_{1} <r_{2}$ and $N\rightarrow \infty $, this proves that $f_{N}$ and $\nabla  f_{N}$ converge uniformly on $D'$. Hence there exists $f\in C^{1} (D)$ s.t.\ $f_{N} \rightarrow f$ and $\nabla  f_{N} \rightarrow \nabla  f$ pointwise on $D$. Finally, taking $r_{1} :=r_{2} :=r$ and any $N\in \mathbb{N}$, we obtain \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des series de mcl}.
<!-- end demo-107 -->
<!-- demo-108: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{preuve: decompo modale des CL} 
Let us prove the result by induction of $p\in \mathbb{P}$. First, let $p=0$. The only $\ell $ s.t.\ $u_{0,\ell } \neq 0$ is $\ell =0$. Since $u_{0,0} \in H^{1} (\Omega )$, \cref{majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog} shows that there exists $(s_{d} )\in \mathbb{C}^{\tau\mathbb{N}^*}$ s.t.\ $s_{d} =O(R^{-d} )$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ and $u_{0,0} =\sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} s_{d} \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0}$ in $B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ with locally uniform convergence. \Cref{convergence des series de mcl} then states that
\[\widetilde{\rho }_{N} := u_{0,0} - \sum _{\substack{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*\\ d\leqslant N\tau}} s_{d} \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} \quad  \mathrm{satisfies} \quad  
| \widetilde{\rho }_{N} (r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \widetilde{\rho }_{N} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{(s_{d} ),R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{(N+1)\tau} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2} .\]
Let us show that $s_{d} =\sigma _{d} (u^0_{0,0} )$ for~any $d$.
\begin{sousdemo}
    Let us assume by contradiction that there exists $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$ s.t.\ $s_{d} \neq \sigma _{d} (u^0_{0,0} )$. Let us assume that $d$ is minimal for this property. On the one hand, the estimate on $\widetilde{\rho }_{N}$ implies that 
    \[u_{0,0} = \sum _{d'\leqslant d} s_{d'} \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d',0} + o(r^{d} ) \quad  \text{when }  r\rightarrow 0.\]
    On the other hand, we have
    \begin{alignjustif}
        u_{0,0} &= T_{\leqslant d} (u^0_{0,0} )+o(r^{d} )\\
        &= \sum _{d'\leqslant d} \sigma _{d'} (u^0_{0,0} ) \cdot T_{\leqslant d} (\Phi^0_{d',0} ) + o(r^{d} ) & \text{by \cref{expression uDA avec mcl}} \\
        &= \sum _{d'\leqslant d} \sigma _{d'} (u^0_{0,0} ) \cdot \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d',0} + o(r^{d} )
    \end{alignjustif}
    because $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d',0} = T_{\leqslant d} (\Phi^0_{d',0} )+o(r^{d} )$ by \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl}. Subtracting the two gives $(s_{d} -\sigma _{d} (u^0_{0,0} )) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} = o(r^{d} )$ when $r\rightarrow 0$. Now, \cref{expression sing homog CL} states that $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0}$ is proportional to $J_{d} (k_{0} r) \sin (d\theta )$, which is~not a $o(r^{d} )$ by the properties of Bessel functions, see \cite{Leb72}. Hence $s_{d} -\sigma _{d} (u^0_{0,0} ) =0$, which is absurd.
\end{sousdemo}
This concludes the initialization.\medskip\smallskip

Let $p\in \mathbb{P} \setminus \{0\}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$. Let us assume that the property holds for~any $p'<p$ and let us show it at rank $p$. By~induction hypothesis, we have $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) =O(R^{-d} )$ for~any $n\geqslant 1$ and $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. So~\cref{convergence des series de mcl} states that the following series, denoted $f$, converges locally uniformly in $\overline{\Omega }\cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$: 
\[f := \sum _{n=\textcolor{red!93!black}{1}} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ d\geqslant -p+n}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} .\]
Note that $n\geqslant 1$ in the above sum, which means that $f$ takes into account the contributions of the previous far fields, but not the $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )$. Since $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} =0$ for~any $(d,n)$, we have $(\Delta +k_{0} ^2 )f=0$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\Omega )$. In addition, we have on $\Gamma $:
\begin{alignat*}{2}
    f &= \sum _{n=1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{d\geqslant -p+n} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\sum _{m=0} ^{\lfloor {(n-1)/2}\rfloor } \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n-1-2m} &\ \ & \text{by \cref{convergence des mcl}} \\ 
    &= \sum _{m=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Bigg( \sum _{n=2m+1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{d\geqslant -p+n} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \, \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n-1-2m} \Bigg) && \text{with convergence in }  \mathcal{D}'(\Gamma )\\
    &= \sum _{m=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} \Bigg( \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p-1-2m}\rfloor } \!\!\! \sum _{d\geqslant -p+1+2m+n} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-1-2m-n,\ell } ) \, \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} \Bigg) && \text{with }  n \leadsto  n-1-2m \\
    &= \sum _{m=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} T_{m} \cdot  (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{m} \partial _{y} u_{p-1-2m,\ell } && \text{by induction hypothesis} 
\end{alignat*}
Hence $f$ satisfies the same Dirichlet condition on $\Gamma $ as $u_{p,\ell }$ (see \cref{construction directe des upl}). Now, let
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: decompo modale des CL preuve def g}}
    g:=u_{p,\ell } -f-\sum\limits _{d\in \textcolor{red!93!black}{-\tau\mathbb{N}^*},d\geqslant -p} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} .
\end{equation}
We will show that $g$ is equal to $\sum _{d\in \textcolor{red!93!black}{\tau\mathbb{N}^*}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0}$. Using the problems satisfied by $u_{p,\ell }$ (see \cref{construction directe des upl}), $f$ (thanks to the previous steps) and $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0}$ (see \cref{convergence des mcl}), we~obtain
\[\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
    (\Delta  + k_{0} ^2 )g & 0 &\text{ in }\Omega \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}}) \\
    g & 0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega  \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}})  
\end{array}\right.\]
\defR'{R'} 
In order to apply \cref{majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog} to $g$, let us show that $g\in H^{1} (\Omega \cap B(0,R'))$ for~any $R' \in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. Note that the sum over $d$ in \cref{eq: decompo modale des CL preuve def g} is the singular behavior at 0 of $u_{p,\ell } -f$ and subtracting it was necessary to make $g$ regular at the corner.
\begin{sousdemo}
    Let $R' \in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. By~construction of $u_{p,\ell }$ in \cref{def: construction des termes}, we know that $u_{p,\ell }$ is in $H^{1} (\Omega  \setminus B(0,\eta ))$ for~any $\eta >0$. By~\cref{convergence des mcl}, the same holds for~any $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$. \Cref{convergence des series de mcl} also shows that $f \in H^{1} (\Omega  \cap B(0,R') \setminus B(0,\eta ))$ for~any $\eta >0$. Therefore it only remains to prove that $g$ is $H^{1}$ in the vicinity of the corner.\\
    Let $N\in \mathbb{N}$. \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des series de mcl} gives 
    \begin{align}
        \Bigg|f(r,\theta ) - \sum _{n=1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant N\tau}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} (r,\theta )\Bigg| 
        &\,\leqslant \, C_{\delta ,n,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{(N+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor } (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \nonumber\\[-3ex]
        & \underset{r\rightarrow 0}{\longrightarrow} 0 \label{eq: decompo modale des mcl preuve ineg f}
    \end{align}
    provided that $N$ is chosen s.t.\ $(N+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor  >0$. Using $u_{p,\ell } =T_{\leqslant 0} (u^0_{p,\ell } )+o(1)$ and $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} = T_{\leqslant 0} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )+o(1)$ when $r\rightarrow 0$, we deduce 
    \[g = T_{\leqslant 0} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) - \sum _{n=1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant N\tau}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } )\, T_{\leqslant 0} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) \,-\! \sum\limits _{d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*,d\geqslant -p} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\, T_{\leqslant 0} (\Phi^0_{d,0} ) +o(1).\]
    This is valid because we are summing a finite number of $o(1)$ (this is why approximating $f$ by a finite sum using \cref{eq: decompo modale des mcl preuve ineg f} was necessary). This implies
    \begin{align*}
        g &= T_{\leqslant 0} \bigg( u^0_{p,\ell } - \sum _{n=1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{-p+n\leqslant d\leqslant N\tau} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } )\, \Phi^0_{d,n} \,-\! \sum\limits _{d\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*,d\geqslant -p} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\, \Phi^0_{d,0} \bigg) +o(1)\\
        &= T_{\leqslant 0} \bigg( \sum _{n=1} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\geqslant (N+1)\tau} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } )\, \Phi^0_{d,n} \,+\! \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\, \Phi^0_{d,0} \bigg) +o(1)
    \end{align*}
    thanks to \cref{expression uDA avec mcl}. Next, for~any $d\geqslant (N+1)\tau$ and $n\geqslant 1$, we~have $d-n\geqslant (N+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor  >0$, so $T_{\leqslant 0} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) =0$. We also have $T_{\leqslant 0} (\Phi^0_{d,0} )=0$ for~any $d>0$. Therefore, we~get $g=o(1)$. Similarly, one can show $\nabla g =o(1)$. This proves that $g$ is $H^{1}$ in the vicinity of the corner.
\end{sousdemo}
Similarly to the case $p=0$ (replacing $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ by $R'$), one can deduce using \cref{majoration coefs decompo modale Helmholtz homog} that $g=\sum _{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0}$ and $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )=O(R^{-d} )$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. This proves \cref{eq: decompo modale des CL}. Then, \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg decompo modale des CL} follows from \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg des series de mcl}. Finally, the convergence is uniform on $\Omega  \cap B(0,R)$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ because, with $R'':= (R+R_{\mathrm{s}})/2$, \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg decompo modale des CL} implies
\[|\rho _{N} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R''} \right)^{(N+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor } (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} 
\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R''} \right)^{N\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor } 
\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{R}{R''} \right)^{N\tau}.\]
<!-- end demo-108 -->
<!-- demo-109: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{preuve: decompo en modes tronques des CL} 
\defm_{N,q}{m_{N,q}} 
\defM{M} 
\def\rho_{N,q}{\rho_{N,q}} 
                 
                 
\deff_{M,q}{f_{M,q}} 
\defg_{M,q}{g_{M,q}} 
\defg_{M,-p}{g_{M,-p}} 
\def -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau { -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau } 
To begin, note that, if $N$ is very large compared to $q$, then a lot of the truncated modes $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )$ in \cref{eq: reste decompo en modes tronques des CL} vanish. Let us eliminate them by defining $M$ as the greatest integer in $(-\infty ,N]$ s.t.\ $M\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor \leqslant q$. Thus, for~any $n\in [\![0,\lfloor {p}\rfloor ]\!]$ and $d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap  (M\tau,N\tau]$ (which may be empty) we have $d-n\geqslant (M+1)\tau -\lfloor {p}\rfloor >q$, so $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) = 0$. Therefore, we have
\[\rho_{N,q} = \rho _{M,q} .\]
Next, we can decompose the remainder as
\[\rho_{N,q} \;=\; \underbrace{u_{p,\ell } - \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \! \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\  -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau }} \!\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} }_{\textstyle :=f_{M,q}} \;-\, \underbrace{\sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \! \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\  -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau }} \! \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\rho_{d,n,q} }_{\textstyle :=g_{M,q}} .\]
with $\rho_{d,n,q} := \Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} -T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )$ for~any $(d,n,q)$. Let $m_{N,q}:=\min ((N+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor ,q)$. We will bound $f_{M,q}$ and $g_{M,q}$ by $C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{m_{N,q}} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1}$ to prove the theorem.\\
Let us start with $f_{M,q}$. Thanks to \cref{decompo modale des CL}, we know that
\[|f_{M,q}(r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  f_{M,q}(r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{(M+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor } (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} .\]
In addition, by~definition of $M$, we have either $M=N$ or $(M+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor >q$. In both cases, $(M+1)\tau-\lfloor {p}\rfloor \geqslant  m_{N,q}$, which gives the desired bound on $f_{M,q}$.\smallskip\medskip

Let us now treat $g_{M,q}$ and prove more precisely
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: preuve decompo en modes tronques des CL} }
    |g_{M,q}(r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  g_{M,q}(r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{q} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} .
\end{equation}
Let $\delta :=-p$ and $s'>s>s_{\delta ,n}$ (to be choosen later). Let $R' :=(R+R_{\mathrm{s}})/2$. By~\cref{decompo modale des CL,eq: vitesse de cvg des mcl}, we have for~any $q\geqslant \delta $
\begin{align*}
    |g_{M,q} (r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  g_{M,q} (r,\theta )|
    &\leqslant  \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau } |\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } )| \cdot \big(|\rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )| + r|\nabla  \rho_{d,n,q}(r,\theta )|\big) \\
    &\leqslant  \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau } C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \, R'^{-d} \cdot  C_{\delta ,n,s,s'} \, \frac{\gamma (d)}{\gamma (q)} \,s^{-d} \,(s' r)^{q} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2n+1} \\
    &\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s' r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau } (s R')^{-d} \, \gamma (d) \\
    &\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s,s'} \, \frac{(s' r)^{q} }{\gamma (q)} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} \underbrace{\sum _{-p\leqslant d\leqslant M\tau} (s R')^{-d} \, \gamma (d) }_{:=A}
\end{align*}
Let us show that $\displaystyle A\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s,s''} \left( \frac{s''}{s R'}\right)^{q} \gamma (q)$ for~any $q\geqslant -p$ and $s''>1$.
\begin{sousdemo}
    \defq'{q'} 
    The proof of \cref{cvg des SF de norme finie} showed that we have  \[\frac{(s R')^{q'} }{\gamma (q')} \leqslant  C_{p,R',s} \frac{(s R')^{d} }{\gamma (d)}\]
    for~any $q'\geqslant d\geqslant -p$. Since $M\tau\leqslant q+\lfloor {p}\rfloor $ by~definition of $M$, we can applying this to $d\in [-p,M\tau]$ and $q':=q+\lfloor {p}\rfloor $, which gives:
    \[\textstyle A \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s} \cdot  \operatorname{card}(\@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}* \cap [-p,M\tau]) \cdot  (s R')^{-q'} \gamma (q')\] 
    Next, the above cardinal is bounded by $C\cdot (M\tau+p) \leqslant C\cdot (q+\lfloor {p}\rfloor +p)\leqslant  C_{p} \, q$ because $q\geqslant -p$.                                                                                                      
    Then, $q\cdot  (s R')^{-q'}$ can be bounded by $C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s,s''} \cdot  s''^{q} \cdot  (s R')^{-q}$. Finally, using again \cref{eq: majoration de quotients des fonctions gamma} from the proof of \cref{norme SF de mcl cas general} to bound $\gamma (q+\lfloor {p}\rfloor ) / \gamma (q)$ by $C_{p,s''} s''^{q}$, we deduce the desired estimate of $A$.
\end{sousdemo} 
Therefore we have shown
\begin{align*}
    |g_{M,q} (r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  g_{M,q} (r,\theta )|
    &\leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R,s,s',s''} \left( \frac{s' s'' r}{s R'} \right)^{q} \, (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1}
\end{align*}
\defq_0{q_0} 
Let us take $s:=s_{\delta ,n}+1$ and $s':=s\cdot s''$, and choose $s''$ s.t.\ $\frac{s''^2 }{R'} = \frac{1}{R}$. This proves \cref{eq: preuve decompo en modes tronques des CL} when $q\geqslant -p$.\\
Finally, for~any $q<-p$, we have $g_{M,q} = g_{M,-p}$ because $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )=0=T_{<-p} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )$ for~any $n\in [\![0,\lfloor {p}\rfloor ]\!]$ and $d\geqslant -p+n$. Using \cref{eq: preuve decompo en modes tronques des CL} on $g_{M,-p}$, we obtain
\[|g_{M,q} (r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  g_{M,q} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{-p} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{q} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} .\]
because $r/R \in (0,1)$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end demo-109 -->
<!-- demo-110: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{preuve: convergence de uDA} 
Let us write $T_{<q} (u^0_{p,\ell } )$ as a truncation of the modal decompostion of $u_{p,\ell }$ in order to use \cref{decompo en modes tronques des CL}. We have:
\begin{alignjustif}
T_{<q} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) &= T_{<q} \bigg( \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ d\geqslant -p+n }} \!\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^0_{d,n} \bigg) & \text{by \cref{expression uDA avec mcl}.} \\
&= \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ d\geqslant -p+n }} \!\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \cdot  T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} ) & \text{by \cref{rq: fsum commute avec les troncatures T}} 
\end{alignjustif}
Let $N$ be the smallest integer s.t.\ $(N+1)\tau -\lfloor {p}\rfloor \geqslant q$. Then, for~any $n\leqslant \lfloor {p}\rfloor $ and $d\geqslant (N+1)\tau$, we have $d-n\geqslant q$, so $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )=0$. We deduce:
\[T_{<q} (u^0_{p,\ell } )                                                                                                                                                                     
= \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ -p+n\leqslant d\leqslant N\tau }} \!\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \cdot  T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )\]
because any finite $\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}$-sum can be written as a classical sum (see \cref{proprietes de fsum}). Hence, according to \cref{decompo en modes tronques des CL}, we have
\[|\rho _{q} (r,\theta )|+r|\nabla  \rho _{q} (r,\theta )| \leqslant  C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{\min \left((N+1)\tau -\lfloor {p}\rfloor ,\, q\right)} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1} = C_{p,f_{\mathrm{s}},R} \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^{q} (1+|{\ln r}|)^{2p+1}\]
which proves \cref{eq: vitesse de cvg de uDA}. Similarly to the end of the proof of \cref{decompo modale des CL}, this implies $T_{<q} (u^0_{p,\ell } )\rightarrow  u_{p,\ell }$ uniformly on $\Omega \cap B(0,R)$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$.
<!-- end demo-110 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-12: body_md -->
\defq{q}        
All the corner profiles are solutions of problems of the form
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: model pb for corner fields}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  S) & F &\text{ in }\Omega _{1} \\[0.5mm]
	S & 0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega _{1} \\[0.5mm]
	\sigma _{q} (S)& s_{q} & \ \forall q \in \tau\mathbb{N}^*
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
with $S\in V+\chi_\infty \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$, $F\in L^2 _{\mathrm{loc}} (\overline{\Omega _{1} })$ (i.e.\ $L^2 $ on any bounded subset of $\Omega _{1}$) and $(s_{q} )_{q} \in \mathbb{C}^{\tau\mathbb{N}^*}$ with a finite support. Moreover, $F$ satisfies the following assumptions:
\begin{itemize}
	\item there exists $F^{\infty } _{\Omega } \in \mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Omega )$ s.t.\ $\forall q \in \mathbb{R},\; F_{|\Omega } = T_{\geqslant q} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } ) + o_{\partial } (r^{q} )$ when $r\rightarrow \infty $,
	\item there exists $F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} \in \mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Lambda)$ s.t.\ $\forall q \in \mathbb{R},\; F_{|\Lambda} = T_{\geqslant q} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} ) + o_{\partial } (x^{q} )$ when $x\rightarrow \infty $.
\end{itemize}
Using \cref{cadre fonctionnel pour les champs de coin}, one can show that \cref{eq: model pb for corner fields} has a unique solution (this is similar to the proof of existence and uniqueness of the corner fields done in \cref{sec: construction des termes}). To compute the corner profiles, it suffices to be able to solve numerically the model problem \cref{eq: model pb for corner fields}.\\

Let us denote
\[R^- := \operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}} \left( -R_{\partial_Y^2}\circ \partial _{x|\Lambda} ^2  + \frac{\mu _{0} }{\mu _{1}} R_{\mathrm{N}}\circ \partial _{Y|\Gamma ,Y=0^{+}} \right)^{n} .\]
This is an operator $\mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )\rightarrow \mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$. \Cref{DA des champs de coin} states that there exists $S^\infty \in \mathcal{A}^-\hspace{-0.15ex}(\Pi )$ that has the following form 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: SDA compl sing}}
	                                                                       
	S^\infty = R^-\bigg( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} R_{\Delta} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } )+ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} ) + \!\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{q \in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*} \! \sigma _{q} (S^\infty) \,\phi_{q} \bigg)
\end{equation}
such that: \ $\forall q\in \mathbb{R},\ S = T_{\geqslant q} (S^\infty ) + o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{q} )$ when $\mathbf{r}\rightarrow \infty $. For~any $q\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$, $\sigma _{q} (S^\infty)$ is known because it~is equal to $\sigma _{q} (S)$, i.e.\ to $s_{q}$. It belongs to the non-variational behavior of $S$. But the $\sigma _{q} (S^\infty)$ with $q\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$ are unknown and belong to the non-variational behavior of $S$. We are interested in a method to compute these coefficients.\\

We need to answer two questions:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Question 1: how to compute numerically a good approximation of $S$ ?
	\item Question 2: how to compute numerically a good approximation of $\sigma _{q} (S^\infty)$ when $q\in -\tau\mathbb{N}^*$ ?
\end{itemize}
Although in the end we are only interested in the coefficients $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n} )$, the inductive construction of the corner profiles through the relation $\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  \mathcal{S}_{d,n} )=-\rho \,\mathcal{S}_{d,n-1}$ makes it also necessary to compute a good approximation of $\mathcal{S}_{d,n-1}$. So we must compute accurately both $S$ and the $\sigma _{q} (S^\infty)$.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-12 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-13: body_md -->
The first step is to rewrite the problem as a variational one. Let $\chi \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty } (\mathbb{R}^2 )$ be a truncation function that is equal to 0 in $B(0,R_{\mathrm{c}})$ and to 1 in a vicinity of infinity. Let $\beta \leqslant -1$ and 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: def S survaria et S varia}}
	S^{\mathcal{A}} := T_{\geqslant \beta } \circ R^-\bigg( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} R_{\Delta} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } )+ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} ) + \!\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{\textcolor{red!93!black}{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*}} \! s_{d} \,\phi_{d} \bigg) \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )
\quad  \text{ and } \quad  S^V := S - \chi \,S^{\mathcal{A}} .
\end{equation}
$\beta $ will be chosen later (see \cref{estimate of uL-SV}). $S^V$ satisfies
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: eq of the variational part for corner fields}}
\left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll}
	\operatorname{div}(\mu  \nabla  S^V) &f := F-\operatorname{div}[\mu  \nabla (\chi  S^{\mathcal{A}} )]&\text{ in }\Omega _{1} \setminus (\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\})  \\[0.5mm]
	S^V &0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega _{1} \\[0.5mm]
	S^V_{|Y=0^{+}} - S^V_{|Y=0^{-}} & 0 &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\} \\[0.5mm]
	[\mu  \partial _{y} S^V] & g := -[\mu  \partial _{y} (\chi  S^{\mathcal{A}} )] &\text{ on }\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\} 
\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
with $[\mu \partial _{y} \dots ] :=\mu _{0} \partial _{y|y=0^{+}} - \mu _{1} \partial _{y|y=0^{-}}$. Similarly to the proof of \cref{cadre fonctionnel pour les champs de coin}, we have $S^V \in V$, $(1+r)f\in L^2 (\Omega _{1} )$ and $g\in L^2 (\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\})$, and $S^V$ is the unique solution of \cref{eq: eq of the variational part for corner fields} in $V$. The couple $(S^V,S^{\mathcal{A}} )$ is a decomposition of $S$ into a variational part and a diverging part.\\

In~practice, $F$ is $-\rho $ times some previously computed corner profile, say $\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n-1}$. The computation of the first coefficients $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n-1} )$, provides knowledge of $F^{\infty } _{\Omega }$ and $F^{\infty } _{\Lambda}$ up to a given order (i.e.\ we know $T_{\geqslant q} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } )$ and $T_{\geqslant q} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} )$ for some $q$). If enough coefficients $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n-1} )$ have been computed, then enough terms of $F^{\infty } _{\Omega }$ and $F^{\infty } _{\Lambda}$ are known so~that $S^{\mathcal{A}}$ is a known data. Let us assume that we are in this situation. The number of coefficients $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n-1} )$ needed depends on $\beta $. Note that $S^{\mathcal{A}}$ has an explicit expression, thanks to the explicit expressions of $R_{\Delta}$, $R_{\mathrm{N}}$, $R_{\partial_Y^2}$ (see \cref{operateurs R}). Therefore, to compute $S$ it suffices to compute $S^V$.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-13 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-14: body_md -->
Since $S^V$ is defined on an unbounded domain, it~is natural to introduce a truncated domain. Let us recall that the variable $\mathbf{r}$ is equal to $r$ in $\Omega $ and $x$ in $\Lambda $. For~any $L>R_{\mathrm{c}}+1$, we define the truncated domain $\Omega_1^L:= \Omega _{1} \cap \{\mathbf{r}<L\}$.\\

One must choose a boundary condition to apply on the truncated edge. A homogeneous Dirichlet condition is a possibility that provides convergence of the approximated solution towards $S^V$, because $S^V \rightarrow  0$ when $\mathbf{r} \rightarrow 0$. However, $S^V$ may converge to 0 slowly because its behavior at infinity involves $\phi_{-\pi/\Theta}$, which behaves like $r^{-\pi/\Theta}$, with $\tau \in ( \frac{1}{2} ,\infty )$. Thus, the approximated solution may converge slowly to $S^V$. A homogeneous Neumann condition leads to the same issue. It~is thus not easy to answer Question 1 of this section.\\

The truncation condition can be improved using the known expansion of $S^V$ at infinity (which is given by $S^\infty-S^{\mathcal{A}}$). For instance, \cite{Auv18} achieved a better rate of convergence by using a Robin condition in a similar setting with $\Theta =\pi $. One can check that there~is a known function $f  \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$ (depending on the data $F^{\infty } _{\Omega }$, $F^{\infty } _{\Lambda}$ and $(s_{d} )$) s.t.
\[S^V = f  +\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty)\,\phi_{-\tau} + o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{-\tau} ).\]
However $\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty)$ is unknown. Since we have $\partial _{n} \phi_{-\tau} + \frac{\pi }{\Theta L} \phi_{-\tau} = 0$ on $\partial \Omega_1^L \setminus \partial \Omega _{1}$, the condition
\[\textstyle \partial _{n} u + \frac{\pi }{\Theta L} u = \partial _{n} f  + \frac{\pi }{\Theta L} f  \quad \text{ on }\partial \Omega_1^L \setminus \partial \Omega _{1} \]
in an approximated transparent boundary condition with a known right hand side. One can show that the associated approximated solution converges to $S^V$ faster than for Dirichlet and Neumann conditions. Then \cite{Auv18} computes $\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty)$ a~posteriori in the following way. Using the calculation below
\[\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty) = 2r^{\tau} \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty) \,\phi_{-\tau} (r,\theta ) \cdot \sin \!\left(\tau \theta \right) \mathrm{d}\theta  = \lim _{r\rightarrow \infty } 2r^{\tau} \int _{0} ^{\Theta } (S^V -f )(r,\theta ) \cdot \sin \!\left(\tau \theta \right) \mathrm{d}\theta  ,\]
one deduces the following approximated formula for $\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty)$ (where $u_L$ denotes the approximated solution)
\[\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty) \approx  2L^{\tau} \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \big(u_L(L,\theta ) -f (L,\theta )\big) \sin \!\left(\tau \theta \right) \mathrm{d}\theta  .\]\setlength{\reducBoite}{-2.3ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-14 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-15: body_md -->
The approach of \cite{Auv18} works fine to obtain $\sigma _{-\tau} (S^\infty)$. However to obtain more coefficients, that describe a finer behavior of $S^V$ at infinity, one needs a finer truncation boundary condition. So we chose a different approach, closer to the method of singular functions, see \cite[chap.\,8]{StrFix73} and \cite{Loh98, LubNic94, CiaHe03}.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
This method is used on elliptic problems in a domain with a corner. In a neighborhood of the corner, the solution is not very regular, e.g.\ it~is~not $H^{2}$, which deteriorates the convergence of the finite element method w.r.t.\ the mesh step. This difficulty is overcome by adding to the Galerkin space a ``singular function'' $f $ s.t.\ the solution has the form $c\,f +v$ with $c\in \mathbb{C}$ and $v$ a regular function (e.g.\ $H^2 $). In this method, $c$ is unknown, but not $f $. For instance, if the problem is the Poisson equation with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions and the corner has angle $\Theta $, then $f  =\chi \,\phi_{\tau}$, where $\chi $ is a smooth truncation function supported in a neighborhood of the corner. Using this method, the rate of convergence of the finite elements is limited only by the regularity of $v$, and not by the poor regularity of $f $.\\

In our case, we are~not fighting against a lack of regularity at the corner but rather against the slow decay of $S^V$ at infinity. There is a kind of correspondence between the two as the regularity at 0 of $x\mapsto x^{a}$ and the decay at infinity of $x\mapsto  ( \frac{1}{x} )^{a}$ both get better for $a$ large and worse for $a$ small ($a\in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Z}$). To solve our problem \cref{eq: eq of the variational part for corner fields}, we add to the Galerkin space functions located near infinity rather than near the corner. We call these functions ``complements at infinity''. An important advantage of this approach is that we can use as many complements at infinity as we want, providing a high order method (although it seems that usually only one singular function is used).
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-15 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-16: body_md -->
Let $L>R_{\mathrm{c}}+1$. We define the truncated domains $\Omega ^{L} := \Omega \cap \{r<L\}$, $\Lambda ^{L} := \Lambda \cap \{x<L\}$, $\Gamma ^{L} := \Gamma \cap \{x<L\}$ and $\Omega_1^L:= \Omega _{1} \cap \{\mathbf{r}<L\} =\Omega ^{L} \cup \Gamma ^{L} \cup \Lambda^{L}$. Let $N \in \mathbb{N}^*$, $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ and
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: def complement singulier}}
	\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} := T_{\geqslant \gamma } \circ R^-(\phi_{-n\pi/\Theta} )\in \mathcal{A}(\Pi ) \qquad  \text{for~any }  n\in [\![1,N]\!].
\end{equation}
The parameter $\gamma $ will be chosen later in terms of $N$ (see \cref{estimate of uL-SV}). Let $\widetilde{\chi } \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty } (\mathbb{R})$ be a truncation function that is equal to 0 on $(-\infty ,-1]$ and 1 on $[0,\infty )$, and $\chi_L \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty } (\Omega _{1} )$ be equal to $\widetilde{\chi }(\mathbf{r}-L)$. The approximation space is defined as
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: def evcs}}
	V_L := \{u\in V \mid u_{|\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L} =0\} \oplus  \operatorname{Span}(\{ \chi_L \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \mid n\in [\![1,N]\!]\}).
\end{equation}
It~is included in $V$ (see \cref{def: V}). Note that the first term for the direct sum is equal to the set of $H^{1} _{0} (\Omega_1^L)$-functions extended by 0 in $\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L$. In practice, it~is discretised with finite elements, but we do~not consider this discretisation in our theoretical analysis. Besides, the functions $\chi_L \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}}$ are what we call the \emph{complements at infinity}.\\

Moreover, for~any $v\in V_L$, we denote $(\mathfrak{h}(v),\mathfrak{s}_{1}(v),\dots ,\mathfrak{s}_{N}(v))$ the only element of $V \times \mathbb{R}^{N}$ s.t.\ $\mathfrak{h}(v)_{|\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L} =0$ and
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: decomposition of elements of evcs}}
	v=\mathfrak{h}(v)+\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(v) \cdot \chi_L \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} .
\end{equation}\setlength{\reducBoite}{-2.3ex}\vspace{1\reducBoite}
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-16 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-17: body_md -->
Given \cref{eq: eq of the variational part for corner fields}, $S^V$ is solution of the following variational formulation
\[\forall v\in V, \qquad  \int _{\Omega _{1}} \mu  \nabla  S^V\cdot \nabla  v = -\int _{\Omega _{1}} fv + \int _{\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}} gv.\]
Hence we consider the following approximate problem: finding $u_L \in V_L$ solution of 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: approximated problem}}
\fbox{$\displaystyle \forall v\in V_L, \qquad  \int _{\Omega _{1}} \mu  \nabla  u_L\cdot \nabla  v = -\int _{\Omega _{1}} fv + \int _{\Gamma \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}} gv. $} \end{equation}
Using Lax-Milgram theorem in $V_L$ with $\|.\|_{V}$, it~is easy to see that \cref{eq: approximated problem} is well posed. The total approximate solution of \cref{eq: model pb for corner fields} is given by $\chi  S^{\mathcal{A}} + u_L$.                                                                                                                                                                  
Moreover, the coefficients $\sigma _{-n\tau} (S^\infty)$ with $n\in [\![1,N]\!]$ are approximated by the numbers $\mathfrak{s}_{n}(u_L)$.\\

Let us explain how to compute numerically the integrals in \cref{eq: approximated problem}. Using \cref{eq: decomposition of elements of evcs}, \cref{eq: approximated problem} is equivalent to: $\forall v\in V_L$,
\begin{multline}\label{eq: approximated problem with splitted integrals}
	\int _{\Omega_1^L} \mu  \nabla  u_L\cdot \nabla  v + \int _{\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L} \mu \,\bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(u_L)\,\nabla  \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \bigg)\cdot \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(v)\,\nabla  \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \bigg) \\
	= -\int _{\Omega_1^L} fv -\int _{\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L} f\cdot \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(v)\,\nabla  \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \bigg) + \int _{\Gamma ^{L} \cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}} gv + \int _{(\Gamma  \setminus \Gamma ^{L} )\cap \{x>R_{\mathrm{c}}\}} g\cdot \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(v)\,\nabla  \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \bigg)
\end{multline}
The integrals on the bounded domains $\Omega_1^L$ and $\Gamma ^{L}$ do~not raise any difficulty. As~for the other integrals, they have explicit integrands. Indeed, first, the $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}}$ are explicit functions because the operators $R_{\Delta}$, $R_{\mathrm{N}}$ and $R_{\partial_Y^2}$ are explicit and so is $R^-$. Secondly, $f$ and $g$ depend on $S^{\mathcal{A}}$ (explicit) and on $F$. In~practice $F$ is proportional to another corner profile, computed using the same method, so it~is also explicitly known outside $\Omega_1^L$.\\

Theoretically, one could calculate analytically the integrals on $\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L$ and $\Gamma  \setminus \Gamma ^{L}$. But it requires to express the $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}}$, $f$ and $g$ in $\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L}$ with the variables $(r,\theta )$ rather than $z=x+\mathrm{i}y$. The obtained expressions usually involve tens of terms, so the integrands can have hundreds or thousands of terms (after expanding the products in the integrals). In the end it~is~not very efficient compared to a quadrature method, and it requires more work to implement.\\

Therefore we chose to compute the integrals on $\Omega _{1} \setminus \Omega_1^L$ and $\Gamma  \setminus \Gamma ^{L}$ in \cref{eq: approximated problem with splitted integrals} using a high order quadrature method. Before the quadrature, we apply the following changes of variables in order to integrate on bounded domains ($f $ denotes one of the integrands that appear in \cref{eq: approximated problem with splitted integrals} and $a$ is a parameter that belongs to $\mathbb{R}_-^*$)
\[\int _{\Gamma  \setminus \Gamma ^{L} } f  = \int _{L} ^{\infty } f (x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int _{0} ^{L^{1/a}} f (t^{a} )\,at^{a-1} \,\mathrm{d}t, \qquad  \quad  \int _{\Lambda \setminus \Lambda^{L} } f  = \int _{0} ^{L^{1/a}} \int _{-1} ^{0} f (t^{a} ,y)\,at^{a-1} \,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}t,\]
\[\int _{\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L} } f  = \int _{L} ^{\infty } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } f (r,\theta )\,r\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}r = \int _{0} ^{L^{1/a}} \int _{0} ^{\Theta } f (t^{a} ,\theta )\,at^{2a-1} \,\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}t.\]
Note that the algebraic behavior of $f $ at infinity implies that the integrand after the change of variable has a limited regularity at 0.                                                                                                           
This regularity must be sufficiently high for the quadrature method to converge at its the optimal rate.
By~choosing an appropriate value of $a$, we can achieve the needed regularity.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-17 -->
<!-- demo-111: body_md -->
To compare $u_L$ to $S^V$, let us first build an approximation of $S^V$ in $V_L$, denoted $S^V_L$, defined as follows
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: def of SVL}}
S^V_L := \underbrace{(1-\chi_L)\,S^V}_{\displaystyle =\mathfrak{h}(S^V_L)} + \sum _{n=1} ^{N} \underbrace{\sigma _{-n\pi/\Theta} (S^{\infty } )}_{\displaystyle =\mathfrak{s}_{n}(S^V_L)} \cdot \chi_L \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} .\end{equation}
Céa's lemma yields \[\|S^V-u_L\|_{V} \lesssim  \|S^V-S^V_L\|_{V}\] with a constant independent of $L$. Let us estimate $\|S^V-S^V_L\|_{V}$. We have $S^V-S^V_L = \chi_LS_{\mathrm{r}}$ with
\begin{align*}
	S_{\mathrm{r}} &:= S^V - \sum _{n=1} ^{N} \sigma _{-n\pi/\Theta} (S^{\infty } ) \,\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \\
	&= S - \chi  \cdot  T_{\geqslant \beta } \circ R^-\bigg( \frac{1}{\mu _{0}} R_{\Delta} (F^{\infty } _{\Omega } )+ \frac{1}{\mu _{1}} R_{\partial_Y^2} (F^{\infty } _{\Lambda} ) + \!\operatorname*{\mathchoice
        {\contour*{.}{$\displaystyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\textstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptstyle\sum$}} 
        {\contour*{.}{$\scriptscriptstyle\sum$}}}_{d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*} \! s_{d} \,\phi_{d} \bigg) - \sum _{n=1} ^{N} \sigma _{-n\pi/\Theta} (S^{\infty } ) \cdot T_{\geqslant \gamma } \circ R^-(\phi_{-n\pi/\Theta} )
\end{align*}
by~definition of $S^V$ and $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}}$, see \cref{eq: def S survaria et S varia,eq: def complement singulier}. Let $\delta  :=-(N+1) \tau$. Provided that $\beta \leqslant \delta $ and $\gamma \leqslant \delta $, we deduce
\[S_{\mathrm{r}} = S-T_{\geqslant \delta } (S^{\infty } ) + \sigma _{\delta } (S^{\infty } )\,\phi_{\delta } +o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{\delta } )\]
because: $\forall d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*,\; s_{d} = \sigma _{d} (S^{\infty } )$ and $T_{\geqslant \delta } \circ R^-(\phi_{\delta } )= \phi_{\delta }$ and $\forall d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\cap (-\infty ,\delta ),\; T_{\geqslant \delta } \circ R^-(\phi_{d} )=0$. Therefore $S_{\mathrm{r}} = \sigma _{\delta } (S^{\infty } )\,\phi_{\delta } +o_{\partial } (\mathbf{r}^{\delta } )$, which implies
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: estimates of Srest}}
	\forall (i,j)\in \mathbb{N}^2 , \qquad  \partial _{x} ^{i} \partial _{y} ^{j} S_{\mathrm{r}} = 
	\left\{\begin{array}{@{\;}l@{\;}l}
	O(\mathbf{r}^{\delta -i-j} ) &\text{ in }\Omega  \;\text{ when }  r\rightarrow \infty  \\
	O(\mathbf{r}^{\delta -i} ) &\text{ in }\Lambda \;\text{ when }  x\rightarrow \infty .
	\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
This yields
\begin{align}
	\|S^V-S^V_L\|_{V} &= \|\nabla (\chi_LS_{\mathrm{r}})\|_{L^2 } = \|\nabla \chi_L\|_{L^{\infty }} \|S_{\mathrm{r}}\|_{L^2 (\Omega _{1} \cap \{L-1<\mathbf{r}<L\})} + \|\chi_L\|_{L^{\infty }} \|\nabla  S_{\mathrm{r}}\|_{L^2 (\Omega _{1} \cap \{\mathbf{r}>L-1\})} \nonumber\\
	&= O(L^{\delta + \frac{1}{2} } ) \label{eq: estimate of SV-SVL}
\end{align}
since $\|\chi_L\|_{L^{\infty }}$ and $\|\nabla \chi_L\|_{L^{\infty }}$ do~not depend on $L$.
<!-- end demo-111 -->
<!-- demo-112: body_md -->
For~any $n\in [\![1,N]\!]$, let us denote $s_{n}^{L} := L^{-(n-N-1) \tau - \frac{1}{2} } \big(\mathfrak{s}_{n}(u_L) - \sigma _{-n\pi/\Theta} (S^{\infty } )\big) = L^{-(n-N-1) \tau - \frac{1}{2} } \mathfrak{s}_{n}(u_L-S^V_L)$ and $\psi_n^{L} := L^{n \tau } \partial _{r} \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}}$. We have
\begin{align*}
	\bigg\|\sum _{n=1} ^{N} s_{n}^{L}\,\psi_n^{L} \bigg\|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L} )} &= L^{(N+1) \tau - \frac{1}{2} } \bigg\|\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \mathfrak{s}_{n}(u_L-S^V_L)\,\partial _{r} \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \bigg\|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L} )} \\
	&\leqslant  L^{(N+1) \tau - \frac{1}{2} } \|u_L-S^V_L\|_{V} \\
	&\leqslant  L^{(N+1) \tau - \frac{1}{2} } (\|u_L-S^V\|_{V} +\|S^V-S^V_L\|_{V} ) =O(1). \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation}\label{eq: sum snL psinL is bounded}
\end{align*}
by \cref{estimate of uL-SV} and \cref{eq: estimate of SV-SVL}.\smallskip

Let us assume by contradiction that there exists $m\in [\![1,N]\!]$ s.t.\ $\mathfrak{s}_{m}(u_L) - \sigma _{-m\pi/\Theta} (S^{\infty } ) \neq  O\big(L^{(m-N-1) \tau + \frac{1}{2} }\big)$, which means $s_{m}^{L} \neq O(1)$ when $L\rightarrow \infty $. Without loss of generality, we can assume that there exists a sequence $(L_{j} )_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ s.t.\ $L_{j} \rightarrow \infty $, 
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: properties of m}}
	|s_{m}^{L_{j} }| \underset{j\rightarrow \infty }{\longrightarrow} \infty  \quad  \text{ and } \quad  \forall j\in \mathbb{N},\ \ |s_{m}^{L_{j} }| = \max \!\big(|s_{1}^{L_{j} }|,\dots , |s_{N}^{L_{j} }|\big).\end{equation}
Up to a subsequence, we can also assume that for every $n\in [\![1,N]\!]$, $s_{n}^{L_{j} } / s_{m}^{L_{j} }$ converges. Let $\ell _{n}$ be its limit. We have for~any $j\in \mathbb{N}$
\begin{align*}
	\bigg\| \frac{1}{s_{m}^{L_{j} }} \sum _{n=1} ^{N} s_{n}^{L_{j} }\,\psi_n^{L_{j} } \bigg\|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L_{j}} )}
	&= \int _{L_{j}} ^{\infty } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \frac{s_{n}^{L_{j} }}{s_{m}^{L_{j} }} \,\psi_n^{L_{j} }(r,\theta ) \bigg)^2  r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}r \\
	&= \int _{1} ^{\infty } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \frac{s_{n}^{L_{j} }}{s_{m}^{L_{j} }} \,\psi_n^{L_{j} }(L_{j} t,\theta ) \,L_{j} \bigg)^2  t\,\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}t
\end{align*}
with $t := \frac{r}{L_{j}}$. Now we have in $\Omega $ when $r\rightarrow \infty $ that $\@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} =\phi_{-n\pi/\Theta} +o_{\partial } (r^{-n\pi/\Theta})$, so $\partial _{r} \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} \sim \partial _{r} \phi_{-n\pi/\Theta} = -n \tau \cdot r^{-n \tau -1} \sin \!\big(-n \tau \theta \big)$. Applying the dominated convergence theorem gives
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: limit of sum snL psinL over smL}}
	\bigg\| \frac{1}{s_{m}^{L_{j} }} \sum _{n=1} ^{N} s_{n}^{L_{j} }\,\psi_n^{L_{j} } \bigg\|_{L^2 (\Omega  \setminus \Omega ^{L_{j}} )} \underset{j\rightarrow \infty }{\longrightarrow} \int _{1} ^{\infty } \int _{0} ^{\Theta } \bigg(\sum _{n=1} ^{N} \ell _{n} \cdot  n \tau \cdot t^{-n \tau -1} \sin \!\Big({-n \tau \theta }\Big) \bigg)^2  t\,\mathrm{d}\theta \,\mathrm{d}t	\end{equation}
(the domination hypothesis is satisfied because $\exists r_{0} ,\forall r>r_{0} , \forall n\in [\![1,N]\!],\; |\partial _{r} \@ifnextchar_{\open@subscrf_{n}}{f_{n}} |\leqslant  2n \tau \cdot r^{-n \tau -1}$). Since the functions $t^{-n \tau -1} \sin \!\big({-n \tau \theta }\big)$, $n\in [\![1,N]\!]$, are linearly independent and $\ell _{m} =1 \neq 0$, the limit in \cref{eq: limit of sum snL psinL over smL} is non-zero. However by \cref{eq: sum snL psinL is bounded} and \cref{eq: properties of m}, that limit must be zero. This is contradictory, and it concludes the proof.
<!-- end demo-112 -->
<!-- demo-113: body_md -->
\defz_{\mathrm{c}}{z_{\mathrm{c}}} 
We denote $z$ the complex variable $x+\mathrm{i}y$ and $z_{\mathrm{c}} = x_{\mathrm{c}}-\mathrm{i} = -\frac{\cos \Theta +\mathrm{i}\sin \Theta }{\sin \Theta } =- \frac{1}{\alpha \sin (\Theta )}$. For~any $(x,y)\in \Omega $ with $x^2 +y^2 $ large enough, we have:
\begin{align*}
	\widetilde{\phi}_{d} :(x,y)                              
	&= \Im\big[(\alpha  (z-z_{\mathrm{c}}))^{d} \big]\\
	&= \Im\!\left[(\alpha z)^{d} \left(1- \frac{z_{\mathrm{c}}}{z} \right)^{d} \right]\\
	&= \Im\!\left[(\alpha z)^{d} \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \binom{d}{n} \left(- \frac{z_{\mathrm{c}}}{z} \right)^{n} \right]\\
	&= \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \binom{d}{n} (\sin \Theta )^{-n} \,\Im\!\left[(\alpha z)^{d-n} \right]
\end{align*}
where $\binom{d}{n} := \frac{1}{n!} \prod _{k=0} ^{n-1} (d-k)$. Similarly, when $(x,y)\in \Lambda$, we have
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\phi}_{d} :(x,y) &= \Im\left[(\alpha x)^{d} \left(1+ \frac{\mathrm{i}y-z_{\mathrm{c}}}{x} \right)^{d} \right]\\
&= \Im\left[(\alpha x)^{d} \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \binom{d}{n} \left( \frac{\mathrm{i}y-z_{\mathrm{c}}}{x} \right)^{n} \right]\\
&= \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \binom{d}{n} \,x^{d-n} \,\Im[\alpha ^{d} (\mathrm{i}y-z_{\mathrm{c}})^{n} ]
\end{align*}
Let \[f (x,y) := \sum _{n=0} ^{\lceil {d}\rceil +1} \binom{d}{n} \times \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
	(\sin \Theta )^{-n} \,\Im\!\left[(\alpha z)^{d-n} \right] &\text{ in }\Omega \\
	x^{d-n} \,\Im[\alpha ^{d} (\mathrm{i}y-z_{\mathrm{c}})^{n} ] &\text{ in }\Lambda
\end{array}\right.\]
We have $f \in \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$ and $\nabla (\widetilde{\phi}_{d} -f ) = O(r^{-3} )$ at infinity, so $\widetilde{\phi}_{d} \in V+\chi_0 \mathcal{A}(\Pi )$. Therefore by the uniqueness in \cref{cadre fonctionnel pour les champs de coin}
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: expression de phicoin}}
	\widetilde{\phi}_{d} = \sum_{q\in \tau\mathbb{N}^* ,q\leqslant d} \sigma _{q} (\widetilde{\phi}_{d} )\,\mathcal{S}_{q,0} 
	\qquad  \text{with}  \qquad  \forall q\in {\textstyle\tau\mathbb{N}^*},\ \ \sigma _{q} (\widetilde{\phi}_{d} ) = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{N}} (d-q) \cdot  \binom{d}{d-q} (\sin \Theta )^{q-d} .
\end{equation}
To conclude, it suffices to notice that the matrix $(\sigma _{q} (\widetilde{\phi}_{d} ))_{q,d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*}$ is triangular with coefficients 1 on the diagonal, hence it~is invertible.
<!-- end demo-113 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-18: body_md -->
This issue is addressed using a Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) map on an artificial boundary around the corner. Let us introduce the relevant domains. Let $R_{\mathrm{s}} := \operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{supp} f)$ and $\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ} \in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. We have $R_{\mathrm{s}}>0$ because we assumed $\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}(f_{\mathrm{s}}),\Gamma )>0$. We define $\Omega^\circ:= \Omega  \setminus \overline{B}(0,\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})$, $\Gamma^\circ:= \Gamma  \setminus \overline{B}(0,\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})$ and $\Sigma^\circ := \{(\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ} \cos \theta , \@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ} \sin \theta ) \mid \theta \in (0,\Theta )\}$. Note that $\partial \Omega^\circ = \overline{\Sigma_\Omega^\circ \cup  \Sigma^\circ \cup  \Gamma^\circ}$. See \cref{fig: domaine numerique CL}. The ``$\circ $'' exponents are intended to recall that a ball is excluded around the corner.\\

\begin{figure}[h]

\def2.9{2.7}                                               
\def205{205}                                                         
\def1.3{1.3}

	\coordinate (dbtLambda) at ({1.3*cos(205)}, {1.3*sin(205)});
	\fill [pattern={Lines[angle=45,line width=.2pt]}, pattern color=white!70!gray] (dbtLambda) arc (205:0:1.3) -- (3.5,0) -- (3.5,2.9) -- (-3.5,2.9) -- (finLambda) -- cycle;
	\draw [thick] (finLambda) -- (dbtLambda) arc (205:0:1.3) -- (3.5,0);
	\draw [dashed] (dbtLambda) -- (0,0);
	      
	\draw [>=stealth,->] (-3.5-0.4,0) -- (3.5+0.4,0) node [right] {$x$};
	\draw [>=stealth,->] (0,{-3.5*tan(205-180)}) -- (0,{2.9+0.3}) node [right] {$y$};
	           
	\draw (-3.5*0.5,2.9*0.6) node {$\Omega^\circ$};
	\draw [->,>=latex] (0.35,0) arc (0:205-5:0.35) node[near start,above] {$\Theta$} -- (205:0.36);
	                                                                                                                                         
	\draw [<-,>=latex] (3.5*0.65,0) to[bend right=20] ++(0.15,-0.55) node[below]{$\ \ \Gamma^\circ$};
	                                    
	                                                                                                                
	\draw [<-,>=latex] ({1.3*cos(55)}, {1.3*sin(55)}) to[bend left=20] ++(0.4,0.45) node[right]{\raisebox{1ex}{$\Sigma^\circ$}};
	\draw [<->,>=latex] (0,-0.2) -- node[midway, below] {$\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ}$} (1.3, -0.2);
\end{tikzpicture}\par
