\label{fig: domaine numerique CL}
\end{figure}

It is classical that any function $u\in H^{1} (\Omega )$ that satisfies
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: numerique CL pb Helmholtz homog}}
    \left\{\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}ll@{}}
        \mu _{0} \Delta  u +\omega ^2 \rho _{0} u & f &\text{ in }\Omega  \\[0.5mm]
        u & 0 &\text{ on }\partial \Omega 
    \end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
with $f\in \{f_{\mathrm{s}},0\}$ has the following modal decomposition in $\Omega  \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$ for some coefficients $s_{n} \in \mathbb{C}$:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: decompo modale solution H1 Helmholtz}}
    u(r,\theta ) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  s_{n} \cdot J_{n\tau} (k_{0} r) \sin  (n\tfrac\pi\Theta \theta ).
\end{equation}
Here $J_{n\tau}$ denotes a Bessel function of the first kind. In addition, the above series and its gradient converge uniformly on $B(0,R)$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. So we also have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: dr decompo modale solution H1 Helmholtz}}
    \partial _{r} u = \sum_{n=0}^\infty  s_{n} \cdot k_{0} J_{n\tau} '(k_{0} r) \sin  (n\tfrac\pi\Theta \theta ).
\end{equation}
Moreover, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: formule coef Fourier solution H1 Helmholtz}}
    \forall n\in \mathbb{N}^*, \qquad  s_{n} = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ}\Theta } } \cdot  \frac{\langle u ,f _{n} \rangle _{L^2 (\Sigma^\circ)} }{J_{n\tau} (k_{0} \@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})} \qquad  \text{with } \ f _{n} :\theta  \mapsto \sqrt{ \frac{2}{\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ}\Theta } } \sin (n\theta )
\end{equation}
by orthonormality in $L^2 (\Sigma^\circ)$ of the functions $f _{n}$. Combining \cref{eq: dr decompo modale solution H1 Helmholtz,eq: formule coef Fourier solution H1 Helmholtz}, we obtain
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: def opF}}
    \partial _{r} u_{|\Sigma^\circ} = \mathbf{F}(u_{|\Sigma^\circ} ) \qquad  \text{with}  \qquad  \mathbf{F} : v \mapsto  \sum_{n=0}^\infty  \frac{k_{0} \.J'_{n\tau} (k_{0} \@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})}{J_{n\tau} (k_{0} \@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})} \,\langle v,f _{n} \rangle _{L^2 (\Sigma^\circ)} \,f _{n.}
\end{equation}
One can show that $\mathbf{F}$ is well-defined from $H^{1/2} _{00} (\Sigma^\circ)$, the set of elements of $H^{1/2} (\Sigma^\circ)$ whose extension by 0 to $\partial \Omega^\circ$ remains $H^{1/2}$, to $(H^{1/2} _{00} (\Sigma^\circ))'$. $\mathbf{F}$ is the DtN map that we use.\\

Let us use this on $u_{p,\ell }$ for a given $(p,\ell )\in \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}$. By~\cref{decompo modale des CL}, we have the following modal decomposition in $\Omega  \cap B(0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: rappel decompo modale CL pour numerique CL}}
    u_{p,\ell } \.=\. \sum _{n=0} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ d\geqslant -p+n}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} .
\end{equation}
We recall $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ is introduced in \cref{convergence des mcl} as the limit function of the converging series $\Phi^0_{d,n}$, which is defined in \cref{def: mcl}. In addition, \cref{decompo modale des CL} states that \cref{eq: rappel decompo modale CL pour numerique CL} and its gradient converge uniformly on $B(0,R)$ for~any $R\in (0,R_{\mathrm{s}})$. Let us write
                                        
                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                     
                                                                                                                                              
\[u_{p,\ell } := u^V_{p,\ell } + \tilde{u}_{p,\ell } \quad  \text{with }  \left\{\begin{array}{l}
    u^V_{p,\ell } :=\displaystyle \sum _{d\in \textcolor{red!93!black}{\tau\mathbb{N}^*}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} \vrule width0pt height 3ex\relax \\
    \tilde{u}_{p,\ell } :=\displaystyle \smash{\sum _{\substack{d\in \textcolor{red!93!black}{-\tau\mathbb{N}^*}\\ d\geqslant -p}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} } + \sum _{n=\textcolor{red!93!black}{1}} ^{\lfloor {p}\rfloor } \smash{\sum _{\substack{d\in \@ifstar{\tau\mathbb{Z}^*}{\tau\mathbb{Z}}*\\ d\geqslant -p+n}} \sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } ) \,\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n} } \vrule width0pt depth 4ex\relax
\end{array}\right. \vspace{1ex} \]
When computing $u_{p,\ell }$, $\tilde{u}_{p,\ell }$ is a known piece of data (at least approximately) because
\begin{itemize}
    \item the functions $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ are described in \cref{convergence des mcl,def: mcl},
    \item the fields $u_{p',\ell '}$ are built inductively w.r.t.\ $p'$ so the coefficients $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p-n,\ell } )$ with $n>0$ are known,
    \item the coefficients $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )$ with $d<0$ are given by the last equation in \cref{eq: numerique CL rappel eq CL}.
\end{itemize}
On the contrary, $u^V_{p,\ell }$ is unknown and is a solution in $H^{1} (\Omega )$ of \cref{eq: numerique CL pb Helmholtz homog} for a certain $f$. Therefore, we have $\partial _{r} u^V_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} =\mathbf{F}(u^V_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} )$, which yields:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: condition DtN CL}}
    \partial _{r} u_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} - \mathbf{F}(u_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} ) = \partial _{r} \tilde{u}_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} - \mathbf{F}(\tilde{u}_{p,\ell |\Sigma^\circ} ).
\end{equation}
This gives a non-homogeneous DtN condition for $u_{p,\ell }$ on the boundary $\Sigma^\circ$. We use it to compute $u_{p,\ell }$ in the domain $\Omega^\circ$. Numerically, this condition can be approximated by truncating the series that defines $\mathbf{F}$ in \cref{eq: def opF}.\\

Moreover, for~any $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$, we have $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,0} = (-1)^{d\Theta /\pi } \,\Gamma (d+1) \big( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \big)^{d} J_{d} (k_{0} r) \sin (d \theta )$ by \cref{expression sing homog CL}. So, when applying \cref{eq: decompo modale solution H1 Helmholtz} to $u:=u^V_{p,\ell }$, we have
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: lien coef Fourier CL et sigma}}
    \forall n\in \mathbb{N}^*, \qquad  s_{n} = (-1)^{n} \,\Gamma \!\left(n\tau+1\right) \left( \frac{2}{k_{0}} \right)^{n\tau} \sigma _{n\tau} (u^0_{p,\ell } ).
\end{equation}
\Cref{eq: lien coef Fourier CL et sigma,eq: formule coef Fourier solution H1 Helmholtz} allow us to compute the coefficient $\sigma _{d} (u^0_{p,\ell } )$ for~any $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$ once $u_{p,\ell }$ is computed.\\

Thus, the DtN condition \cref{eq: condition DtN CL} addresses at once and in a neat way three issues:
\begin{itemize}
    \item It handles the fact that $u_{p,\ell }$ is in general a non variational solution of Helmholtz's equation, due to its diverging behavior at the corner. Note that this does~not require introducing an auxiliary variational unknown (like we did for the corner profiles), as the condition \cref{eq: condition DtN CL} is directly formulated in terms of $u_{p,\ell }$, not in terms of $u^V_{p,\ell }$.
    \item It allows a good approximation of $u_{p,\ell }$ at the corner despite its lack of regularity.
    \item It provides a way to compute the coefficients $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$ with $d\in \tau\mathbb{N}^*$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-18 -->
<!-- paragraphesansboite-19: body_md -->
\def\approxh#1[#2]{#1[#2#1]^h}                       
\defX^h{X^h} 
\def\mathbf{x}{\mathbf{x}} 
\def\mathbf{x'}{\mathbf{x'}} 
This Dirichlet condition on $\Gamma $ involves the functions $(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma }$, see \cref{eq: numerique CL rappel eq CL}. Let us denote $h$ the mesh step, $V^h$ the Galerkin space used for the far fields (e.g.\ the Lagrange finite elements P1 on $\Omega^\circ$) and $V^h_{\Gamma^\circ} := \{v_{|\Gamma^\circ} \mid v\in V^h\}$. For~any function $f$ that is defined in the continuous setting, we denote $\approxh[f]$ its discrete approximation, which will be properly defined  case by case. In particular, to shorten notations, we denote, for any $(p,\ell ,n)\in \mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{N}^2 $, $u^h_{p,\ell} :=\approxh[u_{p,\ell } ]\in V^h$ the computed far field and $u^h_{p,\ell,n} :=\approxh\big[(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma^\circ} ]$. We look for $u^h_{p,\ell,n}$ in $V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}$, so that $u^h_{p,\ell,n}$ can be directly used in the Dirichlet condition of a far field. Now, let us explain how $u^h_{p,\ell,n}$ is computed from $u^h_{p,\ell}$, starting with the case $n=0$.\\

For~any $v\in H^{1/2} (\Gamma^\circ)$, we have:
\[\int _{\Gamma^\circ} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } \,v = -\int _{\Omega^\circ} (\nabla  u_{p,\ell } \cdot  \nabla  w + \Delta  u_{p,\ell } \,w) + \int _{\partial \Omega^\circ \setminus \Gamma^\circ} \partial _{n} u_{p,\ell } \,w \]
where $w\in H^{1} (\Omega^\circ)$ is s.t.\ $w_{|\Gamma^\circ} =v$. Assuming that $w$ vanishes on $\partial \Omega^\circ \setminus (\Gamma^\circ \cup \Sigma^\circ)$ and using that $u_{p,\ell }$ satisfies $\Delta u_{p,\ell } +k_{0} ^2  \.u_{p,\ell } =f_{p,\ell }$ with $f_{p,\ell } := \delta _{p,0} \.\delta _{\ell ,0} \.\mu _{0} ^{-1} f_{\mathrm{s}}$, we obtain:
\[\int _{\Gamma^\circ} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } \,v = \int _{\Omega^\circ} \big({-\nabla  u_{p,\ell } }\cdot  \nabla  w + k_{0} ^2  \.u_{p,\ell } \.w + f_{p,\ell } \.w \big) - \int _{\Sigma^\circ} \partial _{r} u_{p,\ell } \,w.\]
This equation gives a way to compute an approximation of $\partial _{y} u_{p,\ell }$ by solving the following problem:
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 1}}
    \begin{multlined}
    \text{find $u^h_{p,\ell,0} \in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}$ s.t.\ }  \forall v\in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}, \qquad  \qquad \\
    \qquad  \qquad  \int _{\Gamma^\circ} u^h_{p,\ell,0} \,v = \int _{\Omega } \big({-\nabla  u^h_{p,\ell}}\cdot  \nabla  w + k_{0} ^2  \.u^h_{p,\ell} \.w + f_{p,\ell } \.w \big) - \int _{\Sigma^\circ} \approxh[\partial _{r} u_{p,\ell } ]\,w.
    \end{multlined}
\end{equation}
Here $w$ is taken in $V^h$ and built in the following way, that is classical. Let us denote $X^h$ the set of vertices of the mesh and, for any $\mathbf{x} \in X^h$, $w_{\mathbf{x}}$ the canonical basis function of $V^h$ associated to $\mathbf{x}$ (i.e.\ the unique element of $V^h$ s.t.: $\forall \mathbf{x'} \in X^h,\, w_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x'}) = \delta _{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x'}}$). We define
\[w := \sum _{\mathbf{x} \in X^h \cap \Gamma^\circ} v(\mathbf{x}) \,w_{\mathbf{x}} .\]
In addition, in \cref{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 1}, $\approxh[\partial _{r} u_{p,\ell } ]$ is computed thanks to the DtN condition \cref{eq: condition DtN CL}.\\

Actually, we use a variant of \cref{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 1} to compute $u^h_{p,\ell,0}$. The computation of high order derivatives of $u^h_{p,\ell}$ introduces numerical instabilities, as any small parasite oscillation at the scale of the mesh step gets amplificated when taking derivatives. To solve this issue, we introduced a regularization in the computation of $u^h_{p,\ell,n}$, by solving instead the following problem
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 2}}
    \begin{array}{l}
    \text{find $u^h_{p,\ell,0} \in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}$ s.t.\ }  \forall v\in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}, \\[1.3\jot]
    \displaystyle \int _{\Gamma^\circ} \big(\textcolor{red!93!black}{h^2 }\.\partial _{x} u^h_{p,\ell,0} \,\partial _{x} v + u^h_{p,\ell,0} \,v \big)= \int _{\Omega^\circ} \big({-\nabla  u^h_{p,\ell}}\cdot  \nabla  w + k_{0} ^2  \.u^h_{p,\ell} \.w + f_{p,\ell } \.w \big) - \int _{\Sigma^\circ} \approxh[\partial _{r} u_{p,\ell } ]\,w. \hspace{-1em}
\end{array} \end{equation}
This regularization reduces the high frequency oscillations of $u^h_{p,\ell,0}$. The factor $h^2 $ in \cref{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 2} is a relevant regularization parameter because, by dimensional analysis, the parameter in front of $\partial _{x} u^h_{p,\ell,0} \,\partial _{x} v$ must be the square of a length. See \cite{LazSig09,LazSig11} for similar filters used in topology optimization and \cite{Sag06} in the context of large eddy simulations.\\

Next, let $n\geqslant 1$. For~any $u\in H^2 (\Gamma^\circ)$ and $v\in H^{1} (\Gamma^\circ)$, we have
\[\int _{\Gamma^\circ} (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )u \cdot v = \int _{\Gamma^\circ} \big({-\partial _{x} u} \, \partial _{x} ^2 v +k_{1} ^2 \.u\.v\big) - \partial _{x} u(P^\circ) \cdot v(P^\circ)\]
with $P^\circ :=(\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ},0)$ the tip of $\Gamma^\circ$. Applying this to $u:=(\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n-1} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell |\Gamma }$, and employing the same regularization technique as in \cref{eq: calcul dy upl Gamma methode 2}, we obtain the following problem which we use to compute inductively the functions $u^h_{p,\ell,n}$ with $n\geqslant 1$
\begin{equation}{\label{eq: calcul (dx+k)n dy upl}}
    \begin{multlined}    
    \text{find $u^h_{p,\ell,n} \in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}$ s.t.\ }  \forall v\in V^h_{\Gamma^\circ}, \quad   \int _{\Gamma^\circ} \big(4h^2 \partial _{x} u^h_{p,\ell,n} \,\partial _{x} v + u^h_{p,\ell,n} \,v \big) = \qquad  \qquad  \qquad  \quad \ \\
    \qquad  \qquad  \int _{\Gamma^\circ} \big({-\partial _{x} u^h_{p,\ell,n-1}} \, \partial _{x} ^2 v +k_{1} ^2 \.u^h_{p,\ell,n-1}\.v\big) - \approxh\big[\partial _{x} (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n-1} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } (P^\circ)] \cdot v(P^\circ) \hspace*{-1em}
    \end{multlined}
\end{equation}
The factor 4 in the right-hand side of \cref{eq: calcul (dx+k)n dy upl} seemed to give the best results in practice. Moreover, $\approxh\big[\partial _{x} (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n-1} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } (P^\circ)]$ is calculated in the following way. As~explained before, \cref{eq: lien coef Fourier CL et sigma,eq: formule coef Fourier solution H1 Helmholtz} give a way to compute the values of the coefficients $\sigma _{d} (u_{p,\ell } )$. Thanks to a truncation of the modal decomposition \cref{eq: rappel decompo modale CL pour numerique CL}, this then allows us to reconstitute an approximation of $u_{p,\ell }$ in $\Omega  \cap B(0,\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})$, i.e.\ outside the computation domain $\Omega^\circ$. Let us denote $\approxh[u^0_{p,\ell } ]$ this approximate reconstitution. It can be:
\begin{itemize}
    \item either a linear combination of Bessel functions, which is possible if and only if the functions $\Phi^{\rm lim}_{d,n}$ that appear can be expressed using Bessel functions (see \cref{sec: expression des mcl,sec: annexe des complements sur le DA}),
    \item or a linear combination of truncations of the form $T_{<q} (\Phi^0_{d,n} )$, which is always possible but can be less easy to implement. In this case, $\approxh[u^0_{p,\ell } ]$ is an approximation of $T_{<q} (u^0_{p,\ell } )$ (see \cref{expression uDA avec mcl}). In addition, it belongs to $\mathcal{A}(\Omega )$, so it can be numerically represented as explained in \cref{sec: implementation des espaces A}. We used this second option because \cref{chap: complements sur le DA} was chronologically posterior to these numerical experiments and this options allows to unified implementation for any angle $\Theta $.
\end{itemize}
In both cases, we define $\approxh\big[\partial _{x} (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n-1} \partial _{y} u_{p,\ell } (P^\circ)]:= \partial _{x} (\partial _{x} ^2 +k_{1} ^2 )^{n-1} \partial _{y} \approxh[u^0_{p,\ell } ](P^\circ)$. This derivative can be computed exactly from $\approxh[u^0_{p,\ell } ]$ as $\approxh[u^0_{p,\ell } ]$ has an explicit expression in both cases.
<!-- end paragraphesansboite-19 -->

\label{notations ME} 
\begin{itemize}
	\item We denote $R_{\mathrm{s}} := \operatorname{dist}(0,\operatorname{supp}f_{\mathrm{s}})$. Since we assumed $\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma ,\operatorname{supp}f_{\mathrm{s}})>0$, we have $R_{\mathrm{s}}>0$. We also assumed $\overline{B}(0,\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ})\cap \operatorname{supp}(f_{\mathrm{s}})= \varnothing $, which is equivalent to $\@ifnextchar^{(R^\circ)}{R^\circ}<R_{\mathrm{s}}$.
	\item For~any $p\in \mathbb{N}$, we define 
	\begin{align*}
		\ell _{p} &:= \max _{p'\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,p]} \max \{\ell \in \mathbb{N} \mid u_{p',\ell } \text{ is generically non-zero} \}\\
		&\,= \, \min \{\ell \in \mathbb{N} \mid \forall p'\in \mathbb{P}\cap [0,p],\; \forall \ell '>\ell ,\ u_{p',\ell '} \text{ is always zero} \}
	\end{align*}
	where ``always zero'' means that the far field vanishes for any value of $(\mu _{0} ,\mu _{1} ,\rho _{0} ,\rho _{1} ,\omega ,f_{\mathrm{s}})$ and the corner profile coefficients $\sigma _{q} (\mathcal{S}^\infty_{d,n} )$. The equality between the two expressions of $\ell _{p}$ is a consequence of \cref{generiqmt non nul ou tjs nul}. By~construction, $\ell _{p}$ depends only on $\Theta $ and $p$, and is independent of $(\mu _{0} ,\mu _{1} ,\rho _{0} ,\rho _{1} ,\omega ,f_{\mathrm{s}})$ and the corner profiles. The existence of $\ell _{p}$ is guaranteed by \cref{borne sur l}.
	                                                                                                                  
	                                                                                                                                                                               
	\item All over this section, $C_{\dots }$ will denote any positive constant that depends \emph{only} on the variables in ``...'' and $(\Theta ,\mu _{0} ,\mu _{1} ,\rho _{0} ,\rho _{1} ,\omega )$ and on $m$. Its value may change from one line to another.
	\item For~any $x\in \mathbb{R}$, we denote $\langle x\rangle:=1+|x|$.
	\item For~any domain $D$ and $u\in H^{1} (D)$, $\snh{u}(D) :=\|\nabla  u\|_{L^2 (D)}$ is the $H^{1}$ semi-norm.
\end{itemize}
